AN OLD-FASHIONED LOVE-SONG. Tell me what within her eyes Makes the forgotten Spring arise, And all the day, if kind she looks, Flow to a tune like tinkling brooks; ' Tell we why, if bat her voice Falls on men's ears, their souls rejoice; Tell me why, if only she Doth come into the companie All spirits straight enkindled are, As if a moon lit up a star. Tell me thir that's writ above, And I will tell you why hove. Tell tee why the foolish wind Is to her tresses ever kind, And only blows them in such wise As lends her beauty some surprise; Tell me why no changing year Can change from Spring, if site appear; Tell me why to see her face Begets in all folk else a grace rliat makes them fair, as love of her Did to a gentler nature stir. Tell me why, if she but go Alone acrcss thel,fields of snow, All fancies of the Springs of old Within a lover's breast grow bold; Tell me why, when her he sees, Within him stirs an April breme; And all that in his secret heart Most sacredly was set apart, - And most was hidden, then awakes, At the sweet joy her coming makes. Tell 1718 what is writ ahave,'4 And I 'anal tell you why I lose. H. C. BUNWER.

ills proof of high culture to say the greatest matters in the simplest way. The surest sign of wisdom is charity; and the best charity is that which never ostensibly parades itself. Don't hit a man when he's down: hit him while he's up a tree, and run away before he reaches the ground. What struck you most in the equatorial regions?" asked a gentlemah of a traveller. "The sun," was the reply. The childish miss resents a kiss and runs the other way; hut when at last some years have passed, it's different, they say. The had traits in character are passed down from generation te generation with as much care as the good ones. A true friend unbosoms freely, advises justly, assists readily, defends courageously, and continues a friend unchangedly. Never judge a man by the clothes he wears. If you want to form an opinion of him, find out whether he has paid for them. There will never exist anything permanently noble and excellent in character which is a stranger to the exercise of resolute self-denial. Whatever is coming, there is but one way to meet it— to go straight forward, to bear what has to be borne, and to do what has to be done. Hold last to the present. Every position. every moment of life, is of unspeakable value as the represen- tative of a whole eternity.—Goethe "Isn't it lonely bore. deorge? Did you ever know any- thing so still?" "Oh, yes. Once." "When was that ?" .4 I hired a plumber once to do a day's work for me, and he never moved from morning to night." A foolish fellow was taunting a neighbour on the length of his ears. "It's true," replied the latter. "that my:ears are rather long for a man, but how uncommon short yours are for a donkey !" Many a woman dusts billiard chalk off her husband's coat with groat big drops of tears in her beautiful eyes, as she reflects how hard and how late he has to work at his desk close to that nasty whitewashed wall..

Wife: "Keep quiet, Charlie. The new doctor says I must not talk to you." Husband, feebly: "Mary! Beery !" Wife: "What is it, Charlie?" Husband: "Engage that doctor for our family physician." "What a good thing it would be if men were angels!" said one young lady to another. "Well, my dear, all those who made love to me were." "How so ?" eagerly asked the former. "Why, because they have all flown!' Retaliation is like the storm which sweeps tbrough the forest in destruction. Kindness is like the combined in- fluence of the sun and the rain of the cloud, which ger- minates seed and upholds their leaves, flowers, and *lours. OLD JONES'S Pentosomr.—Modesty is a great rudder but a bad engine. Lickin' may teach a boy to dance, but not to do sums. You may get learnin' at school, but sense comes nat'ral or not at aIL You just bring a couple of little quarrels into your family, an' they'll breed like sparrows. Don't go Pack on your friends when you're in luck, nor give away your unaberel just because the sun shines. You can't always judge's, man by the blood he's got. Corn bread an' whisky come from the same family. A runaway hoss is worse'n a runaway wife, because it sometimes takes You with it. THE BEAUTY OF SPANISH WOMEN.— In the January Scribner's, Henry 'l'. Fula says :•—" If I were asked to state in one sentence wherein lies the chief advautage of Spanish women over those of other countries, and to what they chiefly owe their fame for beauty, I should say that if a Spanish girl has round cheeks, and has medium-sized, deiicately cut nose and mouth, she is almost certain to be a complete beauty; whereas if an American or English girl has a good nose, mouth, and cheeks, the chances are still against her having a beauti- ful complexion and fine eyes, hair, and teeth, which Spanish girls are always endowed with as a matter of cour-e. But, over anu above everything else, it is the unique grace and the exquisite femininity, unalloyed by any trace of masculine assumption or caricature, that constitute the eternal charm of Spanish women." THE DEVIL AS A VIOLINIST.—One night, as the com- poser Tartini was asleep iii bed, he dreamed that, after the fashion of Faust, he had made a compact with tile devel for his soul. The Evil One was to do for him everything he wanted so long as he lived, after which Tartini was to pay the orthodox penalty. . . After a time the idea occurred to him that he would hand his fiddle over to the representative of the lower regions, bid him play, and see what sort of music his Satanic Majesty could produce. . . The devil took the instrument, and "great was my astonishment." said Tartini afterwards, "when I heard him play, with consummate skill, a sonata of such exquisite beauty that it surpassed the boldest flight of my imagination. I felt enraptured, transported, enchanted; my breath was taken away, and I awoke. Seizing my violin I tried to retain the sounds I had heard: but it was in vain. The piece I then composed, • The Devil's Sonata.' although the best I ever wrote, was far below the one I had heard in my dream." Such was the origin of the world-famous sonata, "II Trillo del Diavlo."—Casseirs Saturday Mayazine. Then LIKE A BERO.—The following,pathetic incident is related by one of the surgeons of the American Civil War. :—l)r. Westmoreland was one day dressing the wound of a soldier who had been shot in the neck near the carotid artery. It had not been regarded as a par- ticularly dangerous case. Suppuration had set in, however, and while the surge na was cleansing the wound the blood vessel suddenly gave way. Dr. Westmoreland as quickly put his finger into the aperture and stopped the flow. Tae soldier glanced questioningly into the surgeon's face. "Doctor," lie asked, " what does that mean ?" "It means death, my poor fellow," answered Dr. Westmoreland, with a strong sympathy in his voice. A moment the soldier lay with dosed eyes as if stunned by the fatal words, then he looked up and calmly asked, "Sow long can I live?" "Until I remove my finger," answered the doctor. "Will—you wait a little," the poor man asked, "till I can—write a few words to my wife ?" The doctor bowed his head affirmatively. Tne soldier wrote his brief letter, and then, with the pathos of resignation, said, "I am ready, doctcr." I removed my linger," said the surgeon, "and in a litfTe while the brave fellow was dead. I'd have given a good deal to save that man's life. But he died like a hero." THROUGH THE CIGAR FACIORY IN SEVILLE.—One of the sights of Seville. which no tourist misses, is the cigar factory, in which the llovernment employs about five thousand women and girls. The showing about of visitors is accordingly looked upon as a ...regular source of income by the porter and the matrons. After getting permission to enter, you are placed in chargeLof matron, who_ shows you through her own department, and then passes you on to another, and soon, until your stock of pesetas and half-peseta; put aside for fees is exhausted. These matrons accompany the visitors, not in order to prevent the girls from flirting with them (notating could do that), but to see that no tobacco or bundles of cigarettes may .disappear. Before entering each room a bell is rung to warn the girls, who are in great deshabine on account of the heat, to put on their wrappers, and as the door open- scores of round arms and pretty- shoulders are seen disappearing, while several hundred pairs of coal-black eyes are fastened on you. The passages are lined with cradles, and the poor young girl-mothers to whom they belong im- plore us with eyes and hands for a penny for the Murillos of the futurelying in them. These girls are more frank than subtle in their flirtations. There is not one in the crowd who will not be immediately conscious of a man's gaze fixed on her, nor will she be the first to turn her eyes away. Some will wink, and even throw a kiss from a distant corner at the rich Inglese (all foreigners are supposed to be wealthy Englishmen). They areta merry lot, on the whole, these poor girls, the cleverest of whom make only two pesetas, or forty cents a clay, for which tney have to toil twelve or fourteen hours in a , tobacco-reeking atmosphere. Itiot that they object to - the tobacco at all. They are allowed to smOkal if they wish, and many make use of this privilege. They are I remarkably deft at rolling the cigarettes, bu. not ail seem eager to make as many as possible; for SOMA are idling, and others are asleep; but no one cares, as each is paid according to the number she rolls.—Scrilmer. CADBURY'S COCOA is absolutiv pure.—The Public Ana- lysts have submitted CAnansy's Cocos to close testa, and the result has always proved its great value as a sustain- ing and nourishing,beverage.—ildet.
COUNT TOLSTOPS bTORIES FOR CHILDREN.

"The Long Exile and ether Stories for Children" is the title of one of the latest volumes of Count Tolstoi's works published by Mr. Walter Scott. There are many people who, whilst they admire the philanthropy which is the basis of the Russian author's writings find themselves unable to accept some of his teaching. They will have no check on their admiration in the work under notice, for, written as it is for children, it cannot be regarded as in • any sense controversial. It reveals Count Tolstoi in quite a new light—in his love and know- ledge of nature and in his love of children and prac- tical interest in their education and general welfare. The stories were written for peasant children, but they will piove the delight of children of all condi- tions and all climes. We append one of them, and promise our readers other extracts from the work. HOW UNCLE SEMYON TOLD ABOUT HIS ADVENTURE IN THE WOODS.

Once in winter I had gone into the woods after timber. I bad cut down three trees, and cut off the limbs, and was hewing them, when I look up and see that it is getting late : time to go home. But the weather was bad; it snowed and blowed. I say to myself, 'The night is coming on, and you don't know the way." I whipped up the horse and drove on: still no sign of outlet. Forest all around. I think how thin my shuba is: I may freeze to death.

I still pushed on; it grew dark, and I was en- tirely off the road. I was just going to unyoke the sled and protect myself under it, when I heard not far away the jingle of bells. I went in the direction of the bells, and saw a troika of roan horses, their manes tied with ribbons! their bells were jingling, and two young men were in the sleigh. "Good evening, brothers." "Good evening peasant." "Where is the roan, brothers?" "Here we are right on the road." I went to them and see that strangely enough the road is unbroken, all drifted over.
"Follow us," said they, and they whipped up their horses.

My wretched mare could no keep up with thent. I began to shout, "Hold on brothers I" They waited forme, laughing. "Get in with us," said they; "it will be easier for your horse without a load." "Thanks," said I.

I climbed into their sledge. It was handsome— well lined. A soon as I sat down, how they spurred on the horses! "Now then, my darlings!" The roan horses dashed away, making the snow fly in clouds. What a wonderful thing. It grew lighter and lighter, and the road became as glare as ice, and we flew so fast that it took away my breath, and the twigs lashed my face. It began to be painful. I look ahead: there is a steep mountain, a very sleep mountain, and at the foot of the mountain a ravine. The roans were flying straight for the ravine.

I was frightened, and cried: "Heavens and earth! slow up, you, slow up; you will kill us !" But the men only laughed, and urged on the horses the more. I see there is no saving us: the ravine is under our very runners. But I see a bough right over my head. "Well,' I think, "you may go over alone." I stood up, I seized the bough, and there I hung! As I caught it I shouted, "Held on !" And then I bear women shouting: "Uncle &rayon! what is the matter? Start up the fire, you women ! Something is wrong with Uncle Semyon! He is screaming! Stir up the fire!" I woke u?, and there I was in my cottage, cling- ing to the loft and screaming at the top of my voice. And all that I had seen had been a dream! —From the "Long Exile;' and other Stories.

div.head: WELLINGTON AND THE TAME TOAD.
div.p: WELLINGTON AND THE TAME TOAD.

A gentleman who is a great collector of auto- graphs has a very singular one of the Duke of Wellington, which ho prizes very highly, as he con- siders it characteristic of a noble-hearted man. The following is a faithful transcript—"Strathfieldsaye, July 27, 1837. Field-Marshal the Duke of Welling- ton is happy to inform William Harries that his toad is alive and well." An explanation of this singular letter is given on a paper appended in these words—The Duke of Wellington was one day taking his usual country walk when he heard a cry of distress. He walked to the spot, and found a chubby, rosy-faced boy lying on the ground, and bending his head over a tame toad, and crying as if his bean would break. "What's the matter, my lad ?" said the Duke. "Oh, sir; please sir, my poor toad—l bring it something to eat every morning. But they are going to send me off ever so far away to school; nobody will bring it anything to eat when I am gone, and I am afraid it will die" "Never mind, don't cry, lad—l'll see that the toad is well fed, and you shall hear all about it when you are at school."

div.head: NEW MAIL COACHES.
div.p: THE NEW MAIL COACHES.

In. confirmation of an announcement made last summer, we learn that the Post Office authorities are now formally inviting tenders for the convey- ance of mails between Manchester and Liverpool by coaches drawn by three horses, which coaches are to run from each city six nights a week. The mail coaches will leave the General Post Office, in Man- chester, every evening, and, it is understood, will take the old coach road from Manchester to Liver- pool. This road includes Pendleton, Eccles, Petri- croft, Irlam, Cadishead, Hollins Green, and Warrington (where the coach is timed to arrave soon after midnight); thence proceeding by Rain- hill, Prescot, and Knotty Ash to the General Post Office, Liverpool. Before the cfmveyance of the mails by the Manchester and Liverpool Railway (now nearly sixty years .ago), some thirty cdaches were running every working day from Manchester Ito Liverpool via Warrington. Acc•rding to the late Mr. J. T. Slugg, one of the most popular of these was the "Doctor," which ran every evening at six o'clock from the Swan and Flying Horse, Market- st., and Bush, Deansgate. Amongst the latest Ipopular coaches leaving Manchester for Liverpool, "i.e., from 1830 to 1832, was the " Delight," from the Swan, Flying Horse, and Bush, which left the town every morning at 9.30. Just before the railway was opened, the Liverpool mail coach left the Royal Hotel and New Bridgewater Arms at 12.30 p.m., go- ing through Irlam, Warrington, and Prescot, arriv- ing at the Saracen's Head and Golden Lion, Liver- pool (alternately),in time for the Post Office packet from that port to Dublin. Other coaches left the same well-known Manchester •hostelry and coach office for Liverpool at 4.45 a.m., 5.45 a.m., 9.45 a.m., 4.30 p.m., and 5.45 p.m., all being timed to perform the journey in four hours. In 1828-9 (a year before the railway was opened)a perfect swarm of coaches left the town for Liverpool from the Royal Hotel; Star and Bush, Deansgate, The Palace, Mossley Arms, Peacock, Talbot, Swan, and Flying Horse, Market-street; King's Arms, King-street; and New Boar's Head, Hyde's Cross—most, if not all, taking the road by Irlam, Warrington, and Prescot.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAMRDA JANUARY 11, 18fl0.
NEW, BOOKS, &c.

• " Little Saint Elizabeth, and other storieb," is the title of a new and charming book for children, by Frances Hodgson Burnett, author of " Little Lord Fauntleroy." It is a matter of course to say, that anything which Mrs. Burnett writes is sure to be worth reading, and "Little Saint Elizabeth" is in its way a delightful and finished picture. It is a story which can be enjoyed by the old as well as by. the young, and will be found helpful and stimulating to both. The book is most artistically illustrated by It. B: Birch, Arthur Brennan, and "0. A." The other portions of the volume include the "Story of Prince Fairyfoot," "The Proud Little Grain of Wheat,' and "Behind the White'Brick." The volume is published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co. It is handsomely printed on thick toned paper, and, as it is beautifully bound, it makes a capital gift book. "Tricks with Cards" is a complete manual of card conjuring, by Professor Hoffman, author of "Modern Magic." It is from the same firm, and the pries is is. The reader will be astonished to find bow numerous are the conjuring tricks that can be accomplished with the aid of a pack of cards, but he will be equally surprised to learn how numerous are the ways in which most of

the tricks can be done. The descriptions are clear and intelligible, and they are aided when necessary with original diagrams and illustrations. Messrs. Warne and Co. also publish a is. volume, with the title of" Home Doctering." It is a guide to domestic medicine and surgery, and is written by Mr. W. B. Kesteven, M.D., F.R.C.S. It is not intended to assist thereader in " quacking "himself, but to be of use in the hundred and one emergencies which may arise when a doctor is not at hand. It is written in simple lan- guage, suitably illustrated, and completed by having an admirable index. " Advice to singers" may be des- cribed as the good wine which needs no bush, for the manual has already reached the fourth edition. It is from the pen of Mr. F. J. Crowest, and contains so much that is valuable in the way - of advice and instruction, that no singer, trained or untrained, can fail to profit by it. In the Camelot series, published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have to hand "Elizabethan England, from a 'Short description of England 'by Mr. William Harrison, (in Holinshed's Chronicles), edited by Lothrop Withing- • ton, with introduction by F. J. Furnivall, LL.D." Har- rison went to the heart of the matter in describing what he saw, and gave a finished picture of the England of ihis day. Referring to what may be called the degene- rate tendency," he says—" When our houses were builded of willow, then had we oken men, but now that our houses are come to be made of oke, our men are not onlie become willow, but a great manie, through Persian delicacie, crept in among us, altogether of straw, which is a sore alteration." " Humourous Poenis "is the title of the latest issue of the Canterbury Poets. It covers the humourous verse of a century, and is edited, with biographical notes, by Mr. Ralph H. Caine. It is hardly necessary to say that there is much in this volume which thestusent will have come across elsewherein one form or another, but it is due to say that there are many poems which will probably be new to him. It is altogether a treat to get such a collec- tion,in such a form, at such a cheap rate. The biographi- cal notes are exceedingly valuable, and the preface is pertinent and discriminating. "The Life of Gotthold Ephraim Leasing" is issued as one of the "Great Writers.' It is written by Mr. T. W. 1 Rolleston, who has spared no pains in getting together the best material for writing thelife of the great German critic. Lessing had unquestionably a striking influenee upon the literatureof his country, and, for that matter, upon the literature of all countries. Goethe, in his autobiography,has a special reference to the effect which Lessing's publication of the" Laocoon " produced in his young days. Goethe concludes by saying that with Lessing's review of the " Laocoon," "All former criticism was flung away like a worn-out garment." Mr. John Heywood issues an "Introduction to the Study of Commercial Geography," by Mr. John J. Card- well, of St. Bede's College, Manchester. It deals with map drawing and projection from memory, and there is a chapter on the teaching of commercial geography, the work being a summary of the lectures introductory to the course of commercial geography and practical commerce at the Technical School, Manchester. This first part will probably be followed by other volumes, and meantime the technical student cannot do better than make himself thoroughly acquainted with this new text book, which has obviously been most carefully pre- pared. The third series Of "Manchester Science Lectures" has reached the 15th thousand, which may be taken as evidence of. the popularity of these cheap, and yet in- valuable, science works. The subjects of this series of lectures are—" Yeast, coal-colours, food of plants, un- cortscious action of the brain, epidemic delusions, and progress of sanitary science." We have also received from Mr. John Heywood "The charge delivered to the clergy and churchwardens of Manchester, at the primary visitation, held in July, 1889, by James Moorhouse, D.D., Bishop of Manchester," and Christ and His sur- roundings—three lectures delivered in the Manchester Cathedral on Sundays October 13th, 20th, and 27th, 1889, by the Right Rev. Tames Moorhouse, D.D., Bishop of Manchester.' Both the charge and the lectures ex- cited a considerable amount of interest at the time they were delivered, and it is well that they are issued in this permanent form. The bishop shows himself to be liberal-minded as well as learned, and no one can read his expositions, whatever his views may be, without profiting by them.

True, tha'rt nobbut new among us, Like a chicken, fresh fro' a' shell ; Tha may give us lots o' sunshine, Happen trubble—who con tell? 0 thad singin', an' glad praisin', 'At ther's bin o'er thy new name, Hes bin chimed bi hearts 'at's hopeful— () thi lots bin welcomed t' seine. Tha'rt nod teed th' owd rut to folio', 'At o th' years hey done afooar ; Try to mend ther wark, lift th' humble, Smile an' gladden th' hearts o' t' poor. Strengthen t' wayk 'at pine i' sorro'. div.head: BRUN WIELD.
div.p: BRUN WIELD.
A TALE OF THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY.

The war carried on in Scotland, by the friends and enemies of Queen Mary, after her departure into England, was productive of an almost complete dis- solution of order, and laid the foundation of many feuds, which were kept up by private families and individuals long after all political cause of hostility had ceased. Among the most remarkable quarrels which history or tradition has recorded as arising out of that civic broil, I know of none so deeply cherished or accompanied by so many romantic and peculiar circumstances, as one, which took place between two old families of gentry in the neigh- bourhood of Edinburgh. Stephen Bruntfield, laird of Craighouse, had been a zealous and disintei eeted partisan (if the queen. Robert Moubray of Barn- bougle was the friend successively of Murray and Morton, and distinguished himself very highly in their cause. During the year 1572, when Edinburgh . Castle was maintained by Kirkaldy of Grange in behalf of the queen, Stephen Bruntfield held out Craighouse in the same interest, and suffered a siege from a detachment of the forces of the Regent, commanded by the laird Of Barn. bungle. This latter baron, a man of fierce and brutal nature, entered life as a younger brother, and at an early period chose to cast his fate among the Protestant leaders, with a view 'of improving his fortunes. The death of his elder brother in rebellion at Langside, enabled the Regent Murray to reward his services with a grant of the patri- nronial estate, of which he did not scruple to take pessession by the strong hand, to the exclusion of his infant niece, the daughter of the late proprietor. Some incidents which occurred in the course of the war had inspired a mutual hatred of the most ir tense character ' into the breasts 'of Bruntfield and Moubray; and it was therefore with a feeling of strong personal animosity, as well as of political rancour, that the latter • undertook the task of watching the motions of Bruntfield at Craighouse. Bruntfield, after holding out for many months, was obliged, along with his friends in Edinburgh Castle, to yield to the party of the Regent. Like Kirkaldy and Maitland of Lethington, be surrendered upon a promise of life and estate; but while his two friends perished, one by the hand of the executioner, the other by his own band, he fell a victim to the sateless spite of his personal enemy, who, in con- ducting him to Edinburgh as a prisoner, took fire at some bitter expression on the part of the captive, end smote him dead upon the spot. Bruntfield left a widow and three infant sons. The lady of Craighouse bad been an intimate of the unfortunate Mary, from her early years; was educated with her in France, in the Catholic faith; and had left her court to become the wife of Brunt,. field. It was a time calculated to change the natures of women as well as of men. The severity with whieh her religion eves treated in Scotland, the wrongs of her royal mistress, and finally the eufferings.and death of her husband, acting upon a mind naturally enthusiastic, all conspired to alter the chitracter. of Marie Carmichael, and substitute for the rosy hues of her early years, the gloom of the sepulchere and the penitentiary. She continued, after the restoration of peace, to reside in the house of her late husband; but, though it was within two miles of the city, she did not for many years re•appear in public. With no society but that of her children, and . the persons necessary to attend upon them, she mourned in secret over past events, seldom stirring from a particular apart- ment, which in accordance with a fa.shioe by no means uncommon, she had caused to be hung with black, and which was solely illuminated by a lamp. In the most rigorous observances of her faith she was assisted by a priest, whose occasional visits formed almost the only intercourse which she main- tained with the external world. One strong pug= gradually acquired a complete sway over her mind —llEvEleort—a passion which the practice of the au had invested with a conventional respectability. ATI which no kind of religious feeling, then known, was able either to check or soften. So entirely was she absorbed by this fatal passion, that her very children at length ceased to have interest or merit in her eyes, except in so far as they appeared likely to be the means of gratifying it. One after another, as they reached the age of fourteen she sent them to France, in order to be educated; but the accomplishment to which they were enjoined to direct their principal attention was that of martial exercises. The eldest, Stephen, returned at eighteen, a strong and active youth, with a mind of little polish or literary information, but considered a per. loot adept at sword-play. As his mother surveyed his noble form, a smile stole into the desert of her wan and widowed face, as a winter sunbeam wanders over a waste of snows. But it was a smile of more than motherly pride; she was estimating the power which that frame would have in contend- ing with the murderous Moubray. She was not alone pleased with the handsome figure of her first- born child; but she thought with a fiercer and faster joy upon the appearance which it would make in the single combat against the slayer of his father. Young Bruntfield, who, having been from his earliest years trained to the purpose now contemplated by his mother, rejoiced in the prospect, now lost no time in preferring before the king a charge of murder against the laird of Barnbougle, whom he at the same time challenged, according to a custom then not altogether abro- gated, to prove his innocence in single combat. The king having granted the necessary licence, the fight took place in the royal park, near the palace; and, to the surprise of all assembled, young Brunt. field fell under the powerful sword of his adversary. The intelligence was communicated to his mother at Craighouse, where she was found in her darkened chamber, prostrate before an image of the Virgin. The priest who had been commissioned to break the news, opened his discourse in a tone intended to prepare her for the worst; but she cut him short at the very beginning with a frantic exclamation—. I know what you would tell—the murderer's sword has prevailed, and there are now but two, instead of three, to redress their father's wrong!" The melan- choly incident, after the first burst of feeling, seemed only to have concentrated and increased that passion by which she had been engrossed for so many years. She appeared to feel that the death of her eldest son only formed an addition to that debt which it was the sole object of her existence to see discharged. "Roger," she said, "will have the death of his brother, as well as that of his father, to avenge. Animated by such a double object, his arm can hardly fail to be successful." Roger returned about two years after, a still hand- somer, more athletic, and more accomplished youth than his brother. Instead of being daunted by the fate of Stephen, he burned but the more eagerly to wipe out the injuries of his house with the blood of Moubray. On his application for a licence being presented to the court, it was objected by the crown lawyers that the case had been already closed by tnaljortune of the former challenger. But while this was the subject of their deliberation, the applicant caused so much annoyance and fear in the court circle by the threats which he gave out against the enemy of his house, that the king, whose inability to procure respect either for himself or for the law is well known, thought it best to decide in favour of his claim. Roger Bruntfield, therefore, was permitted to fight in banes with Moubray; but the same fortune attended him as that which had already deprived the widow of her first child. Slipping his foot in the midst of the combat, he reeled to the ground, embarrassed by his cumbrous armour. Moubray, according to the barbarous practice of the age, immediately sprang upon and dispatched him. "Heaven's will be done I" said the widow, when she heard of the fatal incident; "but, gratias Deol there still re- mains another chance." Henry Druntileld, the third and last surviving son, had all along been the favou: ire of his mother. Though appareetly cast in a softer mould than his two elder brothers, and bearing all the marks of a gentler and more amiable. dieposirion, he in reelity cherished the hope of avenging hie father's death more deeply in t he receeses Of his heart, and longed more ardently to accomplish that deed than any of his brothers. His mind, naturelly suseeptible.of the softest and tenderesb imptessions, had 'c'ontracted the enthusiasm of his mother's wish in its strongest shape; as the fairest garments are capable of the deepest stain. The intelligenc.e, which reached him in France, of the death of his brothers, instead of bringing to his heart the alarm end horror which might have been expeceed, only braeed him to tee adventure which he no,/ knew to be before him. From this period, he *he nlos,s.nt lnrninat, which he had heretofore delighted to cultivate. His nights were spent in poring over the memoirs of distinguished knights—his days were consumed in the tilt-yard of the sword-player. In due time he entered the French army, in order to add to4tho mere science that practical hardihood„ tin went of which he conceived to be the cause of tie death of his brothers.' Though the sun of chivalrs was now 'declining far in the occident, it was no yet altogether set: Montmorency was but jus, dead ; Bayard was still alive—Bayard, the knigle of all others who has merited the mdtto. div.p: men, Henry firunttleld was a imitator. No young knight kept a Crater sAa! tit his horse—none complained less of th.. ,evori • campaign-ing—none cherished lady's love with fonder, purer, or more devout seosation. On li,- being introduced at the court of Ilenry 111., he h signalised, hala matter ,of course, Cat heriue Min- bray, the disinherited niece of his father's :tor derer, who had been educated in a French convent by her other relatives, and was now provided Itrr In the household of the queen.. The connection o 7 this young lady with the tale of his own family, end the circumstance of her being a sufferer in co:tinted with himself by the wickedness of one individual, would have been enough to create a deep interest respecting her in his breast. But when, in addition to these circumstances, we consider that she was beautiful, was highly accomplished, and, in many other-respects, qualified to engage his affections, we can scarcely be surprised that that was the result of their acquaintance. •

• At length, accomplished with all the skill which could then be acquired in arms, glowing with all the earnest feelings of youth, Henry returned to Scot- land. On reaching his mother's dwelling, she clasped him, in a transport of varied feeling, to her breast, .and for a long time could only gaze upon his elegant person. "My last and dearest," she at length said, "and thou too art to be adventured upon this perilous course I Much have I bethought me of the purpose which now remains to be accom- plished. I have net been without a sense of dread lest I be only doing that which is to sink my soul in flames at the day of reckoning; but yet there has been that which comforts me'also. Only yestemight I dreamed that your father appeared before me. In his hand he held a bow and three goodly shafts —at a distance appeared the fierce and sanguinary Moubray. He desired me to shoot the arrows at that arch traitor, and I gladly obeyed. A first and secoud he caught in his hand, broke, and trampled on with cotnempt. But the third shaft, which was the fairest and goodliest of all, pierced his guilty bosom, and he immediately expired. The revered shade at this gave me an encouraging smile, and withdrew. My Henry, thou art that third arrow, which is at length to avail against the shedder of our blood. The dream seems a revelation, given I especially that I may have comfort in this enter- prise, otherwise so revolting to a mother's feelings."

Young Bruntfield saw that his mother's wishes bad only imposed upon her reason, but he rnade no attempt to break the charm by which she was actuated, being glad, upon any terms, to obtain her sanction for that adventure to which he was himself impelled by feelings considerably differ- ent. He therefore began, in the most deliberate manner, to take measures for brieging on the com- bat with Moubray. The same legal objections which had stood against the second duel were maintained against the third; but public, teeang was too favourable to thmobject to be madly virth- stood. The laird of Barnbougle, though somewhat past the bloom of life, was still a powerful and active man, and, instead of expressing any tear to meet this third and more red oubted warrior, rather longed for a combat which promised, if successful, to make him one of the most renowned swordsmen of his time. He had also heard of the attachment which subsisted between Bruntfield and his niece; and, in the contemplation of an alliance which might give some force to the claims of that lady upon his estate, found a deeper and more selfish rea‘on for accepting the challenge of his youthful enemy. King James himself protested against stretching the law of the per duellum so far; but, sensible that there would be no peace between either the parties or their adherents till it should be decided in a fair combat, he was faint to grant the required licence. The fight was appointed to take place on Cramond Inch, a low grassy island in the Frith of Forth, near the Castle of Barnbougle. All the preparations were made in the most approved manner by the young Duke of Lennox, who had been the friend of Bruntfield in France. On a level space, close to the northern beach of the islet, a space was marked off, and strongly secured by a paling. The spectators, who were almost exclusively gentlemen (the rabble not being per- mitted to approach), sat upon a rising ground .beside the enclosure, while the space towards the sea was quite clear. At one end, surrounded by his friends, stood the laird of Barnbougle, a huge and ungainly figure, whose features displayed a mixture of ferocity and hypocrisy, in the highest degree unpleasing. At the other, also attended by a host of family allies and friends, stood the gallant Henry Bruntaeld, who, if divested of his armour, might have realised the idea of a winged Mercury. A t eat was erected close beside the tams for the Duke of Lennox and other courtiers, who were to act as judges; and at a little distance upen the sea lay a small decked vessel, with a single female figure on board. After all the proper ceremonies which attended this strange legal custom bad been gone through, the combatants advanced into the centre, and, planting foot to :oot, each with his heavy sword in his hand, awaited the command which should let them loose against each other, in a combat which both knew would only be closed with the death of one or other. The word being given, the fight commenced. Moubray, almost itt the first pass, gave his adversary a cut in the right limb, from which blood was seen to flow profusely. lint Brunt field was enabled, by this mishap, to per- ceive the trick upon which his adversary chiefly depended, and, by taking care to avoid it, put Moubray nearly hors de combat. The fight then proceeded for a few minutes, without either gaining the least advantage over the other. Moubray was able to defend himself pretty successfully from the cuts and thrusts of his anta- gonist, but he could make no impression in return. The question then became one of time. It was evident that, if no lucky stroke should take effect beforehand, he who first becamesfe.tigned with the exertion would be the victim. Moubray felt his disadvantage as the elder and bulkier man, and be- gan to Ham most desperately, and with less caution. One tremendous blow, for which be seemed to have gathered his last strength, took effect upon Bruntfield, and brought him upon his knee, in a half-stupefied state; but the elder Combatant had no strength to follow up the effort. He reeled to- wards his youthful and sinking enemy, and stood for a few moments over him, vainly endeavouring to raise his weapon for another and final blow. The be could accomplish his wish, Bruntfield receveresi sufficient stiength to draw his dngger, and thrust it up to the hilt beneath the breastplate of his exhausted foe. The murderer of his race instantly lay dead beside him, and a shout of joy from the spectators hailed him as the victor. At the same instant, a scream of more than earthly note arose from the vessel anchored near the island; a lady descended from its side into a boat, and, rowing to the land, rushed up to the bloody scene where she fell upon the neck of the comanerer, an%l pressed him, with the most frantio eagerness, to her bosom. The widow of Stephen Bruntfield at length found the yearnings of twenty years fulfilled—she saw the murderer of her husband, the slayer of her two sonls, dead on the sward before ber, while there still su'r- vived to hems noble a child as ever blessed a mother's arms. But the revulsion of feeling produced by the event was too much for her strength; or, rather Providence, in its righteous judgment, had resolved that so unholy a feeling as that of revenge should not be too signally gratified. She expired in Ihe arms of her son, murmuring ":,:eac Donzine," with her latest breath.

The remainder of the tale of Bruntfield may be easily told. After a decent interval, the young laird of Craighouse married Catherine Noubmy ; and as the king saw It right to restore that young lady to a property originally forfeited for service to his mother, the happiness of the parties might be considered complete. A long life of prosperity and peace was granted to them by the kindness of Heaven; and at their death they had the satisfac- tion of enjoying that greatest of all earthly bless- ings, the love and respect of a numerous and virtuous family.

CHAPTER • XLV. FERDINAND'S END.

A NOVNISBER day in Italy—in Naples—when sum- mer reigns over the glorious fruits of that sunny land, which hang ripe arld luscious on the bough. In a house there, with long open windows and green verandah, cool stone facading, and temple•like aspect, in the front room, lies Ferdinand de Resimont, his dying eyes fixed on the window, where the closed Venetian blinds exclude both sun and air. "Shall I die like this, and never look on God's earth again ? Oh, that I could drag myself to that window and tear the blind away! I cannot—alone, alone! God and man have forsaken me !”

And be sobbed wildly for a time, and beat his pil- lows in his despair. After that, he seemed to grow calmer. He took up a book lying on his bed, and attempted to read; but the effort was too great, his weak eyes closed, and he fell into a fitful sleep. To be broken soon by some one entering the room and walking softly up to the bed. Ferdinand opened his eyes, and saw Philippe standing there, looking down upon him. '
"I have seen Dr. Principi. He says you are dying." "1 know it—feel it, and you have killed me !" Philippe's lip curled. _ . . _ _ .

"How is that? I, who would have preserved your life for my own purposes? Your death will defeat many of them; for you play an important part in the drama of my life. At the risk of losing a limb. I would save you, if possible. But you are dying." "And I thank God for it. I look for rest beyond the grave; my sins are forgiven me, and I can say I am rejoiced to die." Here he stopped, and drew his breath with a painful effort. "I cannot understand why you should wish me to live, or what value my life can be to you. From no natural affection, Philippe, I know; for you do not love me." "Love you! no," cried the other with a laugh; "I hate you, and have since the hour in which you were born. I tell you now, because it is useless keeping the knowledge from you, when you are escaping from my hands. I tell you that you have no claim upon my natural affection. Your are not of my kin or of my people; you are not my brother; no blood of mine, or of my race, is in your veins. To serve my own purposes I reared you; to serve my own ends I would save you; but you must die." Ferdinand rose from the bed and sat up; his large, dreamy eyes fixed steadily on the other's face. "Say that again—swear it—that you are not my brother!"

"I swear it, although," he muttered in an under- tone, "an oath has no sanctity to me." "From my heart I thank God! I feel very, very happy," and he sank back again among the pillows, his wasted hands clasped together. Philippe ground his teeth. "Oh, that I could inspire life, and you should live!"
"You cannot, and I shall have rest ;" and a tran• quil.sunle settled on his lips._ _ _

The man saw it, and his dark face frowned as he greedily watched the beautiful expression come and go. "Only to preserve that likeness of her—only to keep that smile always, near me, you should live. Boy, I bate you! and yet when that look of your mother's steals over your Saxon face--when I see the most glorious light that ever shone from a woman's eyes reflected from hers in yours, I could grovel on the ground, your slave! It is hard to part with you now—you are all I have of her." "Then you loved my mother?" said the youth. un- easily. "Philippe, will you not tell me who and what I am, and why you took the care of such a wretched waif as I upon yourself? There is much that is strange and mysterious in your habits and life —much that I often wondered at, ' yet never sougnt !nfortnation upon; but the strangest thing pf all is your adoption of Me." "Hut 0.110 feeling prompted it—revenge! To gratify that, I took you from a child and made you mine—body and soul, made you mine—at least, I thought to 'do so, but Fate wills otherwise. Your body is Death's, your soul is God's. You have escaped me; but I vow double and treble vengeance on those who survive—your mother for one." "Ah ! then my mother is living ?'' • "She is living." "And in your power? Ah ! my poor mother P' De covered his face and wept aloud. Philippe regarded this weakness with a mocking smile, and then, without another word, turned round and left the room.

Ferd;nand's tears were still falling, when the door opened again, and a second personage entered the room—a tall man' in a priest's dress, and with a shovel-hat slouched over his eyes. The boy looked round, and then turned away hastily. "Is that you, Father Pedro r he said. "I want nothing; lam very comfortable. Leave to2e a little longer, please." But the good father did not go; he came nearer to the bed, and looked curiously at the dying boy. "Poor fellow! you look confoundedly bad," was the very unpriestlike exclamation of the intruder, delivered, too, in very excellent English. Ferdinand started up. _

How did you come here?" The priest pulled off his hat, and sat down on the chair by the side of the bed, before he answered. "I had no easy job to get care, I can tell you; for, It seems, they won't let any but priests come near you. You are suspected of being a heretic; and they are afraid the devil will pay you a visit, I suppose. But that he did, I will answer for, just now, in the shape of that fiend, De Rdsicnout. Have you forgotten me ?" And he threw off his priest's cloak, and tossed back hie pile of bright chestnut curls, and smiled a broad, wholesome, English smile on the poor dying man.

"I have seen you somewhere, but I cannot re- member where; yet you bring back the memory a a happy time." "At Redfern, in England. I am Ingram Ross Ingestre, a cousin of the Redfern Ingestres. I saw you once in the garden at Westwood; I have come all the way to Italy to see you again. Don't tremble so; He still for a while, you are so weak."

Ah ! you bring with you the glorious scent of those English moors; you bring with you visions of sunny glades and shadowy dells—of cottage, farm, and park—of happy faces—of cheerful voices! Oh, England! Dying, I feel that you gave me birth. I love you With a tender and holy passion; and I pray that my bones may lie bitneath your sod." Ingram feared this burst of passionate emotion would bo the young man's death; but he rallied again from the half-fainting fit it brought on, and sat up, eagerly questioning his visitor. "Why have you come so far to see me?" Did she —Catherine—send you?" "Catherine? Ali! you mean Miss Wace, the governess at Redfern. No; Lina von Bernstein sent me to try and hunt down this man, who calls himself Count de Resbnont, and your brother. But he is neither. Do you know that?" "I have known the latter only ten minntes ; he told me. Give me your hand, you are a friend; you come from the midst of faces I have loved. Give me your strong hand to hold while you tell me the strange things I see written in your honest eyes. That man," and here he shuddered, "who and what is he? Tell me." "It would be difficult to do that yet. I have hung on his track like a bloodhound, and well nigh hate myself for the tricks I have played and the disguises I have worn, only to get a link in the chain of evi- dence I am charged with against him. It is not com- pleted yet; for he has not played out the most impor- tant card in his hand—the one that will betray him. But his time is up here soon, aud he will be off to England again, to work out his devilish schemes, and there I expect to have him. Oh! for the time when I may use my strength on the fellow !" Anckhere he threw out one of his great, muscular arras, clenched his fist, and made savage passes at an imaginary head before him. Ferdinand seemed growing weaker and weaker: he tried to speak, but the words died feebly away upon his lips; and it was not until Ingram had moistened them with a little water he found upon the table, that he could manage to articulate— " Then you are going back to England soon ?" "I have taken my passage in the same ship in which De Rksimont sails. I am going to work as a common sailor in it, the better to advance my task. caYot, uepotroarnsfpelalorewn!t" fhaceeexocflaitmheed,yloooutkiiing at "Fores,d)cralie- cursed reason or other he has wound you up in his cunning web of trickery ! not rest satisfied until I find out why, fcr Lina declared you had some interest or other in property he wanted to get hold of —not for himself; I'll do him. that justice., but for his master. Eh? what do you say? Can't you tell me anything about yourself, my poor boy ?" • "Nothing. God only knows why he claimed and brought me up as his own. My earliest remem- brances are of his dark face—his inscrutable ways— his mysterious habits. Not until the last few years 44tVa I been in his constant comnanionsbin, for it was

Ins wtsti trati swan). &tatty at IlivSG ul 111,c ..G colleges of France and Germany. I feel that I can- not revile this man. I have loved him dearly. He has given me much good, even if he intintied evil. I should die easier if I thought you would not isa sh him for any wrong he may be guilty of to you yours. Forgive him !" "No ! Even if I had no other crime to punis4, your dying face would inspire vengeance in me. has murdered you. I say !" • Ferdinand smiled and shook his head. 4' Not in the bAdy ; he killed me n.orally, and then my physical strength gave w4y. tie took i:ont roe my self-respect, my untarnished honour.:--he told we that I was an outcast, a child of infamy--I whese lofty aspirations--- Ah ! me, that was death in- deed!" He paused and closed his eves for a short time, and then resumed : "That was the only, murder I experienced at his hands, for he had calcunied visely the effect such a revelation would have upon me. It made me desperate. I plunged into the wildest excesses, gave myself up to dissipation, such as men do when, for a brief thipe, they are mad. You see the result. God's punishment works, and I die for the sin of rebellion—rebellion against the ban He set upon MI lam glad you are come. Do not take your hand away. lam glad you are come, for now I can ask you to do something for me. In all this place I have no friend—no one but priests and spies.. surround me."
"Do something for you? Only say what; only tell me how. I can help you—what I can do for you, and It shall be done—done to the utmost of my ability. Tell me."

"He said just now—Philippe said —that my mother • was still living; and his vengeance should fall heavily on her, because death had taken me from him. Will you find her out, and protect her from it, if you are able? I do not know her, I have no clue by which you could trace her; but I am content to leave it in God's hands, and He will guide you to her. Promise this, and I shall die much happier than I thought to." "I'll promise it, gladly enough, and do my best to- find the lady. I believe I shall, for already I have found out a great deal of this man's history; and what. you tell me may explain a thing or two that seemed. puzzling enough before. He bates your mother, you. say?" "He also confessed to having loved her; I believe, from my heart, he does so now. He spoke almost. tenderly of my resemblance to her." Ingram looked at his face for a moment, scanned it. narrowly; then he said, as if the thought Bashing; through his mind found speech in spite of himself— ". Your mother is an Ingestre, then?" "What's that you say i" 'Strange that I notice it now for the first time; but, lying there, I could almost swear you were tii:. murdered son of George Ross, come back Agitill to.- life! Rest content, I have got the clue, and I will set to work. I will save her, if I can, trust we. Hove.. you no message to her, supposing you-- --" .tire dead?—cut off a piece of my hair and give it - to hti, and tell her that if I had known her mother'n. love, I should have been living now to blesd her!

Tell her that I thought of her when I was dying, and would have even many hours of the few left me only to look on her dear face and kiss it. • Tell her lift as! lam flinking so low; raise me" Ingram did it, tenderly as a woman, and the young man, supported in his arms, ciao And tell her that I should wish her to know and love one who was very kind and dear to me— Catl terino Wace."

But here his breath ; he paved, and the- lips emitted no sound. Ills eyi s turned °a the face of Ingram, and their pleading, dying expression moved the heart of the young man mobt vmslv ; team bung op his thick, short lashes, and his huge, bautlzolue bps quivered.

"Poor fellow !—poor boy !" Still the dying eyes continued to sp,..ak. They said most eloquently the soul within was peaceful, and forbade the sorrow the other showed. A brighter radiance seemed to gather in them, and a tranquil and most beautiful expression settled on his young, wan. features. His lips moved once, and Ingram s.ooped. his ear to listen. _ _ _ _
" My mother!—eave my mother !" he heard, :md nc. more. - - -

His head sank back among the pillows, and be, closed his eyes gently. Ingram felt the hand .he held tighten round his own, clutch it with a sharp, convulsive grasp; then it slowly relaxed, the hand opened, the fingers unclosed, and the boy was dead, with the radiant light lingering yet upon his face. Ingram composed the dead limbs, resumed his hat and cloak, and stole out of the room, but not before he had cut a lock of the bright chestnut hair trom the head of the dead. (To be continued.)

WARRING TON TOWN COUNCIL. A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francornb) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Harrison, Davies, Sutton; Councillors Monks, Plat t, W. Pierpoint, F. A. Roberts, Tinsley, Fleming, Shaw Green, Muir, Marsh, Ashton, Voisey, Jenkins, Flood, R. T. Fair- dough, James Fairclough, Bolton, Heaton, Black- hurst, Percival, Hepherd ; Messrs. Brook (town Clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Dr. Gornall (medical officer), Longelin (borough surveyor), and Chorley (borough treasurer). VINANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended payment of several SIMS of money, including some large sums in connection With the gas department. Orders had also been made for the payment of interest on the bond debt of £87,200 at 3.1 per cent. The Committee also announced that the Local Government Board had sanctioned the borrowing Of £8,954 for the purpose of making additions to and alterations at the depots. On the motion of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor Slikw GREEN, these minutes were confirmed. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended approval of the follow- ing plans :-3 Lock-up shops in Buttermarket-st., for M-r. J. R. Young conditionally • 9 cottages in Cart- wright-st , for d'r. George Wallington; Workmen's Mission Chapel, at Bank Quay; 5 shops and dwelling - houses in Bridge-st., for Mr. John Mynekyn. Also that the offer of Messrs. J. & T. Edwards, of Liverpool, to Pay 10s. per yard for a piece of land in front of two cottages in Winwick-st., be accepted. Councillor PLATT moved, and Councillor MARSH seconded, adoption of these minutes which was agreed to. SANITARY COMMITTEE.—A HIGH DEATH RATE.—THE HOSPITAL MATRON'S SALARY. The Sanitary Committee recommended that an order for 100 plans • of the Borough' for the use of the Medical Officer 9f Health, be given to Mr. P. Pearse, the cost not to exceed £5. That the tender of Mrs. Charlotte Lunt, to supply horse hire for 12 months, at 7s. 3d. for horse and man per day, be accepted. The Mayor being an a?"efficio member of all Committees with the object of Placing Mr. Councillor Hepherd on the Committee, Alder. 111 Francomb's resignation as a member of the Com- Mit_ tee, was accepted, and it was resolved that Mr. L:ouncillor Heplierd be appointed inhis stead. Resolved, that the salary of the Matron of the Hospital for Infectious Diseases, be increased to £6O per annum, from the Ist January, 1890; and that a suitable Public Urinal be erected on a site to be selected by the Chairman and tbeb Rector, adjoining the wall on the west side of the ra.rish Church yard, in Church-st. Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the nlinutes, said the contract with Mrs. Lunt for the supply horse and man at 7s. 3d. per day was a reduction on 'l7t Year's contract. With regard to the increase of the 'c'aPital matron's salary, he said that salary was at Present £4O, and the Committee were recommending the tailvance on the advise of the medical officer, which they • a cllght judicious. He pointed outthat matrons holding nflar positions all seemed to receive higher salaries `.9au they were at present paying in Warrington. Refer- :ling to the recent death-rate of 27.73, 428 of which were ..,ue to zymotic diseases, Alderman Burgess said that l•teath-rate was not quite satisfactory or encouraging. OM he thought the death-rate seemed larger than it featly Was owing to its being calculated on the recent local cennus, which he did not think showed the full Pollulation of the borough. Councillor VOISEY seconded the adoption of the nlinutes. Councillor .TENKINS remarked that at a meeting of the etery Committee on the previous day the registrar fePorted that during the past fortnight there had died no io..lo_iver than 44 minors as against 11 in the same period .:trar. He thought that was a serious increase, and, e medical officer was in the room, they might ask if could be accounted for. Councillor Jenkins also Lhoolight that many people had had influenza without n wing it—he believed he had suffered severely from it '4lll2Telf.

, Alderman HARRISON was glad that Alderman Burgess nad alluded to the abnormally large death-rate because he was not slow to inform them when their death-rate Was very small. Councillor J FAIRCLOUGH asked if it was intended to allow the cinders which had been placed on the riverside to remain there. Alderman BURGESS said that, owing to the economy in fuel which had resulted from the conversion of the fur- naces as Longford to the new principle, they had now hadcinders than they could burn, and these cinders Bad to he placed somewhere. They would remember that before they converted the furnaces they were con- suming a large quantity of slack as well as the cinders. Councillor F. A Roman : That was in the summer. Alderman BURGESS said he was afraid it was both Winter and summer. With regard to the high death- rate of minors mentioned by Councillor Jenkins, he fAlderman Burgess) mentioned that measles had lately °Ben very prevalent. The minutes of the Committee were then adopted. SOME STREETS TO BE PAVED.-WOODEN PAVEMENT IN FRONT OF THE INFIRMARY. The Paving and Sewerage Committee recommended that the following apportionments of the cost of forming and Paving of the following streets be approved : -Beat rice- ' Bg. Mr. P. Rowland £3B 9s. 10d, The Refuge Assurance Company £156 Os. 5d., Mrs. Barker £25 19s. Bd., Mr. E. _Aurkland £45 12s. 7d., total £266 2s. 6d. General-st. :1 . 5.N. B. Percival £24 17s. 10d. Mr. R. Butterfield £22 2s d., Mr. John Wilding £23 2's , Mr. A. W. Brundritt £64 is. 6d., Executors of the late William Litherland, 58 15s• 2. ; Executors of the late Thos. Lamb £24 45., Misses Cannel', £23 25., Mr. Robt. Bolton, £22 14s. Bd., total £262 19.5. 7d. Florence.,: The Refuge Assurance Company £145 4s. The Executors of the late Mrs. 'run- stall £lO 3s. 6d., Mr. James Tonge £l2 18s. Bd., total £l6B 6s. 2d. The Borough Surveyor submitted plans, Specifications, and estimates for the forming and paving of Chorley-st. and Hardy-st., and it was resolved that the Town Clerk serve the necessary notices, and take all necessary proceedings under the Public Health Act, requiring the work to be done, and for the recovery of the expenses from the owners, in the event of their being In default. Resolved, that the tender of Messrs. H. Campbell and Son to supply 600 tons of granite cubes at Co.,t 6d. per ton, and the tender of the Warrington Slate t-t Ltd., to supply 600 tons of granite cubes at 17s. 6d. .Per ton, be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway to supply 40,000 tiles at 645. per 1,000, according to sample, be accepted ; that the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway to supply 60 tons of Portland cement at 385. 6d. per ton be accepted ; and that the tender of Mr. J. Lunt for horse hire at 6s. 10d. per day for six months be accepted. The Town Hall, Park an I Baths Committee recom- mended that the hest thanks of this Committee be given to Mr. Clare for his gift of a pair of starlings for the aviary ; also, that that portion of the minute of the 14th November last, viz. : " That Mr. Councillor Bolton be appointed, the Doputy-Chairman of this Committee for the ensuing year," be again submitted to the Council for approval. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman Haw:astir; seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Councillor Ptarr moved that the minute relating to the appointment of Councillor Bolton as deputy chairman of the committee be not approved. He said that one would have thought after the opinion expressed in such unmis- takeable terms at the last meeting of the Town Council by 16 votes to seven, that the Committee would not again have submitted that minute. It would be well for the Council, however, to know how it was that the minute had been again submitted. He might say that I at the meeting of the Committee there were eight members present, and four voted in favour of the re- appointment of Councillor Henry Roberts and four against it. That left the casting vote in the hands of the Mayor, who gave his decision in favour of Councillor Wm. Bolton, so that there was no overwhelming desire on the part of the Committee for the minute to be again submitted to the Council. The Mayor had, he admitted, a perfect 'right to give his casting vote in favour of the candidate who met with his approval, though the estab- lished usage was to re-appoint the gentleman who had already been elected deputy-chairman of a Committee. To displace him in favour of someone else had ho (Councillor Platt) believed never happened before, and it was a thing that would lead to very serious conflicts of opinion in the Council, and in fact it would lead to a scrambling every November for the post of chairman or deputy-chairrnan of a Committee. A great deal was said at the last meeting of the Council by Alderman Harrison, to the effect that the Council had no power to upset the decision of a Conimittee on a point like this, but it was forgotten that that was by no means a new thing. Two years ago the same thing was done in the case of the Markets Committee. Alderman HARRISON : Not the same thing. Councillor PLATT said it amounted to the same. When the Council refused the recommendation of the Markets Committee, appointing Mr. John Pierpoint chairman and Mr. Hokin vice-chairman, the matter was sent back to the Committee for reconsideration. The matter was re- considered, and the decision come to—and which had the approval of the Council—was that the position of , affairs were reversed. Councillor JAMES FAIRCLOUGH, who seconded the amendment, said that the way in which Councillor Bolton had behaved was to his mind mean and contemp- tible, because he did not think a man had a right either to propose or second himself. Alderman SUTTON suggested that the Council ask both Councillor Roberts and Councillor Bolton to resign. (Cries of "No, no.") If they appointed one gentleman half the Council would be dissatisfied, and it was a loss of dignity to discuss the matter further on the part of the Council. (Hear, hear.) Councillor F. A ROBERT said the principal argument in the consideration of the matter was the question of one man being superseded by another. The opinion was decidedly expressed by the Council that,as the Committee had given no justifiable reason why they should over- look the services of a man who had already sat as deputy-chairman, the matter should be reconsidered. In the previous debate Alderman Harrison stood aloof, but when it came up for re-consideration he took a posi- tion, not in favour of Mr. Bolton or opposiid to Mr. H. Roberts, but simply on the ground that the Council had I no jurisdictiov in the matter, and he therefore voted for , Mr. Bolton. He did not think the Mayor had behaved fairly in giving the casting vote in the way he did. He did not want to create any animosity, but he could not conceive how the Mayor could give his casting vote in fav- our of Councillor Bolton in face of the decision at the last Council meeting-16 votes against seven. If there was nothing else in it but that, one would say that the judg- ment of the Mayor was at fault, but little birds told little tales. (Laughter.) A little tale had been told that the Mayor afterwards gave his reason why he had done so.

The MAYOR: That is very unfair, Mr. Roberts. When it was a question of giving a casting vote I asked the Deputy-Town Clerk what I ought to do, and he at once said "You must vote." "Can I put it off and take further advice ?" I asked. "No, you must decide it now," was the reply. I decided the matter to the best of my ; but it is wrong to drag tittle-tattle in. I could tell a lot that was said there. I think it is very unfair indeed. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS : If it is not based on truth, I am very sorry, but it is a matter of great importance when the Mayor of this borough uses—as I delcare it has been told me, that he he did use what I considered— The-afavon I don't think you ought to repeat things you have only heard. It is most unfair to do so ; it is mere gossip. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: If there was any motive of spite towards Mr. Roberts underlying that vote, I say it is unworthy of the Mayor of this borough. The MAYOR: If there was, but I have no spite against Mr. Roberts or anyone else. Alderman HARRISON contended that the Committee had their own rights to defend. The Committee felt that their rights and privileges—if privileges they were— had been trampled upon in a very inconsiderate manner by the Council ; indeed, in such a way that had no parallel since the incorporation of the borough. He con- tended that the incident in connection with Mr. John Pierpoint was not a parallel case. The Standing Orders said the first business of a Committee after appoint- ment was to choose a chairman and a de- puty-chairman. That was done by the Town Hall Committee, in accordance with the Or- ders. The Committee was not a Committee till it had appointed its chairman, and it could do nothing judicially until then. If, therefore. a Committee had power to appoint a chairman or deputy-chairman, it was not within the province of the Council to undo what they had done. Singe they last met an opinion of a high order—a legal opinion—had been sought on the question through the columns of a publication dealing with municipal matters, and the gentleman who had given that opinion was very much more favourably inclined to the opinion he (the Alderman) had expressed than to the opinion expressed by the Council at the last meeting. There was no reflection upon Mr. Roberts by his being superseded, as he was only appointed for the termination of the year, and every Committee had a right if it thought fit to change the chairman or deputy- chairman; otherwise, why should not they be appointed for a longer period? Mr. Bolton had been in the chair on one or two occasions, and what a reflection it would be upon him, if, after having been appointed by the Coin- , mittee, the Council nullified the appointment! It would I convey a most serious reflection upon him. Councillor MoNgs contended that the Council had I entire authority over every Committee. Otherwise it I was Istossible that by intrigue a Committee might appoint a chairman who would do infinite harm to the interests of the borough. Councillor BOLTON said that he would like, after what Councillor Monks had said, the Standing Orders to be so framed that the Council should have power to appoint every chairman and vice-chairman. A little spleen had been thrown into this matter, but it was of such a character that he would not insult the Mayor with tittle- tattle, nor would he introduce personalities. It had been suggested that he and Councillor Roberts should retire. He (the speaker) had offered to retire if Councillor Roberts would do so, but now, the Committee thought fit to put him up again he should allow the nomination. Councillor WILLIAM PIERPOINT believed it was quite time the end of this unfortunate dispute had been reached, but it was four members of the Committee who were defying the whole Council. There was a little history in this transaction that had never been told. Perhaps it would bring them into better humour if they went into a little ancient history. Councillor Bolton was the senior member of the Committee. When Mr. Roberts and Mr. Bolton were put up for election—he was speak- ing of the appointment of Mr. Roberts—Mr. Bolton foolishly withdrew. There was no d aibt he was a very clever and shrewd fellow, Pad wide awake to his own interests, but if he had shown his usual good sense he would have insisted upon his claims, which were certainly more weighty than those of Mr. Roberts; and the Com- mittee would have had no other course open but to appoint him, but Mr. Roberts rather got on the blind side of Mr. Bolton and induced him to go oat of the room, (Laughter). Councillor BOLTON: I deny that. Councillor W. PIE RPOINT said it was rather a funny episode. These two gentlemen retired and had a little discussion, not as to their respective merits, but chances, and Mr. Roberts induced Mr. Bolton to toss. (Laughter.) He (Councillor Pierpoint) had never heard in all his ex- perience of municipal matters of such an office being tossed for. Mr. Roberts tossed and Mr. Bolton lost ; Mr. Bolton went back into the room and Mr. Roberts was appointed. (Laughter.) He appealed to Mr. Bolton's love of English fair play. He had tossed and lost, why didn't he stick to it? (Renewed laughter.) He thought ' it was a little bit un-English of Councillor Bolton to wish to go behind that very historic toss. Alderman HARRISON: It was on another occasion alto- gether. Councillor BOLTON said Councillor Piernoint had left something out. A member who wished to make a state- ment about a certain matter should do so in such a man- ner that the members would understand the correct facts. There were certain portions that were not correct. That transaction had nothing to do with the Town Council as a body. A little bit of spleen was at the bottom of it all. Councillor VOISEY said this was a question of precedent, and he must leave the onus of settling it on the Town Clerk. Councillor JENKINS remarked that, after Councillor Roberts had been proposed and seconded, no one present at the meeting offered to propose any one else. That was, he thought, a very important point to be considered, but which to some exte,nt had been overlooked. In order to bring the matter again before the Council, Councillor Bolton actually himself proposed the resolution which
