appeared on the minutes. He contended that it would be unseemly for the Council to allow their powers to, be overruled by any Committee. He believed there would be an end of order and discipline if the Council were ric,r allowed to have the power to overrule everything which was done by a Committee. The TOWN-CLERK, in replying .to Councillor Voisey, SA id that the advice the Council had from his deputy Was perfectly good, that they had power not to approve.; but at the same time, he could not disguise from himself the opinion expressed by the paper, that the appointment of chairman and deputy-chairman are not appointments within the meaning of the execution of the acts which the Committees and the Council are appointed to carry , out. Therefore he thought strongly that they were not matters that required the confirmation of the Council. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS pointed out that the appoint- it-lent gave a seat on the General Purposes Committee. The TOWN-CLERK said that the Council authorised the Committee to make appointments, and decided that those appointed should be members of the General Pur- poses Committe. The voting resulted as follow :—For the amendment —Aldermen Holmes and Burgess ; Councillors Percival, Blackhurst, R. Fairclouv,h, Flood, J. N'airclough, Jenkins Shaw Green, Fleming, F. A. Roberts, Pierpoint, Platt, Monks-14 ; against the amendment—The Mayor, Alder- men Harrison and Davies ; Councillors Hepherd, Heaton, Bolton, Muir, Ashton, and Marsh-9. The MAYOR.—The amendment is carried by five votes.

GROSS TORY SLANDERS, The publication in the Liverpool 'Courier" and "Express," on Tuesday, of an article headed "The London and North-Western Railway and Politics : Gladstonian Screw at Eatlestown," formed the most lively topic of conversation in the district which has arisen for many months past. Not that any weight attached to the article itselt, but the state- ments it contained, and which purported to have been supplied by their " Own Commissioner," were so palpably inaccurate to all who knew anything of the parties mentioned by name, or of the man- agement of the Viaduct Waggon Works belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Co., that local politicians, both Liberals and Conservatives, were astounded at their publication. There was a consensus of opinion that the " Commissioner " had been duped, or that the article was the mendacious concoction of some reckless ultra-Tory, anxious to counteract, by either fair means or foul, the revela- tions as to the coercive tactics adopted at another branch of the railway company's system at Crewe. The latter view was most generally entertained, but instead of having the effect intended, the article will recoil upon the paper which has given expres- sion to the slanders it contained. ' The article, after alleding to the charges made against the managers of the Crewe works, went on to say : "It is time the public knew that at Earlestewn the same charges have been for years, and are now made against Mr. J. W Emmett, the superintendent, Mr. Francis Harwood, the works manager, and nearly all the foremen under them ; but in this case the shoe is on the other foot. These officials belong to the Liberal party. The Gladstonians are alleged to be the persecutors, and it is the Tory workingman who has been persecuted." Alter an allusion to past Parliamentary elections, the article continued: "Mr. Emmett, the superin- tendent, makes no disguise of his political colours as an enthusiastic Gladstonian. Ile flaunts them whenever any political fight is going on; and out of the many foremen between him and the men only three are Conservatives. The superintendent is also chairman of the Board of Commissioners for Earles- town, who are the local sanitary authorities, and he is the only direct representative on that body of the North-Western Railway Company. Therein Earlestown differs from Crewe. But politics have entered into even so local a board, and at elections for this body, our Commissioner was informed by several persons who are in a position to speak from personal knowledge. Gladstonian foremen have been seen canvassing both inside and outside the works. It is hardly a year since the first county councillor was elected for the district. The representative was to have been non-political, and for that purpose the Earlestown Commissioners, including Mr. Emmett and other Gladstonians, agreed with the Haydock local authority that Mr. Pearson, of Newton-le- Willows, should be the candidate. But Mr. Pearson was a Conservative of prominence, and so Mr. C. C. Rawlins was nominated by the Gladstonians to oppose him on the purely political ticket. Mr. Emmett was found supporting the latter, and as it became necessary to explain this volte-face, he appeared at Mr. Pearson's meeting for this purpose. Many of his subordinates were present, and there occurred this peculiar coincidence, that, after Mr. Emmett repudiated any support of Mr. Pearson and expressed his decided preference for his own politi- tical candidate, the meeting became most disorder- ly, and the accusation was freely made that the persons responsible for this disturbance were rail- way employes." The article went on to insinuate that certain workmen had been discharged because of their Conservative opinions, and added that workmen had found it expedient to withdraw from their membership of the local Conservative Club. '" Not one alleged any fault against the club," con- tinued the article, "or a change of political belief; more than one hinted that Conservatism did not spell promotion or comfort at the works, and that like I cautious men they desired to have their employment I certain." Continuing, it stated "A most significant I fact is that no Conservati've worker cares to canvass in the cottages where railway workmen live, be- cause of the general belief that to do so 'would be detrimental to the interest of any Conservative em- ploye. * * * Conservative workers would be assured by voter after voter employed in the wagon works "Its all right; but don't come with me, in case the foreman sees me." Other Conservatives, to throw off suspicion, even went in company with Gladstonian workers to the poll; while others sought to protect themselves by giving a card to each of the agents outside the polling sta- tions. Those workmen, on the contrary, who be- longed to the Gladstonian party, showed a demons- trative eagerness to let their colours be known." The conclusion of the remarkable Tory production was as follows :—" Workmen of whose Conservatism there is no doubt have declined to join the Tory club because it is more than we dare do.' And the general position, in the opinion of many who have had experience of lalectioneering in the past, was I expressed thus to our Commissioner by one who could speak from a personal knowledge. 'No via- ductman dare take any part in an election if he is a Tory.' On the other hand, any workman can be as militant a Gladstonian as he likes, and the more the better for himself and his prospects." The falsity of the article is apparent to every- one who knows anything of Mr. Emmett, the works superintendent, Mr. Harwood, the manager, or of the events of the past few years in Earlestown. On Wednesday, in a conversation with our representative, Mr. Emmett described the article as "A tissue of falsehoods from beginning to end," and there is not the slightest doubt that nearly all who have perused the article will agree with Mr. Emmett's forcible description. Mr. Harwood, whom our reporter subsequently Paw, expressed himself in almost the same identical terms. Indeed, they both stated that the facts, as against the untruths, were so well-known to everybody in Earlestown and the district that any reply beyond a general denial was unnecessary. Their well-known abstention from all political meetings, the freedom which they accord to all the men, both Liberals and Tories, to exercise their political rights and privileges with- nut Jet or hindrance, their honest and straightfor- ward management of the works, their popularity among all shades and classes of the men under them, and their quiet and unassuming attitudes on all public questions, are facts which are as familiar as " household words," and are a lasting refutation of the unfounded t barges levelled at them.
R. EMMETT'S D EN/AL :"A TISSUE OF FALSEHOODS."
Mr. Emmett courteously supplied our representa- tive with the following copy of a letter he had forwarded to the Tory newspaper in which the articles had appeared:
" TO THE EDITOR OF THE LIVERPOOL COURIER.

Sir,—My attention has been drawn to your issue of the 7th instant, with respect to a leading article, and also a report by your Special Commissioner on the political aspect at Earlestown, wherein I, to- gether with my foremen (of course excluding the three Conservatives you are good enough to name), are charged with political intimidation. To the whole of your charges I give a most emphatic denial, and I challenge you to prove any single statement which appears in your paper. The articles are neither more nor less than a tissue of falsehoods from beginning to end. And I shall feel obliged if you will insert this letter in your next issue.---Yours, &c.,
J. W. Emil Err. London and North-Western Rmilway Wagon Depart- ment, Earlestown, January Bth, 1890." COUNTY COUNCILLOR RAWLINS EXPOSES THE "GROSS DECEPTION."

Mr. G. W. Rawlins, county councillor for the Newton district, writes to the "Courier." I see in your impression of to-day a report by your Commissioner upon the supposed political relations between Mr. J. W. Emmett and the workmen at the Earlestown Wagon works. I have no intention of entering upon a newspaper controversy, but my sense of justice compels me to write this letter, which I am sure your sense of fairplay will lead you to place in a prominent column of your next issue. As chairman of the Newton Division Liberal Association I have a full knowledge of the subject about which I write, and I feel it my duty to say in the must explicit terms that the statements of your Commissioner with regard to Mr. Emmett and his managers have absolutely no founded= , whatever in fact. The assertion that the former "flaunts" his political colours " whenever any political fight is going on " is known by everybody in the neighbourhood to be totally devoid of truth. On the contrary,. Mr. Emmett, during the three parliamentary elections held since the redistribu- tion act was passed, has never at any time been either seen or heard ,as a politician, and on all occasions positively declined to take any action, feeling sure that be would be misrepresented, and that any such action might have a tendency to

unduly influence those under him. He has there- fore studiously avoided any connection with election committees, and we from a knowledge of his position never 'sought his assistance. One of the most prominent of the Conservatives employed at the works himself informed me that the men were left entirely alone, and not one of the man- agers would act upon my committee last January because they said Mr. Emmett would not like it.l As to the County Council election' Mr. Pearson was the nominee of the local boardsof Newton and Hay- dock, and the ratepayers were within their rights in running a candidate of their own choosing. The political character of the contest may be inferred from the fact that some of the leading Conservatives signed my nomidation papers. It is not true that Mr. Emmett Was a supporter of mine. When I called to solicit his vote, he said he had refused to promise it to Mr. Pearson, and he would refuse to promise it to me. He attended one meeting On each side to hear what the candidates had to say, took no other part, either active or passive, beyond recording his vote. With regard to Crewe, I have no knowledge beyond what I have read in the pub- lic prints, but with regard to Earlestown, I repeat, with the utmost confidence, and from a full know- ledge of the facts, that your Commissioner has been grossly deceived.—Yours, &c., GERALD W. RAW- LiNs, Chairman of Liberal Association. Rainhill, January 7, 1890." A WORKMAN AND "THE COWARDLY LIES." The following letter, from a well-known Earles- town man, employed by the Company,also appeared in the" Courier": "Sir,-1 desire a little space to combat the cowardly lies supplied to "Your Own Commissioner" on the above. Having read in to- day's issue Lord Dunraven's well-weighed speech at the Conservative Club, I hurried to the post with matters for Liverpool bearing on the forthcoming Trade Union Congress there, and on returning advised a friend, who was on the eve of entering the Conservative Club, to read Lord Dunraven's speech, little thinking that by further perusal of your issue I should be so ruthlessly disturbed by finding such a nest of lies as that contained in your commissioner's article. I feel compelled from a sense of fair play to deny what your commissioner heard during his flying visit to Earlestown, last Saturday after- noon. I have been employed at the Viaduct Works over 20 years, and my official connection with trade unions—first as secretary to the nine-hour league, afterwards secretary to my own society, also sec- retary to the United Iron Trades—constitute me a kind of receptacle for all kinds of complaints, yet never have I heard even one word impeaching the officials referred to. My fellow-workmen have often felt curious to know what political views the chief officials held, as they seem so very indifferent and inactive on such matters. •I will venture to say that if your commissioner's picture was true I should be the greatest victim, from the fact that in my desire to combat Gladstone's blunder on the Irish business, I flooded the district with political literature, before either the Conservative or Liberal clubs moved, and I have yet to learn who the workman is that has to sink his individuality on political questions at the Viaduct Works.—Yours, &c., DAVID WILLIAMS, 240, Earle-st., Earlestown, Jan. 7, 1890.

div.head: INFIRMARY EXTENSION.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY EXTENSION.

Alderman DAvixs said that an application had been made by the Infirmary Board of Management for the Council to grant them a piece of land on which to make their proposed extensions. The extent of the land was 409 yards, which, if sold at the price the Corporation bought it at would only come to £75. This piece of land was not part of the recreation ground. That was a matter which would have to be considered—land hav- ing been acquired for purposes of recreation had to remain as such for ever; but according to law the Cor- poration could hold five acres on its own account to do what it liked with, and it happily happened in the pre- sent case that they laid out the land in such a manner that the piece of land now asked for happened to be a piece of the land the Corporation could do what they liked with. _

....... Alderman BURGESS approved of the land being granted to the Infirmary, subject to an agreement similar to that which had been entered into when land was previously granted to the Infirmary, namely, that if the Infirmary was at any time removed from the present site the lama should be surrendered back to the Corporation. Alderman HOLMES and other members also approved of the proposal. The minutes of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Com- mittee were then adopted, with the exception of the minute relating to the approval of Councillor Bolton's appointment as deputy-chairman. The opinion referred to in the discussion on the appointment of Councillor Bolton is from "The Justice of the Peace," and is as follows :—"No doubt the appointment of a Deputy-Chairman is an act of the Committee, but we have much hesitation in saying that it is an act requiring approval by the Council. It may be that the acts which require approval are acts done in the way of carrying out the purposes for which the Com- mittee has been appointed, and not formal proceedings of this kind. But in the tace of our correspondent's decided opinion on the point, we are not prepared to say that he is wrong."

The Gas Committee reported that the average illumin- ating power of the gas for the past six weeks was equal to 18.2 candles at both works.

Alderman HOLMES saki a number of the gas stokers and of the Gas Committee had met and made a mutually satisfactory arrangement. The minutes were approved, LOOKING AHEAD.

div.head: CRAIIER'S NEW ORCHESTRAL ORGAN.
div.p: CRAIIER'S NEW ORCHESTRAL ORGAN.

Musioal men have often— and naturally enough— wonderea, :why all or nearly all so-called American organs should li;"...lade in America, and why sufficient enter- prise has not been displayed to construct in our own country a really good instrument of this class. Although ' there are some most excellent American organs capable of producing beautiful effects' yet there is usually notice- able in most of them a defect in the way of sluegish- ness of speech. What has been so long wanted has at length been accomplished by Messrs. J. B. Cramer and Co., Church-at, Liverpool, who after some years of care- ful study have produced an instruYaent which combines all the sweetness of the very best American organs with a perfect sensitive double touch very similar to the Mustel organ, which is known everywhere for the mar- vellous effects which can be g.ot out of it, but which, however, cannot be purchased for less than £l5O or £l7O. The instrument under notice is styled " Cramer's New Orchestral Organ." Not only stately sacred music but the most rapid and difficult music can be played , upon this organ in the most effective manner. A per- former who understands what can be produced from an American organ, has here a complete orchestra at his command. There are sixteen acting stops and ten com- plete sets of reeds, the voicing of which is of the most pleasingly modulated description. A new stop—the Harpe Eolienne—has been introduced as a solo stop ; it supplies a perfect imitation of a muted violin of the purest tone There are several other delightful solo stops, including the violoncello, which when coupled with the vox humane produces the nearest possible approach in tone to that lovely stringed instrument. One great achievement in this organ is the wonderful control the performer has over the bellows, for the crescendos and diminueludos are instantly obtained by the simple pressure of the foot pedals. In the ordinary American organ these effects can only be produced by the knee-swell, while this adjunct unless carefully used gives a jerky and uncouth result, which is entirely absent in this instrument. The new orchestral organ is particularly suited for home use, as the tone, whilst be- ing full, round and melodious, is at the same time com- pletely under control, and will not be found too much for any room of ordinary size. It is gratifying to be able to say that the instrument in its entirety is made upon Messrs. Cramer's Church-st. premises. The cases vary from veneered woods, such as rosewood, Italian walnut, or ebonised, with marqueterie panels, to solid woods such as oak and American walnut, with carved panels ; they are all thoroughly good specimens of English workmanship. Now that a want has been supplied there should be a large demand for the article supplying that want, especially as it can be obtained for a mere trifle more than the amounts usaally paid for the instruments which have hitherto had a monopoly in the musical mart. —From the Liverpool Courier.

div.head: DARESBIJRY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBIJRY HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held in the Court- room on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Cliffe (vice- chairman) presided, and there was a full attendance of members. A DARE AND DANGEROUS LANE AT LATCHFORD.—A letter was read from Mr. John W. Reynolds, of Beech House, Latchford, in which he called attention to the dangerous state of Acker's-lane to the west of Mr. Dun's house. On the dark winter nights he had several times run into the hedge or wall, and since the Ship Canal works started a further danger was added in the shape of tramps. On ' a previous Tuesday night,as his wife was returning from Warrington about 910 she was attacked suddenly by a man she met in Ackers-lane at the point referred to, and she was deliberately thrown down in the mud. She, however, screamed and the man disappeared, and, fortunately, with the exception of a few bruises, she escaped unhurt. Mr. REYNOLDS suggested that two lamps should be put in the lane, and also that the road be put into a better state of repair.—The CLERK said the Highway Board had nothing to do with lighting roads, but the attention of the surveyor had been called to the state of the footpath.—Mr. J. DARBYSHIRE thought that if any road in the Board's district required to be lighted it was the road from Wilderspool brewery towards London Bridge.—The Chairman agreed with these remarks of Mr. Darbyshire.—Mr. MCINTYRE said it might become necessary for that Board to have a special light- ing district.—The CLERK said the ratepayers of the localities, ought to move first.—The subject then dropped. THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY DECLINE TO PAT.—The CLERK read a letter in which the Ship Canal Company disputed their liability to repair a piece of road at Lower Walton.—Mr. T. S. BURGESS said he had positive proof that the road had been repaired for 40 years by the old canal authorities, but unfortdnately there was no record to that effect in Walton township records.—Mr. JOHN DARBYSHIRE supported the remarks of Mr. Burgess, and it was decided to press the Canal Company to do the repairs. A MUDDY LANE AT MOORE.—A letter was read from Mr. H. Golightly,calling attention to the disgraceful con- dition of several parts of Moss-lane, Moore, but the Sur- veyor stated that he had put the road in better condi- tion. This road, Mr. Pearman added, was going to be totally diverted by the Ship Canal Company. THE ROAD BETWEEN RUNCORN AND WESTON POINT.— A letter from the office of the Runcorn Commissioners was read. It mentioned that the Coroner had called attention to the dangerous state of the road between Runcorn and Weston Point, and the Commissioners wished to know if the Highway Board were willing to join with them in dealing with the road. The Clerk, however, added that he had had another letter from Mr. Marshall, clerk to the Commissioners, stating that the matter was being left in abeyance. Mr. Aaron wanted to know what benefit that Board would get from dealing with the road. The Clerk replied that the Commissioners were at present withdrawing from the matter, so that it hardly came before the Board. There was no further discussion on this subject. THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND THE MAIN ROADS.—It was decided by the Board to petition the County Council of Cheshire in favour of arrangements being made which would enable the repair and maintenance of main roads to be carried out as far as possible under the superintendence of the district surveyors of the various Highway Boards throughout the county. This decision was come to on the motion of Mr. MaNyvan,seconded by Mr. HADDOCK. —Mr. AARON asked if they had no power to stop the County Council from taking over those main roads. The CLERK said they had no power except by petition.—Mr. MCINTYRE : You must not fight your masters.—Mr. PARR: A great many people do it now. (Laughter.)— Mr. AARON referred to the increase of the rates by the County Council, and Mr. J. DARBYSHIRE said that where the local authorities would spend £5OO, the County Council would probably spend £l,OOO. THE STATE OF THE ROADS.—MT. W. Long, writing from Westmoreland, complained of the bad state of the roads in the Board's district, and said they compared un- favourably wish those of their neighbours in Lanca- shire and Cheshire. For some years the question of a steam roller had been more or less before the Board, and they had tried experiments two or three times by hiring the Warrington roller, he believed with good results. He mentioned that in the district of Westmoreland where he was, three Local Boards had combined to purchase a roller which had given satisfaction. Mr. Long also suggested the advisability of that Board obtaining a steam roller.—Mr.Parr thought the letter had better lie on table. He (Mr. Parr) had seen some roads near Winder- mere which were a disgrace to the management —Mr. J. DARBISIIIRE said that as Mr. Long had previously promised to assist the Board in obtaining a steam roller, further consideration of the subject had better be left over till Mr. Long was present.—The matter then

dropped. A COMMICIIsh'S REPORT.—The Ship Canal Committee recommended that steps be taken to provide for the bridges over the canal at Twenty-step bridge, and at Knutsford-road being made 36ft. wide. The Committee having carefully considered the plans and bill of the Widnes Brine Company, it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Long, seconded by Mr. Parr, that the Board be recommended to dissent from the bill. This report was adopted.

In the Edinburgh Court of Session, on Wednesday, the record was closed in the action of Mr. Sexton, M.P., against the proprietors of the "Scotsman," claiming £5,000 damages for slander. A Madrid telegram announces the failure of all Senor Sagasta's attempts to form a Ministry. It is thought that a Provisional Cabinet will be formed to pass the Budget and legalise the financial situation. A St. Petersburg letter published in a Munich paper attributes the Czar's recent illness to some of the epilep- tic attacks to which he has been subject since the Borki railway accident. Mr. Thomas Bright, younger brother of the late Mr. John Bright, died on Wednesday afternoon. He was but little known in the world of politics. He had taken a I very active part in the management of the business of John Bright, Brothers.
BUTTE IZMARk ET-ST RE ET W ESLEYAN MISSION, WA It RINGTON . . . . .

The committee of this wiQ.sion. in their annual eeport. state that on the third Sntidtly in October, 1881 [Children's Sunday], there was a revival in the , ButtermarKet-St. building, then used as a Sunday ' School in connection with the Bold-st v% esleyan Society. Under the leadership ot tie then Superin- tendent (Mr. J. B. Isaac), and Mr. Nicholson, a mission was commenced in the upper room on Sunday evenings, after the usual service at the chapel. This was carried on with some success ' • until the year 1886, when a room was opened in ' Hall-st., and the work carried on there, where a Sunday School was opened. In consequence of the number of children who gathered round while the singing band connected with the mission was out, who appar- ently did not attend any school, it was decided to com- mence a Sunday School, and on the 17th October, 1886, the room was opened in the afternoon, and about 30 scholars were enrolled as the nucleus of the school. The attendance increased rapidly, until it was found that the room was too small, as many as 120 being crowded into the room. On Mlrrch 27th, 1887, the school was transferred to the Buttermarket-st. premises. The number of scholars now on the books is 170, the average attendance being 27 in the morning and 75 in the afternoon. In the meantime the missions was con- tinued in Hall-st. until it was thought desirable to have the school and missian in one centre. Permission was given by the trustees to several structural alterations, and the present room opened as a Mission Hall and Sun- day school in June, 1887. The Committee and workers commenced the present winter sew.son in good earnest. After most serious and lengthened discussion it was decided to commence a series of popular entertainments every Saturday evening, the principal object being to provide a means of reasonable recreation and amuse- ment for the people, and to act as a counterattraction to the public-house. A refreshment bar was provided, and so far the results have beett,most satisfactory. A girls' club has also been commenced this season, the number now on the books being 66. There is also a Society Class meeting, with a membership of 24, Mr. Hickman being the leader. In conclusion the Committee look to the future with hopefulness and trust that the Mission may become a power for good to many in the neighbour- hood, and a useful adjunct to the Bold-st. Wesleyan Society.

The annual free tea was given the other evening to the scholars of the Sunday school. After tea the scholars amused themselves by various games until 9.0, when the prizes for regular attendance were given. It should be stated that the funds for this tea are raised by the teachers and friends by carol singing at Christmas time.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL PARISH CHURCH.
ANNUAL TEA PARTY'.

_ There were about 250 persons present at the annual tea party held in connection with Grappen- hall Parish Church on Tuesday. The gathering was held in the schoolroom and assistance was given by the following ladies :—Mrs. Greenell, the Misses Greenall, the Misses Kidd, the Misses Atkin, the Misses Heaton, Mrs. Lomas, Mrs. Woods, Mrs. Car- ter, the Misses Chandley, Tew, and Howson. The tea party was one of the most successful that have been held, and at the subsequent entertainment there was an audience which filled the room. The Rev_ CANON GREENALL, in opening the meeting, wished all of his parishioners and friends in the best and highest sense of the word a happy new year. The year 1889 had been a singularly mournful one, for it had carried away many of their helpers and friends. Those present were met once again in connection with the , Grappenhall Parish Church, a church of which they I might feel pioud, as, judging from the font and corbels it dated back to the year 1120. They ought to be thank- ful to be permitted to take up the work of those gone before, and who were connected with the old church of Grappenhall, and he hoped they would try to be loyal and faithful b it. The church had seen changes by restorations, changes of officers, rectors, and congregations still there it stood as strong as ever. It was a glory to the village, and he only wished they used it better to the glory of God. (Applause.) He trusted the village would be spared an invasion of the epidemic known as the Russian influenza. (Laughter) At the same time, he' warned them that if it did make its appearance, they would be careful to attend to the first symptoms. He hoped they would not alarm themselves about it. (Laughter.) Be would like to remind them that they had two great works in hand in Gra ppenhall. One was the Tinsley memorial, and the other the restoration of the church bells. Both of these had been warmly taken up, and would be carried out. They wished to perpetuate amongst them the memory of a great, good man, a friend of everybody, who had recently passed away from them. He referred to the late Mr. John Tinsley ; and it was pro- posed to erect a chancel screen in memory of him. He might tell them that on the 20th of the present menth they would not hear the sound of the old church clock. Their bells were then going to be taken down, and the work of restoration would commence. To effect this work they had had subscriptions promised, and the ladies of the parish had kindly come forward and.were preparing for a bazaar or sale of work, which would be held towards April. (Applause.) The chief part in the subsequent entertainment SIMS taken by the St. James's (Latchford) Christy Minstrel Company, under the superintendence of Mr. J. Wright. Songs were, however, successfully rendered by Mr. Fairhurst and Miss Fairhurst, and a pianoforte solo by Miss Tow. The minstrels' programme, which was very highly enjoyed, contained humorous dialogues between Messrs. Atkinson, Scarsbrick, and Ground, and songs by Messrs. A. Griffiths, Perkins, T. Goodwin, J. John- son, J. Ashton, Scarsbrick, Grounds, and Keenan, several of which were encored. The second part of the entertainment consisted of a very amusing sketch entitled "The Bouncer," also by the St. James's Minstrels. The gatherieg was brought to a conclusion with the singing of the National Anthem and cheers for the rector.

BOLD STREEI WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening the annual social gathering of the officers, teachers, scholars, and friends of the Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School, took place in the school-room. About 200 sat down to tea, their

wants being attended to by Mrs. Gunnell, Mrs. Kerry, Mrs. Collin, Mrs. Gleave, Mrs. Mills, Mrs. Gandy, Miss Smith, Miss Greening, Miss Collin, and Miss Fairhurst. Trays had been given by Me4dames Allen, Barlow, John Bennett. Benson, Blackhurst, Bodle, J. Carter, T. Carter, W. P. Chorley, P. Clare, Collin, Dale, Dixon, Dutton, Evans, Fairhurst, Gandy, R. Garnett, D. Garnett, Greening, Grime, Guest, Hartley, Henshall, Horrocke' J. B. Isaac, Kent, Kerry, Lilly, Lunt, Peaeocke, Prince, Roff, Savage, IV. Silcock, Sobey, S. Smith, J. Taylor, J. Toft, and E. Weaver, Miss Stelfox, and Mr. W. Barlow. The Rev. JOHN GUNNELL, superintendent minister, presided over the subsequent proceedings, and amongst those pre- sent were—The Rev. W. Brookes, Messrs. W. Silcock (superintendent of the Sunday school), R. G. Henshall (treasurer), J. Evans (general secretary), E. Lunt (teachers' secretary), C. 13. Kerry, W. C. Nicholson, and Fanshaw.—Mr. EVANS presented the Committee's report, which stated that the teaching staff for the past year consisted of 30 male and 29 female teachers. The num- ber of scholars on the books was 526. The average at- tendance had been—morning 168, afternoon 350. The library contained 430 volumes. The Band of Hope had a membership of 60. The school finances were not as favourable as could have been wished, inasmuch as a balance of £ll 18s. 10d. was due to the treasurer. The Chairman remarked that the report on the whole showed progress, but he could not help thinking that there was very much which they could nat report at a gathering of that kind—real work done, work that would tell in time to come, in the future of those boys and girls, that they could not put into black end white. There was going on week by week that very important work —the formation of character ; and he wanted the teachers to remember that althouzli they could not in some instances report all the manifest good which they would like to, yet the work of forming, creating, and developing Christian character was certainly in progress. The progress which had taken place in Sunday school work was very marked when the somewhat short period of tneir existence was taken into account. In 1818 a Parliamentary return which was called for showed that there were at that time not half a million of people connected with Sabbath schools in England and Wales; the exact number was 477,225 In 1833 a second return showed that 1,548,890 children were in attendance at Sunday schools, being ever eleven per cent, of the entire population. An education census which was taken in 1851 gave the figures for that year as 2,407,642, or 13-3 t per cent, of the population. Since then no such authoritative returns had been pub- lished, but there could be no doubt that at the present time something like six million boys and girls attended the various Sabbath schools in the country. The popul- ation since 1851 had increased 45 per cent., whilst the attendance at Sunday schools had i:icreased 120 per ceht. ; so that he was not speaking too strongly when he said that they had made marvellous strides in the last 30 years, and he hoped that the pre,ent prattresq would be further increased as the years passed by. He trusted that the year upon which they had just entered would be to every teacher one of joy .nd prosperity.—Mr. C. H. KERRY distributed the prizes which had been awarded for punctual and regular attendance. There were in all 44 recipients, and the Committee wished it toibe explained that the fund devo'ed to the purchase of the prizes is raised separately, and has no connection with the ordinary school funds.—The interval between the speeches and prize-giving was filled by Miss Dutton, Mr. G. Guest, and the choir, ender the leadership of Mr. Fanshaw, who went through an entertaining pro- gramme comprising songs, anthems, readings, and in- strumental selections Mr. Harrison playing the accom- paniments.—Votes of thanks to the Chairman and to all who bad assisted in promoting the success of the gather- ing, brought the proceedings to a close:

THE Technical Instruction Act ducation. Technical passed last year is a disappoint- be, merit to those who believe that it is t° begin with the elementary schools. It is Putting the cart before the horse to commence with those who have left these schools; but the Ccv erument preferred to do this rather than any . berincur the reproach of doing nothing at. all ithe result is that the Act has been received with ‘l4,ditference in many parts of the country. It is rth while, however, to consider how far it may th advalityage be brought into 'operation, and Waia' in some quarters is already being done. jitles is not in high repute as a place of residence; thu-,4 is due to its leading manufacturers to say that e wtoe,clauheoatwiotilemselves zealous in matters relating The question of Technical Education vra Pul3li3ly referred to the other weak, and there ope i evidence of a desire to bring the new Act into raton i a;3, one form or another. Last week the 11:1'T, s'euncil of St. Helen 9 broached the subject, tieu e°nunittee was appointed to take the ques- reeetilllta consideration, arid report to another Conti Tile members of the Warrington Town notice -Lilltve had the Act brought under their tilos f: t, they have taken no action; they have an as the matter slide. There ia, however, Teeteiatinti in the town for the promotion of active eal _lntstruction ; it includes a number of cryin .educationists ; but they are as men in g 111 tile wilderness. At the last meet - e.g of the association, the honorary secretary, Mr. pared atiele3', read a lucid and carefully pre-1 Paper on the need for a Technical Institute.l ennarised and explained the provisions of the to•A'et, and referred to what is being done in other ' wns• Tho paper was so valuable and pertinent rthat we are pleased to 'see that it has been re- , inted and issued in pamphlet form. It is to be hoped it will be widely distributed ; that it will be has good seed sown, and that in due time there will , a a goodly harvest. It has been resolved, it should " riQted, "That immediate stops be taken to establish a and it Technical Institute for Warrington ; " i 8 understood that this is to be accomplished " primarily by voluntary effort." It may be that, when a fairly large sum has been subs cribed, the Town Council will exercise the power which the

Act confers by voting a grant in aid, which can- not, bye-the-bye, at the outside, exceed one penny in the pound. It is rather unfortunate ,for the scheme that it is projected at a time when War- rington is under obligation to incur considerable expense by tl e promotion of a bill in Parlia- ment, and when, under that bill, it is sought to increase the Library rate from one penny to two- pence in the pound. It seems to us that it blocks the way, in some measure, to ask for more for the Library and Museum than is absolutely necessary. An advance in the Library rate from a id. to lid. would possibly leave the ratepayers in no humour for supporting, some time hence, a proposal to vote something from the rates in aid of technical educa- tion. There is such a thing as grasping at too much and losing all.

THE word "betterment" is more " Betterment." generally in use in America than it is in this country; but Englishmen will become familiar with it if-the London Cotinty Council succeed in their endeavour to obtain the sanction of Parliament to the principle of charging a portion of the cost of public improvements upon those who most benefit by them. So far as London is concerned, it is of great importance that such a principle should be recognised before the Council proceed with the vast changes which they are likely to efiect. It would be altogether inequitable if hundreds of thousands of pounds of the ratepayers' money were spent in widening streets and making new thoroughfares, and not a penny of it could be recovered from those who most profited by the improvements. It is no doubt true that hitherto owners of land—and especially town land—have benefited enormously by improvements which have been effected at the cost of the public. The "unearned increment" has gone into their pockets, and they have "waxed fat and kicked." But kick- ing of another kind has commenced—kicking against the privileges of the few when they result in injustice to the many; arid this demand for payment for "betterment" is a case in point. It is a matter of courie to say that if the prin- ciple be admitted into an Act of Parliament for the metropolis, it will soon be applied throughout the country. This, in the end, will mean that a portion of the wealth which ' has flowed from" betterment" into the pockets of landlords will find its way into the public purse. For instance, it has been suggested that a street should be made in Warrington by cutting through frop Bridge-st. to Winmarleigh-st. There can , be no question that it would be a great improve- ment ; but the cost would be great, and that con- sideration, for the present, blocks the way. It ' cannot be gainsaid that if the proposed no/street 1 wQra made, land which is at present back land woulcibec,,onid i'zont land, and would thereby be increased in value. Tbe 9YRIM of thQ 1111/4 would I i soon fitd that it IRS bettered ; and what is to- , 1 'quired is ,that in such a case they should be I called urn to compensate the Corporation for the . " betteraent," and thus help to pay for the cost of the improvement. The new departure is undoubt- edly founded upon justice; but that is not equiva- lent to saying it will immediately be recognised ' by Parliament. The landedinterest is overpower- .1 ingly represented in the House of Commons; and 1 it is an interest which never neglects its interests. , Still, as the principle is a just one, ratepayers and taxpayers m t force it to the front; and they I 'must keep p 1 ging away until it finds a plage on the statute beok.

'SHE members of the Warrington " A Funny Episode." • Town Council were, on Tuesday, again occupied with the question whether Councillor H. ROBERTS Or Councillor BOLTON should be vice-chairman of the Town Hall and Baths Comnittee. Councillor ROBERTS was appointed to the cost on the death of Alderman JOHN PIERPOINT ; but Councillor BOLTON, itching for the honour, coatrivod to get himself substi- tuted at the annual re-appointment of Committees in November. The rule is to re-appoint chairman and vice-chairman, ualess some good reason can be assigned for supercession. ,But there was none to assign in the case of Councillor ROBERTS, for it was admitted that, whilst he occupied the post of vice- chairman, he did his daty ably and courteously. So the Council, at its sleeting in December, de- clined to confirm Councillor BOLTON'S appointment, referring the minute back by a. majority of sixteen votes to seven. The Coramittee have since recon- sidered the matter, and, by the casting vote of the Mayor, held to the appointment of Councillor Bourne-. Hence the further discussion on Tuesday, which resulted in the Conacil again declining to confirm the appointment—this time by 14 votes 'to 9. it should be mentioned that Councillor ROBERTS was, in consequence of indisposition, absent from the meeting on fuesday, and from the meeting at which he was originally superseded. Councillor PIERFOIXT enliveted the Council pro- ceedings, much to the enjoyment of everyone present except Councillor Dormow, by telling how in the first instance—that is when the vice-chairmanship first became vacant—the rival claimants settled who should have the post by "tossing for it." Alderman HARRISON would have it that this " funny episode" took place on another occasion altogether," but Alderman HARRISON is altogether Wrong- Coun- cillor BOLTON, however, spun the fateful coin, and Councillor BOLTON lost. Happily there was no policeman with his eye on the little game, or both the aspirants for honours might have been "run in" for playing at pitch and toss. Councillor BOLTON having lost, was certainly not happy; and when he saw his rival sitting in the coveted seat, he felt as HAMAN felt when he saw" tIORDECAI the Jew sitting at the King's gate." There is honour, it is said, amongst thieves; but where is the honour when Town Councillors toss fur honours, for all the difficulty has arisen through Councillor BOLTON seeking "to go behind that very historic toss ? " Such conduct is un-English, and it is because it is un-English that the majoritY of the members of the Town Council refuse to confirm Councillor BoLrox's subsequent appointment. And they are right in doing so, for" fair play is a jewel."
" TEE GEOLOGY OF E.'T. HELENS AND NETGOBC"F"

HOOD. A meeting of the Liverpool Geological Association, was held in the Liverpool Free Library, on Mt:m(lM' evening, Mr. A.Norman Tate, F.G.S., &C., president, in the chair. A paper, was read by the Rev. Samuel Gaaking, 8.A., F.G.S., on "The geolo.BY of St. Helens and neighbourhood." Startingl with the oldest rocks of the district, the author described successively all the formations whieh were known to occur 111 the area dealt with. The three divisions Of the coal measures naturally claimed most atten- tion, their physical characters and fossil conteats ' being somewhat minutely treated of. The paper was illustrated by a series of fossil plants found at St. Helens, some of which represented new and rare opecies of ferns. all from the cabinet of the lecturer. A diflcussion followed, and the :proceedings closed with a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Gasking for his paper. EMIARATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston' Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner " Office, by Cunard, Guion, American, and other -lines.-- John Walker, agent, "Examiner" Office, Dewsekst., Warriagton.—Advt.

The Government have an idea that they can save something by running mail coaches between Man- chester and Liverpool; hence the advertisement for three-horse coaches to run from city to city six nights a week. " Poaching days and coaching ways" has a pleasant zing with it; but, if there is to be a genuine revival, it must be accompanied by midnight attacks, "Stand and deliver! Your money or your life I"—and other cheerful things.

Mr. James Henderson has been appointed Superintendent Inspector of Factories for Lan- cashire, in succession to Mr. R. W. Coles, resigned. We have known Mr. Henderson for many years. He is at present stationed at Glasgow; but he has had large experience in London and at Blackburn. He is a model servant of the State; iust, kindly capable, and industrious. This appointment is a compliment to Lancashire as well as to Mr. Hen- derson.

Mr. Spurgeon, who is at Mentone, writes :77" I have the gout in one foot, but personally I feel so well,"and am in such fine spirit, that Ido not mind. ,My voice is better, but there is no music in it ; in fact., it is more representative of the 'croaking of frogs." This sounds bad for future preaching.. Mr. Spurgeon is far from being well, but it is to be hoped he will not "croak"• just yet.

How will Mr. Goschen dispose of the surplus which he is sure to have at the end of the financial year? Lords Salisbury has as good as said that it will be applied in making education free; but some of the Tories of the , old school do not like the prospect; they would prefer a reduction in the income tax. Now, if the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer can do both, he willioein a happy position; and it is just plssiblQ that the money will run to it." '

At the annual tea meeting in connection with Grappenhall Parish Church, Canon Greenall said they might feel Proud of the Church, as " judging from the font and corbels, it dated back to the year 1120." But apart from the question of antiquity, who is there that does not like the Jook of church and, vilhige? Thu a charming picture- picture as yet Unspoiled by the hideous jerry builder. Grappenhall is the delight of painter and photographer, and long may it remain so!

M tht 'St. Helens Town Hall, on Thursday Joseph Smith an elderly man, was charged with being drunk. He said he was an old soldier, and as he caine through Rainford, on Wednesday, some people gave him what they called soda water, but which they afterwards said was champagne. As his tale resulted in his being discharged, it must be conceded that he played the "old soldier" to perfection. Champagne to tramps! He ought to have added that it was accompanied with lobster salad.

Sir Lyon Playfair. writing in the "Speaker," says "the acceptance by Lord Randolrli Churchill of the Eight Hours Bill undoubtedly makes it a question of party politics." Since then, another prominent Tory, Lord Dunraven, has addressed the Tories of Liverpool, and he, too, shows himself in favour of the movement for reducing the hours of labour. But what says Lord Salisbury? The Tories are in office • if they mean anything, let them show signs of doing something. Faith witk- out works is dead.

There is a strong feeling amongst dog owners against the muzzling order, and especially as an exception is made in favour of dogs for hunting purposes. The experiment, too, to be fair, and successful, should operate at the same time throughout the kingdom. Here is an epigram on the subject, which has appeared in a Liverpool eontemporary If some dogs have gond mad, what then? For doubtless it's a fact ; But you don't muzzle all the men Because a few are cracked.

Not Home Rule for Ireland only, but Home Rule all round—that is the way in which events are marching, and it i 4 the right way. Scotland and Wales are in touch on the question. It is proposed to hold a conference on the subject on the 28th inst., at which there will be representa- tives of England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales. Four Home Rule Parliaments and one Imperial Parliament will relieve the over-weighted legisla- tive machine; and we shall then get something done without so much friction, and without so mush delay. \

Who is to be the nest Tory leader in the House of Commons? Mr. Balfour has. been in the run- ning since Lord R. Churchill bolted ; but it would seem that he is to be passed over. According to the "World," an arrangement has been made whereby Mr. Smith" will remain responsible for the conduct of business and the management of the House; but Mr. Goschen will on many occa- sions relieve him, and take charge of the business of the Commons." It would be odd, wouldn't it, if Mr. Chamberlafif& "Skeleton of the Feast" should become the figurehead of the House of Commons ?

Sir Edward Clarke has been joining in the chorus, which is being sung by the Tories, as to the peaceful condition ~ef Ireland. He does not say how much this is ilue to faith in a 'future of Homo Rule ; but as a member of the Ministry he ought to say when Ireland is to have local self-govern- ment. "Equal laws and self-government as soon as there is peace that was the pledge, and now that there is peace the nation requires to see some sign of a redemption of the pledge. A little longer, ana*the pledge will be" forfeited."

It is interesting to note the inveterate stupidity of the Tories in making a set at Mr. Gladstone because of alleged Russian atrocities in Siberia-- just as if he—not Lord Salisbury, were at present at the Foreign Office. The Liberal leader is wise, and his critics are not. Replying to a correspon- dent,Mr.Gladstone says :—" Your letter appears to me perfectly fair, anti I will explain, though under I much pressure of business, that my practice has been to wait for authentic statements, or until opportunity has been given for denial or explana- tion, before presuming to take steps." And a very good practice, too. •

A R:unoorn correspondent sends us 'what purports to be an American epitaph, but we suspect he is" having his little joke." We give the first verse, with the introduction, as follows: "In the Jewish burial ground, San Francisco, may be seen _the following epitaph, written presumably on a former priest, who .fell upon evil ways, and became the glare of the wine cup : Lev. 10 c. 8 S.; 9 v. Here lies poor Aaron. decompoeing lies, And closed for ever his large saucer eyes; In life a High Priest,—lie did sacrifice A dozen sparrows—then went to Paradise."

The rumour that the Duke of Westminster was the anonymous donor of the £lOO,OOO for a con- valescent home to he established in connection with the London hospitals is contradicted. "Saying wrung to get right" doesn't always come right. The speculators must try again.

The "Speaker "—the new Liberal paper after the style of the "Spectator "—has made a good beginning. ,There is no lack of variety in the con- tents of the fust number, and some of the signed articles are as brilliant as they are solid. It is to be hoped the new venture will live, and thrive, and do the State some service.

The "Star" strys--" The Queen wishes it to be known that she cannot open Parliament on account of rheumatism. We are sorry to hear it, but her Majesty never thought it necessary to assign any reason for her neglect to open Parliament, when Mr. Gladstone happened to be First Minister of the Crown."

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.

The nest concert is announced to take place on the 17th February, when Cowen's "Rose Maiden" will be performed. Rehearsals take place on Thursday evening in:each week. REDUCTION OF SCHOOL FEES AT RITSCORN.

Through the medium of the pulpits at the various Wesleyan chapels in Runcorn, on Sunday, the managers of Brunswick Wesleyan Day Schools announced a very substantial reduction in the school fees charged to chil- dren, bringing them to a level with those charged in other similar establishments. MR. HEMET FITTON OF RUNCORN. This gentleman, who recently occupied the position of headina.ster at the Brunswick Wesleyan Schools, has been appointed sketch artist to the " MancheSter Examiner and Times." It will be remembered that Mr. Fitton ably illustrated Mr. Nickson's "History of Runcorn," and that some time ago he hada series of sketches in the "English Illustrated Magazine." DEATH OF MR. W. BANKS, J.P., OF WESTON. Mr. William Banks, JP. , of Weston House, Runcorn, died at his residence on Wednesday morning, at the age of 58 years. For some time the deceased gentleman had been suffering from a complication of diseases, and had been under the care of Dr. Robinson, Mr. Banks belonged to an old Cheshire family and for about 20 years had been on the commission of the peace for the Runcora Petty Sessional Division.

RUNCORN' POLICE COURT. On Thursday. before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley, William McCue was charged with begging in Church-st. on the previous night. The offence was proved and it was stated that prisoner was very abusive to pe..ons who refused his demands. He had Is. 4.0. in coppers in his possession. He was sen- tenced to 14 days' hard labour, and his hawker's license was impounded.—Louisa Bbstock, was 5110 ss. and costs for being drunk aild disorderly. ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALE now on. J. &W. Dutton, Sankey-st., Wurrlngton.—Adet. WIDNES CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

A meeting Of Vie-rti- e-int,ers of this club Was held, on Tuesday evening, Mr. R. Lewis in the chair;for the pur- pose of considering the question of registering the club under the Companies Acts, so as to secure liabilities to the members. After an explanation by the Chairman, it was unanimously resolved without discussion to regis- ter the club, and the liability of each member was fixed at Ws. The Committee was instructed to carry the rmolution into effect at once. WESLEYAN TRACT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.

At the invitation of the Rev. U. Burson, the president, the members of this society have been entertained to tea in the Lecture room at Brunswick school. Afterwards the president delivered an appropriate speech, and Mr. Charles Garnett gave an address on the work of tract distribution. The hon. secretaries gave an encouraging account of the labours of the Runcorn society, and the financial statement of the /1011. treasurer (Mr. E. Taylor) was of a very satisfactory character: '

NEW YEAR'S GIFT 'TO A RUNCORN CHAPEL. . Mrs. - Walton. of LeinsMr Gardens, Runcorn, has contributed a New Year's gift of £lO to the funds oaf Bethesda Congregational Chapel. Under the auspices of the Oxford University Exten- sion Scheme, a second series of lectures will be com- menced, on Tuesday evening, in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on the subject of " Physiography." Although the first series were not a financial success, yet th6:2,l''',,iletit an able disquisitions of the Rev. W. div.head: COAL STEALING_ AT_RGNCORN.
div.p: COAL STEALING_ AT_RGNCORN.

Before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. James Handley, at the Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Joseph Taylor, cap- tain of the flat Annie, John Popplewell, mate, William Beech and James Green, labourers, were !charged with having on the 7th inst., stolen a ton of coal belonging to Messrs. Simpson, Davies and Co., salt and coal mer- chants. it appeared that Taylor had taken a cargo of coal from Worsley collieries to a steamer at Liverpool, and on the 7th inst. P.C. Woodrow saw the prisoners unloading coal from the flat at Top Locks. Taylor and Beech were wheeling the coal in barrows to a house in Dodd's Court—'Taylor said he was allowed to take a little coal but not so much as he had done. The other prisoners were only assisting him believing they were doing no harin.—As the prosecutors did n):. p:ess the case Taylor who had been in custody two days, was sentenced to one day's imprisonment. Toe (,t ter pri- soners were discharged. Mr. Brundrit said it had ht.." 03 the custom formany years for boatmen to take coal, although they had no right to do so, and it was a grow- ing evil that must be stopped. The masters were quite ,auniuch to blame as the men, as they had not put a stop to the practice long ago. The practice would not be allowed in future.

THE WEST LANCASWIRE JUNIOR FOIMALL Cup. The victory of Widnes St. Mary's Football Club in the junior cup competition, was celebrated on Friday night last week, by a dinner at Anderson's Hotel. About 40 members and friends were present, and after dinner, Mr. F. T. Parry, secretary of the West Lancashire Union, took the chair, He remarked that the best team won, and it gave hitn great pleasure to present the Cup to Widnes St. Mary's.—Mr. R. Wilcock proposed success to the club, and observed, in a eulogistic speech, that St. Mary's Club had now passed from the junior ranks, and he hoped they would become a prominent team.--Dr. Richards (vice-chairman) supported the toast, which was honoured with eathusiasm, and Mr. Gould, the sec- tary, responded. He said the season, so far, had been a most successful one, as they had not lost a single match, and they had never been in a better financial position. The team had played 16 matches, won 14, and drawn 2. In these matches they had scored 19 goals, 36 tries, and 61 minors, against their opponents one goal, five tries, and six minors. (Apnlause.) Success to the "West Lancashire League" was proposed by Mr. Wailing, and responded to by Mr. Parry and Mr. Wilcock. The pro- ceedings were enlivened with songs, and a most enjoy- able evening was spent. In further eelebration of their victory, the team and a number of friends were enter- tained to dinner on Tuesday eVening, by Mr. Chapman, of the Grosvenor Hotel. The customary toasts were proposed and a convivial evening was spent. ANNUAL CLEAP.ANCIE SALE now on. J. & W. Dutton, Sankey-st., Worrington.—Adrt. Mn. T. Ews, M.P., who has beeri seriously ill at Luxor, is recovering, and is expected to be able to return from ,Egypt in about a week.

div.head: CANNIBALISM AT WIDNES. _
div.p: CANNIBALISM AT WIDNES. _

At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, George Scanlan, of 44, Midwood-St., was charged with having on Saturday night, unlawfully wounded Thomas Haverty a youth 16 years of age. It appeared that a general row was taking place in the house and the pri- soner was fighting with Haverty's father. Haverty- interfered, and the prisoner seized him anfi bit him severely on the cheek. Brood poisoning had since set in and Dr. Hutchinson said the youth was in a serious con- diti9ll P. 114 t 9 attend the court, The prisoner was remanded for A week. moo.? 124.lizisia . .

An excellent entertainment was given in the Girls' School, on Monday, by the members 01St. Mary's Church Choir. The first piece on the programme was anadapta,- don from the" Pickwick Papers" of the famous trial scene, Bardell v. Pickwick, all the characters well sus- taining their parts. This was followed by a sketch, "The Genius, which afforded math amusement. The concluding portion o the programme was : a Christy Minstrel perforrnance,khe songs being well sung and the choruses harmoniously rendered. There was a large and appreciative audience. On the following evening' Lady Brooke distributed the Sunday school prizes to those scholars who had attended most regularly and punctu- ally during the year 1839. After the distribution the choir kindly repeated the Christy Minstrel performance of the night before, to the delight and amusement of the children. An enjoyable evening was brought to close by each scholar being presented:with a bun.

Sr. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHLIRCH. • The removal by death of Mrs. Joseph Hobson, l'Ork- st., has been an inexpresSible loss to this Church. The deceased lady took an active interest.in. the various branches of labour connected with St. Jolne4 and won the profoundest respect sf all with whom she came in contact. On Sunday evening, the Rev. J. Pulford Williams preached her funeral sermon. There was a large congregation. The rev, gentleman took for his text Psalm cxvi. 15. "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." He made mention of the • solemn fact that, although the Runcorn cemetery had only been opened for 30 years, upwards of 8,400 had been borne within its portals. ' •In the course of his sermon, which was listened to with rapt attention, he said that what made the death of the saint really precious to God, was the life of the saint. Some people were particularly anxious to know the last words of those leaving this world. He (the preacher) gave little heed to last words; the question of paramount imports ance is not how we die, but how we live. At the close of the sermon the choir rendered with much pathos "The Christian's Good-night." . ANNUAL CLEARANCE SALE now on. J. S:, W. Dutton, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.' The monthly meeting was held, on Wednesday. Mr. H. Coleburn presided, and there were present Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. J. Handley, W. S. Taylor, W. Whittaker. W. Mellor, W. Littler, and W. F. Salkeld , (secretary). The interments for the year have beers 287 as compared with 259 in the previous year, increase 28. The fees received had been £244 13s. 60., compared with £245 13s. ed., decrease, 1. The Finance Committee reported that during December £6O had been received from the overseers on general account and £6O on Sinking Fund account. The sum of £9 Bs. 4d. had been paid to Lea and Sons for new stoves for the Cemetery Chapels.—The report was adepted.—Mr. Handley said the total amount of mortgages on the C•finetery wai £5,800, some portion running until 1895. The Board could pay off £450 in March, £30.0 in December, £lOO in 1891. £lOO in 1892 and considerable sums in 1893. 'the question for the consideration of the Board was whether these should be paid as they fell due.—Mr. Littler said it was very probable %hat at no distant date that Board would be dissolved and he asked was it wise to accu- mulate a sum by means of a Sinking Fund, for the District Council to disburse in any way they thought proper. Would it not be better to hand over the debt of the Cemetery after reducing that debt as fir as they could--Mr. Mellor: To closethe Sinking Fund account entirely.—Mr. Littler: And pay off these mortgages as they become due.—On the proposition of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mi. Mellor, a former resolution as to the accummu!ation of a Sinking Fund was rescinded, and on the proposition of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Mellor, it was decided to pay off the mortgages as they fell due, and that the Sinking Fund be applied for the purpose. The evidence of identification in the ease 'of Nugent, who has served twa terms of penal servitude, was very weak, but he had penned an anneal to the magistrate in which he pleaded guilty to haveen lll'id'o everything t Ane then thane, although he had no recollectionfohrotwhe m. istahap-e pesd. coatinned : ''have been a wild. youth, sir, b 33 le 1 1) and have been guilty of soma foolish crimes I but, your siiina worship,etea.m h.,uv ahas have t,Ycel ens tvi oce don could tined rlrdBo to atone far the past ; I i have been to sea as a sailor and as a stoker. After coming out of hospital in Liverpool in- curable, and suffering from heart disease, 1 took my wife and child by the hand and • sang on the streets of my native land for a, honest living, and without staih on my name at alll came to Runcorn. SUICIDE IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.

The body of a gentleman which was found in a London and North-western express train from Liver- pool on arrival in Manchester, on Tuesday after- noon shortly before four o'clock, has been identified as that of Mr. Samuel `. Cheetham, formerly a merchant trading on the West of Africa, and latterly residing in Manchester. A series of heavy trade losses had produced a state of mental and physical depression. On Tuesday morning the deceased left Manchester for Liverpool in order to see the captain of a West African boat, and enter- ing a second-class compartment alone he shot him- self in the forehead, and had been dead some time on the arrival of the train in Manchester. He has two sons who are officers in the mercantile marine. FILTERS.—J. S. Garland, ironmonger, Bridge-street, War- rington.—Advt.

div.head: CHEMICAL LABourns' UNION.
div.p: THE CHEMICAL LABourns' UNION.

A meeting of the members of the recently formed Chemical Labourers Union for St. Helens and dis- trict, was held in Mr. Pletcher' coachhouse, Bicker- on Sunday afternoon. There was a good attendance, and Mr. P. J. King, the organiser, gave an address. He read over the suggested rules for the manageme.nt of the Union which, he said, he had named "The Chemical Workers' Union Of Great Britain and Ireland." He remarked that. he did not mean to cease operating until he had every chemical yard in the Kingdom organised as he had them organised in St. ,Helens. He spoke hopefully of the results of the Union,and-said he was convinced that the chemical slave would no longer be compelled to labour as he had been in the past. He spoke at some length as to the hours of labour and urged the men to rise unitedly,determined to crush those who had oppiessed them so long in the past. div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

- A man named Geo. Barnett, of 19, Pleasant-st., was brought before Mr. H. Gaskell jun., at Widnes Police Court, an Wedneaday, charged with having attempted to commit suicide. About nine o'clock on Tuesday night, Barnett spread a piece of bread with some " salve " and commenced to eat it, remarking to his wife that that was the last bread he , would ever eat. In alarm she ran from the house and ' returned with P.C. Moores, who took possession of a por- tion of the bread, and conveyed the prisoner to the police station. —Dr. Hutchinson NY'2,5, ,alleci in, and an emetic was adutinistered to the prisoner. The doctor then examined the bread, and he informed the magistrate that it was covered with a preparation known as ' " troopers' ointment," which contained Mercury and other deadly poisons and there was quite sufficient on the bread to kill a man.--In answer to the usual ques- tions the prisoner said he had done it before and he would du it again. He was remanded in custody until Monday.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The laq meeting 9f tii;Tn-eiii-beT;Oi-i6 old Board was held at the Town Hall, an Tuesday evening. Mr. James Pritchard presided, and there werc pre- sent the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. F. A. Lake, T. Handley, S. C. Beckett and G. Moss (clerk). 4

div.head: RETROSPECT.
div.p: A RETROSPECT.

The Clerk said he had not prepared a triennial report because it would only be a repetition of previous annual reports.—Mr. Lake: Better have annual reports if only for the sake of keeping the new Board Up to the mark. (Laughter).—The Clerk then read the annual report, which stated that during the year ended 31st December there were served by the visitors 5,158 warning notices; preceding year 3,022 ; increase 2.134 ; parents sum- moned before thci Committee 558 ; preceding year 493; increase 55 ; prosecutions before magistrates 122; pre- ceding year 131, decrease 9 ; average number of child- ren on the rolls 3,330, preceding year 3,230 ; increase 100; average atendance 2,685 ; preceding yea' 2,602; increase 83; percentage of average attendance as com- pared with the number on the rolls 81 ; preceding year 81. It would be observed that while the number of parents brought before the Committee showed an in- crease, the number of prosecutions showed a decrease. This illustrated the policy of the Board, which was to do all that could be done by moral suasion before send- ing parents to the Police Court. The percentage of attendance for the first nine months of the year was 82, but . the subsequent epidemic of sickness reduced it to 81 for the whole year, being the &um` as last year. The per centage for England and Wales was 7712. Neighbouring towns raised a per centage of 83 to 85, but these have the benefit of Coun- cils of Education which distribute rewards for regular attendance It would also be remembered that in Run- corn they had te deal with the bad attendance of canal boat children. Without this class the attendance would be one per cent. better than it was. A Committee of the Board of Guardians continues to meet fortnightly in the School Board offices, for the purpose of receiving appli- cations by poor parents for payment of ‘school fees. No children had been sent to industrial schools during the past year.—The Chairman moved the adoption of the report. At the same time:he should have been glad if the Clerk had prepared a summary of the work done by the Board during the past three years; it would only have been fair to the members who were retiring. The Chair- man referred to the very satisfactory census taken by " the Board in 1888, when there were only 67 children ' found who ought to have been on the rolls, and all the children in the school district were accounted for with the exception of fifteen. With regard to the Atten- dance Committee, during the past three Tears the work of the visitors had been re-organised, and been made thoroughly efficient. The Board had adopted moral suasion rather than summoning parents to appear before the magistrates, and the effect had been ' that the average attendance had increased from 74 per cent to 81 per cent, during their period of office. The Board had changed the character of Greenwav-road schools, with the result that the average attendance, which was 233 when they came into office, was at the ' present time 448, showing an increase of 215 children. The school fees three years ago amounted to £l3B, last year 1223, increase £B7 ; the Government grant had also risen from £2OB to £357 ; increase £149. The schools were somewhat burdensome to the ratepayers, hut now they were in such a state of efficiency that they were almost self-sustaining. There was only £24 taken out of the rates in support of the deficiency for the schools last year. And this had been done while at the same time the fees at Greenway-road and Mill Brow schools were.lower than in any other elementary school in the town.—Mr. Lake seconded the motion.—Dr. McDougal supported the motioo, and endorsed the Chairman's re- marks, stating that the Denominatinal Schools had , benefited very considerably from the efficient working during the past three years. The transfermation at Greenway-road School was carried out without grievance of any description, and the reflections made at the recent election were made in ignorance of the facts. The work of the Board was only of an administrative character,limited, by Act of Parliament, and by the Code, and any inter- ference with Denominational Schools on the part of that Board would in his judgment be an abuse of the privileges of the Board. During the past three years the members had discharged their duties in a fair and creditable man- m r and as far as possible without intrenching upon the privileges or prerogatives of any other school managers. —The report as adopted and ordered to be printed. VOTES OF THANES. Mr. Lake proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for his services during the past three years, and referred to his kindness and courtesy in terms of appreciation No seven men, he said, had pulled together with a more friendly spirit, and with a greater desire to benefit the town and the ratepayers at large, than the members of that Board had done, and he said "good bye" with the best wishes for he future welfare of the members who were continuing.—Mr. Beckett seconded the proposition, which was cordially supported by Mr. Handley, Dr. Gastaldi, and Dr. McDougall, and the Clerk read the following letter from Mr. Edwin Imison "Dear sir, I regret that I am unable to attend the School Board meeting to-night, as I should have been glad to join with others in expressing our appreciation of the courtesy and I tact (together with many other good qualities) with which the Chairman has presided over the Board's deliberations." The motion was carried unanimously, and regret was expressed at the sad circumstance which prevented Mr. Imison's attendance.—The Chairman on responding proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. McDougall for his services as vice-chairman, and Mr. Handley seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously, and Dr. McDougall suitably replied.
