The Clerk read the minutes of a special meeting of the Board at which it was resolved that Mr. Glanfield, of Ipswich, be appointed assistant master at Greenway-rd. Boy's School, at a salary of £5O per annum; and that Mr. B. r. Kenyon, of Ilaydock, be appointed assistant master at Greenway-rd. Boys' School, at a salary of £5O per annum.
DEATH AND FUNERAL_ OF MR. J. B. IMISON,
OF WIDNES.

• The town of Widnes It one of its prominent • citizens on Monday, • by the death of Mr. John L Birchwood Imison. pawnbroker, of Waterloo-road, . and of Castle View• House, larnworth. For about three weeks he had been suffering from an attack • of typhoid fever complicated with bronchitis and congestion of the lungs, and his condition became so precarious that, as a last resource, a Liverpool physi- cian was called into consultation with Dr. MacLennan, who was the medical man in attendance. The united. skill of these gentlemen, however, proved unavailing, and Mr. Imison breathed his last at noon on Monday, at the early age of 39 years. Although it was widely known that Mr. Imison was seriously unwell, tho announcement of his death was a sad surprise to the townspeople generally, and a feeling of universal regret prevailed. His uprightness of character, and consistent life earned for him the respect and esteem of all with whom he was brought in contact both in public and private life, and the poor people of the district have lost in him a kind and helpful friend. Any movement for the public weal had ever a warm supporter in Mr. Imison. To the church is eaily demise is especially a sad blow. He had filled the posi- tion of churchwarden for a number of years, and up to the time of his death lie was a memberof the Councils of the Parish Church, and of St. Luke's, Farnworth, was treasurer of the National schools, lay representative to the ruri-decanal conferences, and filled the important and onerous position of organist and choirmaster of St. Paul's church. He was deeply interested in education, and from his position as manager of the National schools, he gained a practical acquaintance with the requirements and working of the Education Act, which led to his appointment as a member of the School Board. While his views did not on many occasions meet with the approval of his fellow members, he was credited with acting according to his conscientious convictions,' and, as a member ofthe School Management Committee, he had considerable power in directing the policy of the Board. In politics he was a staunch Conservative, and was a prominent promoter of the new club which now adorns Victoria-road. The deceased gentleman who had been in business in Widnes for about 15 years, was a native of I Runcorn, where his father was a highly respected public ' man. He was twice married, and leaves a widow and eight children to mourn his loss.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE COMMISERATION.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE COMMISERATION.

At a meeting of the members of Widnes Conservative Club, on Tuesday night, Mr. H. Lewis, the chairman, referred to the death of Mr. Imison, and said they would have to go very far indeed to find a man who was FO thoroughly genuine and .one who was more deserving of their entire respect and esteem. Mr. Itnison was a man of whom it might with truth be said that whatsoever bis hand found to do he did it with all his might. He had been before the public of Widnes in one capacity or another for a considerable number of years; and in con- nection with that club he would be very much missed. He was induced to accept the post of honorary treasurer and in that capacity he would have been of the greatest possible use to them. He moved that this meeting of the members of the Widnes Conservative Club desires, through its chairman, to convey to Mrs. Imison an expression of its heartfelt sympathy with her in the ' terrible loss which she and her family have sustained through the death of her husband. It also desires to put on record its sense of the great loss in many ways which the town in general, and that club in particular had sustained in the same sad event.—The, resolution was seconded by Mr. Herbert White and supported by Superintendent Johnstone and carried unanimously.

THE FUNERAL. The mortal remains of the deceased gentleman were interred at Farnworth Parish Church, on Thursday after- noon, and notwithstanding that there was a very heavy, 'downpour of rain a large concourse of people assembled • to witness the performance of the last sad rites. A short service for the chief mourners was conducted in the house by the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar of Rainfoid, and then the funeral possession started in the following order :—Clergy, church, council, coffin, covered with wreaths and borne by bearers, the chief mourners, and the rear was brought up by a number of townspeople who had attended to pay respect to the memory of the departed. At the erera.nce to the church, the proces- sion was met by the choir of St. Paul's Church, attired in white surplices, who then preceded the cortege into the sacred edifice chanting the opening sentence of the burial service. After all were seated the 90th Psalm was chanted by the choir and the lesson was read by the Rev. J. Wright Williams. The Vicar then delivered an address, in which he said he could not refrain from say- ing a few words, to express his deep sense of the loss they had all sustained in the removal ef their brother from amongst them. They could all afford to spare anyone who endeavoured however humbly, to further the cause of God in their midst, and who worked for the good of his fellow-men, but that day they were conscious of no ordinary loss. They knew that their dear departed brother was no ordinary man, but one gifted with remarkable powers, with rare tact, and rarer talent—one whose self-sacrificing labour and untiring devotion in the Church of God were the marvel of all who knew him. He was not only prominent in public work, and foremost in every effort for God, and and for good, but, he was one whose personal character, whose private life, were in truest harmony with his pub- lic professions. Such lives were rare, and they might well treasure his memory. It needed no words of his to. commend to their loving sympathy the sorrowing family. They knew what John Birchwood IMISOLL was- te them—they could hardly know what he waa •in his home—the stay, the strength, the support of a deeply affectionate family circle. Their loss was great, but the family's was the greatest of all. Pray then, that He, who is the Father of the fatlicrless, and God of the widow might shield and shelter that desolate home, and defend axd reeect and encircle them in the arms of His love. The body wag then conveyed to the grave, where the Rev. G. H. St. Patrick Garrett, read the burial service, and the Rev. J. R. Jones (curate-in- charge of Farnworth), read the prayers and collects. The choir sang "Hush blessed are the dead" and "How sweet the hour of closing 'day." The chief mourners were Masters Arthur, Sydney end Harold Imison (sons), 'Mr. Edwin Imison (brother), Mr. W. Hailwood, Mr. W. J. Cunningham, Mr. A. Bridgley, Rev. NV. Flelden (cur- ate of Aston), Mr. W. Newton, Mr. R. Yearsley. The clergy present were the Rev. G. H. St. Patrick Garrett (vicar), the Rev. J. Wright William (vicar of Rainford), Rev. Hamilton Wilson (vicar of Glossop), Rev. J. R. Jones (curate-in-charge), Rev. J. Holden (Runcorn), Rev. James Leigh, Rev. .1. F. Collins, Rev. G. A. Leßert. Others in the procassion were Messrs. H. N. Wharton, F. Neil. J. Crabtree, J. Walter, Davies, R. Lewis, J. Williams, L Lilcross, J. Lord, D. J. Brookes, John Hough, Chadwick, J. Lowe, James Hough, J. Farrant, INT. Large, IV. Treacy, J. Dickson junior, J. R. Lea, R. Devonald, J. White, W. T. Husband, G. Stead, J. Treaty, J. Davies, Dr. MacLennan, Superintendent Johnstone, Inspector Keigh- ley, and others. Mr. G. H. Denby represented the School Board. Beautiful wreaths had been sent by St. Paul's . Sunday School teachers, St. Paul's choir' Mr. and Mrs. H. N. Wharton, teachers of the National School, Mrs. J. Beach, Mrs. Hunt and family, Mrs. R. W. Roberts, Mrs. J. C. Crawford, Mrs. J. Wright-Williams, Mr. J. M. Hough, Mr. J. and Mrs. Williamson, Mr. and Mrs.. Edwards, Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss M.P., and three• others, Mr. .1. The regis- ter for the year .just closed contained a total of 12,051 electors, including the duplicate registrations ren- dered necessary under the County Electors Act of 1888 ; the present register contains a total of 12.284 .or an increase of 2537 During the year .three of the polling districts have been re-arranged as follows—Northwich, which hitherto has been a large single polling district has been divided and now forms two districts named " Castle" and " Witten" respectively—the Middlewich polling district has been enlarged by adding thereto the township of Clive, which had previously formed part of the Wharton polling district. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A DRUNKARD'S REVENGE.,

A navvy named John Welby got drunk on Saturday night, and, according to particulars given to the War- rington magistrates on Monday morning, took a mean revenge against a publican who refused to serve him with liquor. He went to the Higher Seven Stars, in Bridge-st., and because his demand for drink was refused he kicked and broke one of the panels of the front door. On Monday he was charged with drunkenness, and with having wilfully damaged the door, and he was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs, in addition to the amount of the damage, 15s. VOLUNTEERS FINED.

At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday morning, time privates in the Ist V. 8., South Lancashire Regiment, named Peter Fearnley, John Brandwood, and John T. Wilcock, were each summoned for having neglected to pay a fine of 355., which they had incurred by failing to make themselves efficient. They were ordered to pay the sum in question at the rate of is. per week, or go to prison for a fortnight.—At the same sit- ting of the Court William Simister, also a private in the Volunteers, was summoned for not having paid a fine of 3s. 6d., incurred under the rules. He had failed to return his rifle to headquarters at a stated time. He was ordered to pay the fine and costs.

div.head: . ~ A CRUEL FATHER SENT TO PRISON.
div.p: . ~ A CRUEL FATHER SENT TO PRISON.

A fustian cutter, named John Webby, was brought before the magistrates on Monday, on charges of having deserted his four children, on the 6th of last August, and of having been drunk and disorderly in Chapel-court, on the 30th of July last. It was stated by Mr. Shearer, inquiry officer, that on the 6th August the four children of the prisoner were admitted to the Workhouse, their mother having been sent to prison, and their father hav- ing left the town. When the mother was released she took the youngest child out of the Workhouse, and joined her husband at Rochdale, at which place prisoner was apprehended by Constable Monoghan. Three months' imprisonment, with hard labour, was the sentence that the Bench passed on Welsby.

div.head: VINEGAR AND COCKROACHES.
div.p: VINEGAR AND COCKROACHES.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a shopkeeper named Sarah Jones, summoned Sarah Wakefield, of Catherine-st., for an assault, alleged to have been committed on New Year's Day. It appeared that Mrs. Wakefield, who was entertaining company, had, amongst other things, provided a tin of salmon to tempt the appetite of her guests. She discovered, how- ever, that she had no vinegar, and sent her little girl, with a bottle, for a" ha'porth." On The girl's return, a couple of cockroaches were found floating in the vinegar, which led to all the trouble. Mrs. Jones alleged that defendant,came to the shop, and, after having emptied thovmegar with the cockroaches, on the floor, assaulted 'her by tearing the sleeve of her dress. Mrs. Wakefield, on the other hand, asserted that complainant tried to push her out of the shop, and that the tearing of the sleeve was an accident.—The Bench, atter hearing wit- nesses, bound the defendant over to keep the peace, and ordered her to pay ss. Costs. PRISON OR THE BIRCH P—THE CHOICE OF Two Evxr.s. _ _

_ A youth of fifteen years of age, named Wm. Coyne, who lives in Scotland-road, but who has only recently come out of prison, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday, OR a charge of theft, the specific allegation against him being that he had stolen a pair of boots from the house of John Longshaw, Mill-lane, where he had been employed. The case was proved, and as it was the ninth apptarance of the prisoner the magistrates where somewhat at a loss to know what to do with him. Mr. It. Garnett, who occupied the chair, said that he did not think that he had seen a more mel- ancholy case in the Court, and he put to the prisoner the question whether he would prefer to be birched, or to go to prison. The lad, who cried, was evidently dis- tressed at the prospect of either alternative, and remarked that he did not know what to say, but the magistrates decided the matter by ordering that he should have twelve strokes with the birch rod, six on that day, and six on the next.

TEE Itrvets.—Frederick Duckett was summoned for assaulting John Moores. The latter alleged that on the 31st December he went into the " Glass Barrel" public house, Bridge-st. The defendant was there and up- braided him with insulting his brother. The complain- ant denied the aectisation,ancl was about to drink of the -whiskey he had ordered, when the defendant knocked the glass out of his hand and struck him two blows on the head, the second blow being enough to kill any man. " He had been ill two days, or he would not have .allowed any man to insult him."—The defendant said the complainant walked along the bar to him, threat- ened him, and put himself in a striking attitude. He Called John Minton, the landlord, who said he thought the affair arose through rivalry in trade. The complain- ant put himself in a menacing attitude and he (witness) thought there was to be a fight, but the defendant hap- pened to strike the complainant first. —The Bench, in consideration of the provocation he had received, fined the defendant is. and costs us. 6d. div.p: RUGBY.
RumouN A v. TUEBR-0011-- Runcorn, in miserable weather, and the visitors were defeated by one goal, four tries, to one minor.

WESTON v. RUNCORN TRUE BUTES.-011 Saturday, at Weston, and the home team won by one goal (dropped by Myers) and five minors to two minors. WARRINGTON STAR v. LOWTON IST.—This match was played at Lowton on Saturday. The visitors were poorly represented having to play 12 men. A good game xesulted in a draw. Score Warrington, Star 1 goal, 2 minors; Lowton, 1 goal (dropped), 2 minors, Walmesley scored for the twinklers, Potts improving; and Davies dropped goal for Lowton. _ _

WIDNEII. RADCLIFFE " A " TEAMS.---This match was played at Widnes on Saturday, in miserable weather. Widnes kicked off, and play was carried from one end of the field lo the other, the chemicals drawing first blood by scoring a minor. The Widnes full back put in a long. kick, and followed up. A return was made, and before he could got back to his position Ratcliffe rushed the ball over and scored a try, which was not improved upon. Several runs were made by Morris for Widnes, but he was prevented from scoring each time. At half-time the score was—Radcliffe, 1 try; Widnes, 1 minor. On changing ends Widnes had the beat of the play, and immediately registered another minor. Again they carried the ball down the field, Kenyon getting over and scoring a try, Morris making a splendid attempt at goal. Laws and Morris showed up well, both being again within an ace of scoring. Final score—Widnes, 1 try, 6 minors; Ratcliffe, .1 try. WARRINGTON 2nd V. GRANGE (BIRVINHEAD).—The only minor match of note in the Liverpool district was the one between Grange and Warrington second team, who met at Birkenhead in the return fixture of the season. The home team were pretty strongly repre- sented, but unfortunately the visitors were unable to raise their full strength. Nevertheless the game was well contested, the Grange having all their work cut out to secure victory. The Warrington men went away with a rush at the start, and Rowe scored a try, but without a resulting goal. This placed the Grange on their mettle, and after vigorous play on the part of T. and W. Jones, Eden, John Mullen, and Mitchell, the latter crossed the Warrington line. The play had barely been in progress five minutes longer ere T. Jones again scored, with a resultizil• 1V22,5i4c1E 9( tli; game was finely contested, victory findliy rosting with , Grange by one goal, one try, and five minor points, to , one try and three minors. _ _ .

WARRINGTON Y. TYLDESLEY "&" TEAMS.—This return match was played at Tyldesley on Saturday, before a moderate assemblage of spectators. Owing to the rain and the rapid thaw which had set in, the ground was in a most wretched condition, the players soon after the commencement of the game being in a pitiable condition, and anything like correct play was entirely out of the question. The first minor was conceded by Tyldesley. From the kick-out Miller took operations to neutral territory, but Howarth retaliated by a good kick, and the visiting forwards quickly had the ball near .he goal line. A capital bit of short passing, the only bit of the game, between Davies, Knowles, Boscow, and Barnes, resulted in the latter scoring a try, the place being much too difficult to improve. A mull by the visiting backs let in Tyldesley, and Warrington were in turn defenders. Ultimately the visiting forwards screwed a pack grandly, and led by Eyre and Boscow rushed down the field, the latter claiming a seemingly fair try, but a minor only was allowed. Succeeding this, Molyneux, Isherwood, and Beard were very prominent, but by the aid of a good kick by Miller play was taken to the Warrington quarters, and a minor was obtained by the home team. The drop out was well taken up by Thorniley, Holmes, and Nield, but Davies had to stop a determined. rush at midfield directly afterwards. A new ball was at this stage requisite, the former having burst through the wet. The game was now of a scrambling nature, the players having the greatest difficulty in keeping a footing, and when half-time was called the score was Warrington 0-1-2 to 0-0-1. Warrington re- started, and play for a long period was of a desultory character, until a free kick to Tyldesley was well-followed up, the ball going to touch near the visitors' lines. Some very good kicking followed between Barnes and Chadwick, and a good dribb e, started by Berry,Boscow. , and Eyre, took play well irslde the home quarters. A piece of tricky play, howev ,by Miller and Mahon in a line-out enabled Tyldesle, to reach their opponents' I territory. A lot of very uninteresting play ensued, scrim- mage succeeding scrimmage, and at this stage War- rington were decidedly having all the worst of the game. At length Berry, Beard, and Tfiorniley relieved the pres- sure, and by the aid of a good kick by Holmes the ball was taken to the home line where a capital bit of play by Chadwick brought the ball out of danger. A free kick to Warrington gained a lot of ground, but this was imme- diately lost by the visiting backs taking innumerable flykicks, and a. minor had to be conceded to the home team to avert disaster. The drop out was finely returned by Miller, and Tyldesley almost scored, but Sampson eventually getting possessiop, raced past several oppo- nents, finally winding up with a splendid kick to touch at mid-field. Subsequently Eyre and Beard had a clear field, but kicking too hard a minor only was obtained. Sampson smartly rettirned the drop out, and Holmes almost scored, time being called Warrington were left winners of a most uninteresting game by one try, three minors, to two minors. Teams : —Warrington: Sampson, back ; Lally, Boscow, and Barnes, three-quarters; Davies and Knowles, half backs; Nield, Holmes, Berry, Eyre, Isherwood, Beard, ThornileY, Molvneaux, and Howarth, forwards. Tyldesley : Smith, back ; Mannion, Chadwick, and Buckley, three-quarters. Miller and Hilton half backs; Fearnley, Hindley, Mahon Greenough, Smith, Bleackley, Allen, Heeley, and Kirk- man, forwards.

div.head: WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY LEAGUE.
div.p: WEST LANCASHIRE RUGBY LEAGUE.
WARRINGTON v. TYLDESLEY.

Barnes and Antrobus were absentees from the War- rington team which met Tyldesley on the Wilderspool ground, on Saturday, the former not having recovered from the injury received in the Dewsbury match. It was pleasing to note that Littlewood made his re-appear ance. On the other side, Priestley and Kenyon were away, so that the teams now met on an equal footing. As this was a Leakue match, great interest was taken in it, but the severe frost of the earlier portion of the week, and the rapid thaw arid rainfall of Friday evening, rendered the going very heavy, but despite this, a capital game was witnessed.

There would be nearly 4,000 people present when Berry started towards the railway goal, midfield at once becoming the scene of operations. A combined rush of the Warrington forwards upset the defence of Tyldesley, and the visitors at ouce assumed defensive tactics. Shaw was to the fore with a neat kickto the half-way flag, and Berry following up the movement, Webster was at fault, and the Warrington 25 was reached. It was left to the home forwards to relieve, and this they did with credit, for brushing aside the visiting front rank like chaff before the wind, they were not satisfied until the oval had found a resting place near the pavilion goal. J. Lawless essayed to get in, the greasy state of the ball alone pre- venting him. Shaw again came in for notice with a tackle of Webster near his goal, and only the exception- ally brilliant play of the Warrington forwards prevented Tyldeslev from negotiating a tangible score. E. Dillon and Frank Turner came away together and dribbled to the half-way flag, a smart save by A. Fearnley staying their progress. 'Smart dribbling tactics of Warrington were the chief items of notice, and passing was out of question; indeed, the backs on the Warrington side had very little work, whilst on the opposing side Shaw and his men were continually busy in staving off the strong rushes and effactive dribbling powers of the Warring- ton forwards. To relieve the monotony of the dribbling, the home three-quarters essayed some neat passing, but the *final one to P. R. Lawless was inaccurate, and by this aid the visitors were afforded slight relief. The home front van would not be denied, and again a smart dribbling movement, in which Littlewood, W. Dillon, Povey, arid Fair. Turner were the chief opera- tors, took the game near the Tyldesley goer:Tate kicked across, and a race for the oval took place, and Frank Turner being first up grounded, but he failed to augment the point. Urged on by this success Warrington pressed the game on the Tyldesley line, Evans and Massey dis- tinguishing themselves by smart running and kicking. Littlewood proved what/ a smart player he is by drib- ' bling from the half way to the line, and from a pack

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 11, 1890. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 11, 1890. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

Ihere, Bate, Evans, and P. R. Lawless passed grandly, the last-named punting over the line, Priestly being com- pelled to touch down. The fine play of ,Berry on the re- start alone prevented Warrington from augmenting their score. Massey put in some grand work hn. the right wing, and although Berry' put 'in A gobd pass to A: Fearnley, Lawless collared his opponent before he could get away. Tyldesley were penalized here, but the ball was got safely away, and no score being made half-time was called—Warrington one try one minor, Tyldesley nil. On resuming operations a flying visit was at once paid to the Warrington end, and from some loose play. Shaw received possession, and in the first minute dropped a goal. This unexpected success of the visitors called forth loud cheers from their supporters, but they only held the lead for a very brief period, for on there-start, the fine combinatioa which existed in the Warrington forwards told its tale, and sweeping down in a body, the game was taken to the Tyldesley line. Bate tried hard to get on, but on bell* tackled he started a dribble, which was eagerly snapped up by Frank Turner, and the second try was scored. Again the kick at goal failed. Massey put in some grand work immediately on the drop out, and although Berry got away, the fleetness of foot of Lawless upset all calculations and the Tyldesley half back was pulled up ere the centre flag was reached. Some wild passing by the visiting backs again let Warrington in, and eventually priestly saved. Massey again responded to the drop out, and relief was brought about by the aid of a free kick. Bate passed wide to P. R. Lawless, but the greasy state of the oval prevented a certain score; but the " wirepullers" took up the running and compelled another minor. Warrington still attacked, and Evans passed to Massey, who made a gallant bid to score. Even- tually, another minor followed, but from a wide pass Lawless failed to pick up, but dribbling on he went through the opposite defence and wound up a grand effert by scoring near the corner flag. A feeble attempt was made at goal. The homesters would not be denied, and grand work by Evans, J. Lawless, Nevins, and Massey took the game to the railway end, where Bate threw to Nevans, who in turn transferred to Massey, and in the last minute of the game that player smartly lowered the Tyldesley citadel with a, clever drop. "No side" was called, the final score reading—Warrington 1-3-5, Tyldesley 1-0-0. The game all through was brimful of interest, and it was, indeed, a capital exhibition, considering the ad- verse circumstances under which it was played. The Tyldesley men Were outclassed at every branch of the game,and the chief credit of the victory was undoubedly due to the brilliant display of the Warrington forwards. Rarely has such form been shown on this enclosure, and it is to be hoped that Saturday's display will not be a mere flash in the pan, but that there will be consistency in all their future matches. Of the backs, Massey and Bate were the pick. Teams : Ararrington: Webster, back; P. R. Lawless, Evans, and Massey, three-quarters; Bate and J. Law- less, half backs, Fair. Turner (captain), Frank Turner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, W. Nevins, W. Bandies, R. Little- wood, W. Povey, and T. Donohue, forwards. Tyldes- ley: G. Priestley, back; A. Fearnley, Shaw, and J. Fearnley, three-quarters; Berryand Hanson, halfbacks; Woodward, Smith, Sutcliffe, Forbes, Ward. Battersby, Yates, Harrison, and Derbyshire, forwards.
FOOTBALL—Hi:TM:3' Y, wr` 'to-day's games :—Warrington v. Widnes at Widnes; Runcorn v. Broughton Rangers at Broughton; St. Helens v. Morecambe at St. Helens ; st. Helens Recs. v Barrow at St. Helens.

• • The Yorkshire team had to put in all it knew en Sat- urday to beat the men of Somerset. This inter-county game was played at Wellington and resulted in a win. tor the visitors by one try to nil. tip till about ten minutes of the end there was little to chose from between the teams and neither had scored, but then the the stalwart Lowrie, who always does good work for his county, saw an opening and made use of it to score the one try of the game. Somerset made the pace very hot for the next few minutes but they were successfully held at bay by the "Tykes.'

Another death from football is recorded, and this time it is that of a real player. Lieutenant Lyon, of th 3 Somerset Regibient, stationed at Aldershot, was injured during a football match at Weston-super-Mare on Mon- day in last week and died on Sunday without having recovered consciousness. The deceased who was 22 years of age, was the eldest, son of the Rev. Gilbert Lyon, rector of Blagdon, Somerset. The cause of death was concussion of the brain.

According to the fixture card Runcorn should have journeyed to Wakefield, on Saturday, to meet the Trini- tarians, but, that match having been cancelled, the Cheshire haen arranged to visit Burton-on-Trent. for the second time this season. On the former occasion the ground was so hard that play was impracticable, and instead of a game, the " wearers of the green" who are great favourites with the Burton folk were entertained to a sumptuous banquet and a concert. On Friday night Mr. Longshaw, the Runcorn secretary, received a tele- gram telling him not to send a team as the ground was as hard as iron through the frost. Fate seems against Burton attempting to regain the laurels they lost on their visit to Runcorn.

The following is an abstract of matches played in the West Lancashire Rugby League competition and the points scored by each League club up to date, viz. --- Points Matches Won Lost Drawn scored Wigan 8 7 0 1 15 Tyldesley Aspull 5 3 1 1 7 WaMien 7 3 3 1 7 Leigh , Warrington Wictnes St. Helens 3 0 3 0 0

In spite of the bad state into which the ground had been put by the severe frost and sudden thaw, there was a fine game between Warrington and Tyldesley on Satur- day. The soft ground and slippery ball was against good passing, but the forwards on bioth sides played well. The borne forwards in particular, hive scarcely ever been seen to better advantage. They dribbled and passed with their feet like Associationists, with the result that at times Tyldesley seemed completely bamboozled, and hardly knew how to stop the combined rushes. If the " Wirepullers " forwards keep in last Saturday's form for the rest of the season the" Warrington dribble" will be famous.

The weak point of both teams was to be found at full back. Webster, who had charge of the Warrington line, has hardly ever been seen to worse advantage, while for Tyldesley, Priestley bungled badly on several occasions. This much must be said for. both custodians, that the state of both the ground and the ball were against " safe " play. Frank Turner and Littlewood were two of the most conspicuous of the Warrington forwards. Turner, who is to be credited with two of the tries, is playing in splendid form at present.

div.head: TURKISH 'MISRULE.
div.p: TURKISH 'MISRULE.

In a letter on Turkish misrule in Crete and Asia Minor. the Earl of Carnarvon addresses something like a warning to Lord Salisbury. The Conservative ex- Colonial Secretary says that if Turkey "persists in her blind policy of administering her affairs in 1890 as they might have been in 1790 . . . she will assuredly find that she has alienated all title to British, and even European sympathy." His lordship intimates that the Prime Minister will be put to the question when Parlia- ment meets.

div.head: ENGLAND THREATEM PORTUGAL.
div.p: ENGLAND THREATEM PORTUGAL.

The "Times" Lisbon correspondent says, a further note from Lord Salisbury respecting Major Serpa Pinto's campaign was delivered there on Monday morning. Although the exact contents of the note are unknown, it is thought to be of a c9mininatory nature, threatening an immediate diplomatic rupture, and even going be- yond this, unless Portugal gives, without evasion or equivocation of any kind, an undertaking to give satis- faction for Major Serpa Pinto's attack on the Makololo, and for his ignoring of, if not outrage upon, the British flag in the district of Shire. RECALL OF MAJOR SERPA PINTO.

A Berlin correspondent says he is informed on trust- worthy authority that the Portuguese Government, which has already recalled Major Serpa, Pinto, intends, if it has not already done so, to disavow the Major's acts and give the necessary satisfaction to England, for the insults offered to the British flag in Africa. It is not unlikely that a friendly hint has been thrown out from Berlin, not to push matters rashly to extremities, as it is no secret that the Portuguese Government has always been extremely accommodating and ready to meet the wishes of Germany in East Africa.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AND THE O'SHEA CASE
div.p: MR. PARNELL AND THE O'SHEA CASE

A report has been going the round of the papers that at a meeting of the Ennis Board ef Guardians on Wednes- day, the subjoined letter was read from Mr. Parnell in reply to a resolution respecting the O'Shea divorce suit. It has since been found that the letter is a hoax, but we print it as published

" TO the Clerk of the Ennis Union. " House of Commons Library, January 6. " Dear sir,—Referring to your resolution about me, I venture to suggest that this charge, in so far as it con- cerns public bodies, may be more advantageously met with the deadly weapon of silent contempt. I have noticed in effect a similar communication of Alderman J. Dundon, of Limerick, who in a moment of pardonable weakness brought forward a similar metion, though for the life of me I can't fathom why Gainey, of the same Board, opposed it. I have been to that gentleman guide, philosopher, and friend, at A time when he bad, little hope of occupying a seat at the Council. While lam convinced that my honour is ever safe in the bands of the staunch burgesses of Ennis, I intend at the same time utterly and entirely declining all culpability, for, in the words of Stone'tvall Jackson, there are times when the insignificance of the accusser is lost in the ingratitude of the accusation.—Believe me, &c.,
CHARLES S. PARNELL.
Captain O'Shea's legal advisers have commenced the issue of subpcenas in connection with the divorce pro- ceedinvs O'Shea v. O'Shea and Parnell. - .

It is understood that Messrs Lewis and Lewis on Thursday entered an appearance on behalf of Mr. Parnell and Mrs. O'Shea in the action for divorce. ' The' Freeman's Journal" on Thursday states that Captain O'Shea has filed an affidavit denying certain imputations, and praying that an attachment for con- tempt may be issued against the printer and publisher of the Freeman" for making them. THE ACTION AGAINST THE "TIMES." Ihe Middlesex special jury lists for the Hilary sittings, which begin on Saturday next, have been published, and among the cases which are set down for hearing in the first week is the action by Mr. Parnell against the "Times" for publication of the Pigott letters. The only question for the jury is the amount of damages, the defendants having paid into court 40s. as sufficient to meet the plaintiff's claim. Sir C. Russell will represent Mr. Parnell, and Sir Henry James will be the leading counsel for the " Times."

div.head: HOW TO DEFEAT OUR ENEMIES.
div.p: HOW TO DEFEAT OUR ENEMIES.

Among the most prominent and most dreadful. like so many generals in the attacking forces of the great enemy of mankind—death—may be mentioned the following: —lndigestion, liver complaint, nervous disorders, and chest affections, while the different symptoms by which these dis- eases manifest themselves may be regarded as so many sub- officers in the ranks of the enemy. When anyone of these attacks us we may be certain that some of the others are close at hand. Hence other parts of the body suffer from the derangement of the stomach. The same may be said of the.liver. It is the great filter of the body to purify the blood. Any disorder In either of these organs—the stomach, or the liver, acts injuriously upon the nervous sys- tem, and makes the sufferer over sensitive and irritable, causing sleeplessness, loss of memory, palpitation. and other painful forms of disease. In our climate, affections of the chest are very prevalent in the form of colds, coughs, bronchitis, asthma, etc. By the insidious attacks of these various enemies of man, thousands are annually laid low and brought to a premature grave. div.head: CRICRIU.
div.p: CRICRIU.

At the annual meeting:Orti;"-forkshire Cricket Club on Tuesday, Mr. Ellison, the president, made some very striking observations on one of the causes which led to the collapse of the county team last year. He said, that some of the professionals had been induced to take drink by "so called supporters of cricket," and their position had in consequence been seriously affected, whilst the interests of the county had also suffered largely. :He protested against the practice of "standing drinks" to players.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

Mr. J. Wright, formerly a well-known athlete in the Widnes district, has been successful in winning the Junior Individual Cross Country Championship of Scot- land, and he has been awarded a splendid gold badge. The distance travelled was seven mhos. His brother George, who is also a member of the Clydesdale Harriers, holds the championship of the Dunbartonshire section of the club.

div.head: MRS. MAYBRICK IN PRISON.
div.p: MRS. MAYBRICK IN PRISON.

The Baroness Rogues Mrs. Maybrick's mother, denies the report that she found her daughter atWoking convict prison in the best of health and spirits when she visited her a few weeks ago. Her daughter, she says, looked deadly pale and very weak. She laid her head against the wall of the cell and wept bitterly. Both were so affected that the time allowed for the interview—twenty minutes—did not suffice for an explanation of family matters.

div.head: FIRE AT A POOll-LAW SCHOOL
div.p: THE FIRE AT A POOll-LAW SCHOOL
FIINEAAL OF THE VICTIMS.

The 26 children who perished in the Forest Gate fire on New Year's morning, were buried on Monday afternoon at West Ram Cemetery, in the presence a a large con- course of relatives and spectators. The scene was most distressing. The 26 coffins, covered with blue cloth and surmounted by a quantity of floral wreaths and crosses, were first taken in hearses to St. James's Church. followed by relatives in carriages and on foot. Canon Scott and the Rev. Dr. Cholson officiated at an impressive service during which many persons wept. After the service the coffins were replaced in the hearses and conveyed to the cemetery, where the deceased were interred in seven graves. Canon Scott delivered an appropriate discourse. and darkness set in before !he crowd left the cemetery. Among those who attended were several officers who represented the Local Government Board, and Mr. Theobald, M.P. for the Romford Division. Among the followers also were 20 boys and 20 girls from the schools, I who acted as choristers. -

div.head: HOME RULE FOR SCOTLAND AND WALES.
div.p: HOME RULE FOR SCOTLAND AND WALES.

At the meeting of the Executive of the South Wales Liberal Federation. on Tuesday, at Mid-Neath, (irla- morganshire, a letter was read from Mr. IVaddie, secre- tary of the Scottish Home Rule Association, suggesting that a conference should be held in Londonthis month, at which representatives of England, Irelanil, Scotland, and Wales could exchange opinions, chiefly on these points—How could Home Rule on federal bases be best promoted, and how could Scotland and Wales work together to best promote their mutuel interests ? There was, he said, a proposal to found a.Federal League for the four countries, with its headquarters in London and to which the four Home Rule Associations could be affi- liated. Such an association could speak authoritatively to the party. The Executive agreed to take part in the conference, and the 28th instant was suggested as a con- venient date. It was stated that invitations would be sent to Welsh Liberal members of Parliament, and that Welshmen residing in London would also have adequate representation at the conference.

div.head: LABOUR QUESTION.
div.p: THE LABOUR QUESTION.

Lord Dunraven was the guest on Monday evening at a house dinner of the members of the Conservative Club. Responding to the toast of his health, he described the Separatists as the vivisectionist party, who wished to rend the United Kingdom limb from limb while it was still instinct with life. Dealing with labour questions, he said he knew of nothing contrary to the sound prin- ciples of social science or political economy which would prevent a curtailment or the hours of labour. He advocate] such a curtailment in the interests first of all of the workingmen themselves, next in the interests of the Conservative party, because it was desirable that workingmen should have leisure to thoroughly under- stand political questions, and also in the interests of the wellbeing of the empire, seeing that workingmen had votes on which-depended the policy of the future. His Lordship spoke in favour of boards of conciliation for the discussion of disputes, and of a department of labour for the collection of information with regard to labour. He thought that, in a number of instances capital might bear the increased cost of produttion which would be brought about by the curtailment of hours. This cur- tailment would not, he felt, be attended with disastrous effects to such of our industries as were in fierce com- petition with those of foreign countries.

div.head: ANOTHER MUMMY LAID BARE.
div.p: ANOTHER MUMMY LAID BARE.

Mr. Wallis Bridge, of the British Museum, hag just returned from Wales, where he has been engaged in the interesting occupation of stripping a famous mummy that was presented a short time ago to the Royal In- stitution of South Wales by Major Grenfell. The mum- my turned out to be all that was left of one who held high rank in the Egyptian temple at Panopolis nearly a thousand years before the Christian era.

div.head: WOOD GREEN MURDER.
div.p: THE WOOD GREEN MURDER.

The inquest was held at Wood Green, London, on Saturday, on Harold Ernest Whorlow, aged'eight years, who was murdered by his mother on New Year's morn- ing. According to the evidence of the husband and a medical man, Mrs. Whorlow was mentally deranged. A verdict of wilful murder was returned, and Mrs. Whor- low was committed for trial. The jury added that the husband should have taken precautions to protect the children.

div.head: EXECUTION AT WARWICK.
div.p: EXECUTION AT WARWICK.

Charles Lister Higginbotham (63) was hanged at Warwick gaol, on Tuesday morning, for murdering Winifred Whittaker Philips, aged 76, with whom he lodged, in Birmmgham. Berry was the executioner. The culprit had no friends, and no one took the slightest in- terest in his fate, to which he appeared indifferent. He had attempted suicide by cutting his throat, and when the: drop fell the wound re-opened, blood gushing from it into the gallows pit. Death ensued immediately.

div.head: MRS. GLADSTONE'S SEVENTY-EIGHTH
div.p: MRS. GLADSTONE'S SEVENTY-EIGHTH
BIRTHDAY.

Mrs. Catherine Gladstone, wife of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, M.P., celebrated her seventy-eighth birtli- day at Hawarden, on Monday, she having been born on the Bth January, 1812. Mrs. Gladstone is thus a little more than two years her distinguished husband's junior. There was no formal celebration at Hawarden, but Mrs. Gladstone was the recipient of a large number ofcon- gratulations. Tuesday was the 38th anniversary of the birth of Mr. Herbert J. Gladstone, M.P., the fourth an youngest son of Mr. and Md. Gladstone. The member for Leeds was born on the 7th January, 1854.

div.head: YACHTING DISASTER. TEN LIVES LOST.
div.p: YACHTING DISASTER. TEN LIVES LOST.

A telegram received in Madrid from Cadiz announces that an English yacht, named the Inva, bound from Portsmouth to Gibraltar, was wrecked on the Aceiteras Rocks, on the night of the 3rd inst. The vessel sank within a few minutes after she struck, and it is feared that all on board perished, with the exception of four men. Eight of the crew jumped into the lifeboat, which, however, capsized, all the occupants being drowned. The four survivors saved themselves in another boat. Up to the present ten bodies have been recovered. The Governor of the province of Cadiz has directed that all aid possible be given to the shipwrecked men.

div.head: RAILWAY FATALITY NEAR
div.p: RAILWAY FATALITY NEAR
HALEWOOD.

On Saturday night, between five and six o'clock, a shocking discovery was made on the Cheshire Lines Railway, between Hough-green and Hale- wood Station. Thomas Willis, the driver of the 5.15 train from Widnes to Liverpool, reported. toi the Halewood stationmaster that he felt a jerk be- tween the above stations as if the engine had passed over something. A porter was despatched to make an examination, and some distance from the station came across the body of a man fright- fully shattered lying in the four-foot. The left side of the face and head were ranch smashed, and the left arm was severed from the body and lay in the six-foot, both legs also being broken. The remains, which were not identified, were conveyed to the Hammer and Pincers public-house to await an in- quest. Deceased was apparently about 35 years of age, sft. sin, high, and is thought to be a foreigner. He had dark brown hair, sandy moustache and whiskers of about.a month's growth, and wore a drab brown overcoat with dogskin collar and cuffs.
WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN
ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of this Association was held on Wednesday evening, at the Rooms in Bold-st. In the absence of the President, Mr. J. C. Parr, who was unable to be present in consequence of his hiving caught a chill, the chair was occupied by Mr. S. B. Stringer, who called upon the Secretary, Mr. T. Wallington, to read the

ANNITAL REPORT. In his report Mr. Wallington remarked by way of pre- face that he had dealt in a detailed manner not long ago with the affairs of the Association, so that the present report need only be a short one. It was very satisfactory to note that the membership was still increasing, and that promises were coming in almost daily of new ad- herents to the Association. The membership roll now numbered 130. The attendance at the Rooms was not so good as they should like it t..) be, for he thought that the average would not exceed an attendance of twelve per evening, reckoning from the time the rooms were opened some months ago. The programme for the winter had so far been fairly successful, and the attend- ances at the various meetings had been encouraging. The Snorthand Class now had about twelve members. The Rible Class was in active operation, and had a membership of about N. The members of the class would like to see a greater number joining, and they strongly recom•nended those not already associated with the class to become so. Owing to unavoidable circum- stnces, the Writing Class had not been commenced. Sunday evening services were still held, but the attend- ance wai only small. The Cricket,. Club formed in the summer had been a great success.' In conclusion the report said it was to be hoped that the remainder of the winter session would be attended with even greater s'ue- cess than the part already pissed. He hoped that the rest of the winter session would show a marked improve- ment in all branches. Be believed that could be accomplished if they were all united in their aims; and he trusted that at no distant date they would be able to see the standard of the Association floating over a building worthy of the name, and worthy of the town.

Mr. J. BARLOW, who submitted the report of the Cricket Club, said that seven matches had been played, of which six were won and one was lost. They had now over thirty members on the books, and there was a balance in hand of about 20s.—Mr. BROWN then gave

the report of the Shorthand Class, which is progressing satisfactorily with about a dozen members, and Mr. A. Honnocxs, the treasurer, announced that the receipts had been £66 18s. 9d., and the expenditure £64 165., leaving a small balance in hand, which had been increased by money received since the statement was made out.
These various reports were adopted on the proposition of Mr. J. JEWKES, seconded by Mr. J. CRITCHLU.
ELECTION OF OFFICER-S.

Mr. H. HORDEN, iii proposing the re-election of Mr. J. C. Parr as president of the Association, referred to that gentleman's invaluable services, which, he said, were unanimously appreciated. The resolution, which also conveyed to Mr. Parr the thanks of the Association, was seconded by Mr. T. WALLINGTON, and carried unani- mously.

The' vice-presidents for last year were re-appointed, and, on the motion of Mr. W. B. BAILEY, seconded by Mr. l'unicE, the following additional vice-presidents Were elected :—Messrs. J. Burgess, J. Crosfield, R. W. Francomb, J. Greening, C. Lister, F. Monks, T. Morris, J. C. Ridgway, and the Rev. W. Graham. The Treasurer, Mr. T. llorrocks, was re-elected on the motion of Mr. Jorms.

The following gentlemen were elected to compose the committee •:—Messrs. H. florden, H. E. Garnett, T. Wallington, W. H. Butler,J. Horton, W. H. Bayley, A. E. Horden, S. B. Stringer, James Critchley, H. J. West- brook, J. Shaw Green, J. P. Jones, T. C. London, J. Allen, G. Walker, J. T. rattison, H. H. Dutton, R. Wyllie, E. Jewkes, W. Parsons, T. Prince.

div.head: ALTERATIONS OF RULES.
div.p: ALTERATIONS OF RULES.

Rule No. 8 was amended to read as follows :—" That the affairs of the Association be conducted by a Corn, mittee:of Management consisting of four persons, to be chosen by the trustees for the time being from their own number, ami sixteen members to be chosen by a Majority of the members of the Association present a 2, a meeting to be convened for that purpose, and all such members to retire annually; but tts be eligible fos re- election." Rule 12 was amended as follows, viz "That the annual subscription of members or associates be 55.; but youths under 17 years of age to be cNiorged only 3s. ed. per annum."

div.p: SUFFOCATED, ON A STEAMER..

ALLEGED LIBEL ON MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE.

The Press Association learns that an action is pending between Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., and Colonel George Bruce Malleson. The latter is alleged to be the London correspondent of the "Morning Post" news- paper, published at Allahabad, India, and in course of his letters to have reflected upon Mr. Herbert Gladstone's moral character. The text of the alleged libel is set out in the statement of claim which has been filed by Messrs. Lewis and Lewis, solicitors to the Plaintiff, and is to the effect that another cause calibre had been" hushed up," that a lady was in the case' that the complainant was a Gladstonian supporter in the North, who had been re- warded by Mr. W. E. Glad=tone with a baronetage, and that Mr. H. Gladstone was a 6' chip of ()the old block." The pending action is one of alleged libel arising out of these statements, and it is rumoured that when the case comes on for hearing the ex-Premier will be one of tht witnesses. Unless some arrangement is come to, it is expected that the case will be heard in a fortnight or so.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.
A Kanturk telegram states that on Sunday morning the house of a family named Smith, who are unpopular in the district, was partially shattered by an explosion of gunpowder.

div.head: SIX PERSONS DROWNED.
div.p: SIX PERSONS DROWNED.

A telegram from Skibbereen states :—lt is reported here that six men have been drowned while endeavour- ing to save some of the wreckage from the steam-r Queensmore, in Dunmann's Bay. The boat's oars have been washed ashore. THE MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A FARMER.

Three men named M'Carthy,. Kelly. and Hurley, have been arrested near Bantry, charged with causing the death of a farmer, named Crawley, who was found dead on the roadside seven weeks ago. The coroner's jury returned an open verdict, but the remains have since been exhumed owing to information received by the police.

div.head: SEVERE STORM.
div.p: SEVERE STORM.

Reports from various parts of Ireland state that a storm which raged on Saturday night and Sunday morn- ing was of unusual severity. JA\ Killarney telegram states that two women, named O'Connor and Scully, as they were driving home from market, were killed by a tree being blown upon them„.

div.head: SE6RET SOCIETIES.
div.p: SE6RET SOCIETIES.

Dr. O'Callaghan, the Roman Catholic Bishop of Cork, presided on Sunday at the annual meeting of the Cork Young Men's Society, and made a pronouncement on the existence of a Secret Society for revolutionary purposes in the city. He asked those who were connected wtih this Secret Society to give it up; and to join with all Ireland in their efforts to save the country. There was no greater danger for Ireland than that there should be a Secret Society working in their midst for other objects. SENTENCES AT MUNSTER ASSIZES.

The business- n-lih-e-14171;;;iit; Winrer TsZe. s closed with the passing of some heavy sentences. Robert Han- lon, who fired a revolver in a strugglewith an emergency man named Whitton, wounding him, Flanlon's own brother being shot, and mortally wounded, on the same occasion, was sentenced to twelve months' imprison- ment. Two men, named Riordin and Cronin, for attack- ing a gamekeeper's house and carrying off a gun, 18 months. The two men, Collins and Broderick, 'Who were found guilty of seizing a farmer's daughter, and cutting off her hair, were sentenced to twelve montheimprison- ment ; while Peter Cooney, for firing at Lady West- meath's gamekeeper, received five years. Antes Brien, a Kerry Moonlighter, for firing at a police patrol, also was sentenced to five years' penal servitude. A man named Donoghue, for attempting to blow up a farmer's house with dynamite, was sentenced to 15'years' penal servitude.

div.head: LONDON SCANDALS.
div.p: THE LONDON SCANDALS.

POLICE COURT PROCEEDINGS. • Artkpr Newton, solicitor; Frederick Taylor,, clerk ; and Adolphus de Gallo, interpreter, appeared on remand at Bow-st., on Monday, charged with conspiring to defeat the ends of justice in connection with the alleged offences at Cleveland-st—Algernon Ed. Allis, of Sud- bury, said he gave evidence at Marlborough-st. and the Old Bailey in September. In August, after receiving an anonymous letter, he destroyed the letters from Lord Arthur Somerset. The Brown spoken of in his evidence was Lord Arthur Somerset. Taylor told witness he wanted him to go abroad, as they did not want him to appear against you know who." Taylor said he came , from Mr. Newton. Witness gave information to Inspect- or Abberline, and afterwards met Taylor by appoint- ment, who said it was all clear. Witness, In November, joined in the information against Lord Arthur Somerset. —Cross-examined, he said he had lived some months at Cleveland-st. for committing acts,of indecency. Witness admitted that he was willing to give evidence to save himself from prosecution. He had written to Yeck,who , was afterwards convicted, to get money, but only obtained a little.--After taking further evidence, the case was adjourned. On Tuesday Charles Ernest Tiekbroom, in cross- examination, stated that when he was dismissed from the Post Office he went to Scotland-yard, and told In- spector Abberline he did not want to have anything more to do with the case, and wanted another situation. Abberline said he would speak to Hanks, another detec- tive. He spoke to flanks, but did not say that perhaps Mr. Newton would do something for him. It was sug- gested to him that he and the boy Perki-s should see somebody, and he thought it was meant that they should see Lord Arthur Somerset's father. Two constables sug- gested it. The name of one of them was Sladden. On Wednesday, the witness Perkins, recalled and further cross-examined, said that when he met DeGallo, they wenr,at once to a public-house. De Gallo mentioned about going to Australia, and gave witness and his com- panions half-a-crown each to get their dinners. Neither Newton nor De Gallo ever asked him about the Cleve- land-street case. M. Sera,phia Pollet, jobmaster, of Brussels, deposed to driving two gentlemen to,the Hotel Bordeux, and to a money changer's, and afterwards to the Northern Railway station, Brussels. A man arrived by train from Luxembourg with a boy of fourteen or fifteen. Witness recognised Mr. Newton and Mr. Taylerson as the two gent.emen, and he identified a photo of Hammond as that of the man who accompanied the boy. They after- wards left for Antwerp. Mr.- Hector Pola, of Antwerp, in the service of the Red Star Line, and Otto Von Heller, clerk, deposed to Taylerson.and another man resembling Hatnmond's photo, sailing for NevvYork, on October sth. The further hearing was again adjourned. On Thursday, George Wright gave • further evidence respecting De Gallo's interviews with him. In cross- examination he admitted having been guilty of improper acts before he knew Cleveland-at. Charles Thomas Swinscoe, a boy employed at the Post Office until July 4th, related what passed between Ds Gallo and the boys whom he wanted to go to Australia. They were to go first from Dover to Calais. The case was not concluded at the rising of the court.
DEATH OF THE DOWAGER, EMPRESS AUGUSTA.

The Dowager Empress Augusta died at Berlin at a quarter-past four o'clock on Tuesday afternoon. It became known early in the day that her Majesty's con- dition was critical,. and before noon a, ,great crowd of sympathizing citizens had gather&l. in the Unter- den Linden, reminding one strikingly- of the time when the old Emperor William lay dying. Thou- sands waited until the announcement of the end, and only then began to disperse. Her Majesty's illness has been very short, and its fatal ter- mination has caused a widespread and profound impres- sion, for it was not until Monday that the public were made aware thatthe case was a dangerous one. The Empress gave a small family:dinner on the eve of New Year's Day, and although .she retired early, she seemed to be in her ordinary health, which, however, was never robust. On Friday, her Majesty manifested symptoms of Russian influenza, and physicians were called in. They could see nothing alarming in her condition, but in view of her advance'd age enjoined the utmost pre- caution,. especially against chill. On the evening of the sam_e day, the patient became suddenly and alarm- ingly weak, and the Grand Duchess of Baden—who nursed her Royal mother from the first, as she haze upon previous occasions—telegraphed the fact to her nephew, the Emperor, who was hunting on Prince HateEeldt's estate. His Majesty did not arrive in Berlin until past one o'clock on Sunday morning, and he at once drove to the Palace, to learn that, although the-patient was very feverishethere was no cause it* immediate alarm. Dr. Verlten, whom the Emperor questioned, said her Majesty was certainly suffering L from the influenza,ree but the disease was pursui ( normal course, and his only anxiety was the possibility ef serious bronchial trouble, of which there were already .some signs. Her Majesty became more feverish after the Emperor left, and could obtain little rest, owltig to fits of coughing and difficulty of breathing. Laterite the day the patient improved somewhat, -but theee•was another relapse towards evening, and from that time the physicians began to lose hope. In the middle of the niPdtdt the patient had a severe struggle fo-a-breath,. and eat the members ,of the family at present in Berlin., inched/rig the Emperor and Empress, were summoned to the Ack chamber. At eight o'clock on Tuesday morn* ho. Majesty's condition was pronounced hopeless, and ee 3 quarter-past four she passed peacefully away. The Emprese Augusta will be buried by the.side a/the Etoperor William in the mausoleum at Chreelottenburg. jaer death is universally lamented. She eras the roost popular and beloved of German Princesses,and number- less charity institutions will eternalize her name. Her death does away with all the court festivity projects which had been planned on a large scale, The Emperor of Austria will attend the funeral. - .

The Court mourning, which would have terminated on the 23rd inst., hag been prolonged to sth February for the late Empress Augusta. In Germany the Court has been ordered into mourning for three months, and a Period of six week's general mourning has been j.nsti- tuted. The Queen has telegraphed her sympathy/to the German Emperor. Her Majesty and the Vrittee 4f. Waled Will be represented at the funeral,
