WARRINGTON WORKSHOPS FOR Tili BLIND. Sir.—Will you allow me, through your columns, to thank the subscribers to the fund for establishing a Library for the Blind in the Moon Type, for their gener- ous help. The subscriptions have been expended in the purchase of books, which will form the nucleus of a Library which I hope may be extended in future and prove a blessing to many.—Yours &c., WILLIAM WHITE, Teacher of the Blind. Battersby-lane, January 9th, 1890.

div.head: MUZZLING DOGS.
div.p: MUZZLING DOGS.

Sir,—l quite agree with your remarks on the question -ef muzzling dogs ; but, as there are some who disapprove of the order for muzzling dogs, I shall feel obliged if you will permit me to state that I think the muzzling orders are a step in the right direction. During the year 1887 rabies was prevalent in Lancashire, and many deaths occurred from hydrophobia, and since there have been occasional deaths from that disease. Not twelve months ago, ten persons were bitten in St. Helens by one rabid dog, and if they had not gone to Paris to be treated by M. Pasteur, it is very probable some of them would have suffered the horrors of hydrophobia. Unmuzzled dogs in a public place are often an annoyance and danger, and the public ought to be protected from them. Our dog laws as they have hitherto existed seem to be the relic of a semi-barbarous time. Nearly every man and woman may call to mind many cases where great injustice has arisen from them. In our consideration for dogs human justice ought not to be disregarded, and to permit animals to interfere with human comfort and happiness is to encourage a perverted state of mind and feeling.-- Yours, &c., Warrington, January 7th, 1890.
S. KENYON.
THE NEWTON DIVISION.

--- Sir,—BeiLg a constant reader of your valuable paper I have thought that, amid the bustle and preparation for a general election which we hear so much of in other parts of the country, the Newton Division is dead so far as practical work goes. I suppose at the last moment sornekentlernan,of whom:we know little or nothing, will be pushed to the front, and a lot of noise made for a week or so. As a Liberal elector, I should like to know who are our leaders in the Newton Division? It is high time, if we are to oust Mr. Legh from misrepresenting us any longer, to be up and doing. Our grand old leader is showing the way, Let the Newton electors thoroughly comprehend the objects of the Liberal party ; they will then rally round its stan- dard and carry it to victory. The Borough of St. Helens has set us a fine example; they have a candidate ready at any moment to join issue with Mr. Seton Karr, and be is expounding his views in a way which is winning the confidence of the work- ing-men of St. Helens. Why cannot Mr. LeF.di be op- posed by a man who is able, and who will have time to explain what his real opinions are? I am convinced that Toryism is only another name for ignorance so far as working-men are concerned. Is there no man or body of men, who will lead the way? Haydock, F;rles- town, and the surrounding districts, are capital fields for sowing the seeds of true Liberalism. Working-men are awakening to the fact, that the party of progress in several matters is the Liberal party. My plea is that they may be:further strengthened in these views by a more active policy common at headquarters. Yours respectfully,

div.head: LIBERAL ELECTOR.
div.p: LIBERAL ELECTOR.

"THE BLACK SPOTS OF WARRINGTON." Sir,—You have discharged a public duty by publishing 'the articles on "The Black Spots of Warrington." It was high time the matter was taken up, and I Shink it ought not to be allowed to rest until efficient measures have been taken to remedy the evil. What is needed is a strong expression of public opinion. Without such an .expression, lam afraid things will be allowed to go on much as usual, for if only a portion of what I have heard is true, the hint thrown out by Mr. Yonge in his letter last week is only too well fonnded. I cannot of my own knowledge speak as to the actual truth of what I have been told, namely, that certain members of the Town Council are the greatest sinners in respect ot unsanitary property; that in the case of at least one well-known member of that body notice has been served upon him many months ago—but that the notice is simply ignored. To say the least, such conduct is dis- graceful and is a bad example to other property

Owners. I happen to be a tenant of a house and shoo in Leonard-st., and I should like to point out the abomin- able state of that and several other streets in the imme- diate neighbourhood. These streets are like miniature canals in the present weather—being full of water and puddles of mud from end to end. Several deaths have occurredin Leonard-St. lately from fever, and no wonder, considering the disgraceful condition of the streets and back passages. At times one has to exercise no little ingenuity to cross from one side of the street to the other. The property owners ought to be compelled to pave the streets, and not allow them ts remain in their present shameful state. This neighbourhood ought to be a very pleasant and a very healthy one—being open and breezy and the streets wide and lined with nice comfortable looking working-class houses. If the streets and back passages were in proper condition, I don't think there would be a nicer working-class locality in the town. Every house is Occupied, and there cannot be the slightest reason for not completing the streets. I hope others will speak out on this matter, and we may then expect good results.—Yours truly, JOHN GANDY.

div.head: MUSEUM RATING.
div.p: THE MUSEUM RATING.

- Sir,—Be mild; as you are strong be merciful. When Jupiter tonans fulminates from the Olympian heights of an editorial chair mere mortals can only tremble and be abashed. And this is not a state of mind conducive to a " free and full discussion." Have pity then for mortal weakness and moderate your wrath. You demand either an explanation or an apology. I hasten, sir, to give you both! I hope they may prove satisfactory, and so avert bloodshed. You will remember how the man apologised for saving a certain person was "not fit to carry garbage to a bear" by retracting the words, and saying that "he was fit to carry karbage to a bear." Would this kind of an apology meet your views? You object to my protesting against " wilful perversion of fact." Here it appears the word wilful is at fault. I withdraw it. You could not help it; hence it was not wilful. You may for aught I know have been possessed at the time. It was not you—it was the " other fellow" who did it. No not a lie—merely a "diplomatic sup- pression of the truth." And now for an explanation. Have you, sir, "for- gotten that quite recently" you embodied the Chair- man's letter to the Mayor in your editorial, and that that letter contaitied the same statement as to the unanimity of the Committee on this question. Why did you let this pass without comment and quarrel with it now ? Do you wish to quarrel with the minute book? Whilst I . am in the inquisitive mood may I ask why that unfortu- nate member—the Only One—who voted one way and thought another, as per "Examiner," why should this unfortunate be so often pilloried in your columns for this one lapse from virtue? Fie, Mr. Editor, call you this backing (A your friends? Then, sir, I have to thank you for so persistently dragging into undue prominence the unimportant fact of my being a member of the Museum Committee. This with voUr usual good taste. But still the fact remains. And 'I do not see why my being a member of this Committee should abrogate my rights as a ratepayer, or prevent me from appealing to my fellow-ratepayers, to do what I think right in this matter. It is quite open to the ratepayers, through their elected Council, to , propose and effect the entire abolition of the Museum. Library, and Art Gallery, if they thought proper. The effect Of this on the rates is evident ; the wisdom of such a measure is quite another thing. We are all agreed as ' to the necessity of keeping up this beneficynt institu- tion. The only question is, How? Shall it be ineffi- ciently on id. as now, deficiently on 10., or efficiently on 2d., as the Committee recommend? Again, it must 'always be remembered in this connexion, that however much agreed the Town Council and the Museum Corn- -'inittee might be as to the necessity- of levying a 2d. rate for this purpose, it could not be done at present. It is :merely to render it possible that it is proposed to insert :this clause in the bill. The actual power a spending
still rests with the Town Council, and they can veto any exorbitant expenditure recommended by the Committee. —I am, sir, sincerely yours, _
JOHN PEERS.

Penketh, January Bth, 1890. P.S.—Don't forget to put this letters in small pica, and your own remarks in capitals. In this way you may make some capital remarks, even though you make no capital out of it. J. P.

gust SO: our correspondent knows where to borrow a good pun; one "Joe Miller" thought it " capital " when he saw it in " Hamlet " some 200 years age. Sorry we cannot oblige Mr. Peers by putting his letter in" small pica." It would be a bad precedent, seeing that" small pica" is four sizes larger than ordinary newspaper type ! Still, we can appreciate the modesty of the request. Czar "bade the Romans mark him, and write his speeches in their books." That was the old style ; the new style is—" Put my letter in small pica." We, of course, accept our correspondent's apology; it is not particularly graceful, but we can let that pass, as he is not perhaps used to going down on his knees. He offers in addition an "explanation" which, he says, was" demanded," though it was not even asked for; but we can let that pass, too, now that we are getting accustomed to the fact that Mr. Peers has a way of saying one thing when he means another. The reason why we did not comment on the Chairman's reference to the unanimity of the Committee was that we dealt solely with the points of importance. It was not until our correspondent sought to magnify a molehill into a mountain that it attracted attention. That a • Committee should be "unanimous "in asking for more money is not at all surprising; it is the usual thing. The wonder is that there was one member of the Library Committee to speak and vote in the Town Council against doubling the levy on the rates. Mr. Peers has certainly a right as a new member of the Committee to have his say, and have we not conceded it, week after week? Surely he will not be so unkind as to wish to deprive us of the right on the other side of pointing to the fact that, although three years have elapsed since the agitation for freeing the library commenced, it is cnly since he became a member of the Library Committee— two months ago—that he has found time to write on the subject. But why pursue the matter? We know our correspondent's humour. When the fit is on him, he is like the celebrated " Mr. Easy ;" he will argue a point even when there is no point in his argument.— En. Ex.]

div.head: LATEST TORY DODGE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: THE LATEST TORY DODGE AT EARLESTOWN.

Sir,—lf the unprovoked attack on two of the most respected gentlemen in Earlestown, which appeared in a Liverpool journal on Tuesday,has been prompted by the leaders or representatives of the local Conservative party, it is one of the most contemptible and dishonest actions in the history of electioneering in the district. I hope for the sake of what credit does attach to the Conserva- tive party that the local leaders will at once disavow, and that publicly, their knowledge of and complicity with those who have gone so far to attempt to injure the reputations of Mr. James Watson Emmett, and Mr. Francis Harwood. Ia the short period which has elapsed since the publication of the article there has been a general condemnation of the statements contained therein. That they are false—and maliciously false—is known to every workman employed by the Company at parlestown, and by every right thinking and honest politician in the district. Lest, however, some of your readers may think there is some foundation for the attack I will, with your permission, specify some of the most glaring untruths in the now notorious article. 1. •It is time the public knew that at Earlestown the same charges (i.e., of political intimidation, &c.), have been for years, and are now, made against Mr. J. W. Emmett, the superintendent, Mr. Francis Harwood, the works manager, and nearly all the foremen under them." This is, positively, the first public intimation of any such charges, and it is, positively, too, the first time that ever any such a thing was brought to the knowledge of either Mr. Emmett or Mr. Harwood. Hence we can only conclude that the "charges for many years," have existed only in the imagination of "Our Own Com- missioner," or of his vindictive informants! 2. "Mr. Emmett, the superintendent, makes no disguise of his political colours as an enthusiastic Gladstonian. He flaunts them whenever any political fight is going on," &c. In reply to this I can only use a now common expression to the effect that "The next time Mr. Emmett does so, will be his first." This is known to everybody except "Our Own Commissioner." Both Mr. Emmett and Mr. Harwood have carefully and studiously avoided attendance at political gatherings of any shade or colour, and if either is "an enthusiastic Gladstonian," it has not been pubiicly ascertained through " flaunting " of colours for the simple reason that there has been none. Thousands in Earlestown can tewify to this. 3. The County Council election. The reference to this matter by "dur Own Commissioner" seems to be a mass of inaccuracies all through. I have not time and you, sir, have not space at disposal, on such short notice, to go fully into them. I will briefly specify what is fact in contra-distinction to the many inaccuracies of "Our Own Commissioner." It is not correct that Mr. G. W. Rawlins (and by the bye, not Mr. C. C. Rawlins, as stated by "0. 0. C.") was nominated by the Glad- stonians. He was the nominee of the Earlestown Rate- payers' Association, of whom a hardworking and prominent Tory was then President, and that gentleman became the " agent " for Mr. T. H. Pearson, the defeated Conservative candidate. 4. Mr. Rawlins was nominated to oppose Mr. Pearson "on the purely political ticket." This is not correct ; and is evidenced by the unimpeachable fact that one of Mr. Rawlins' most prominent supporters was Mr. Benjamin B. Glover, as straightforward and honest a Conservative as there is to be found in Earlestown or Newton. This is sufficient for all purposes, but there is the additional fact that several well-known Conservatives signed the nomination papers of Mr. Rawlins. 5. Alleged canvassing by Gladstonian foremen and workers only. The insinuations in respect of this matter can be refuted by any of the workmen, either Tories or Radicals. It is almost incredible that such unfounded aspersions should be cast at the heads of the waggon- making department. It is well-known to everyone in Earlestown that Mr. Emmett and Mr. Ffarwood are above suspicion, that they would at once put their foot down, and that vigorously, on any attempt at parti- ality or to interfere with the free and unfettered rights of each individual workman. Evidently "Our Own Commissioner" must have been judging of their conduct through the lasses which have so long reflected the actions of those employers of his own particular political leanings. 6. "That no Conservative worker cares to canvass in the cottages where railway workmen live." Good old "Our Own Commissioner " ! Surely he cannot have consulted the local Tory officials, or the local managers of that party! The statement carries with it its own refutation. 7. That workmen of whose Conservatism there is no doubt, have declined to join the Tory club because it is more than they dare do. This about beats everything, and is a fitting climax to the inaccuracies which precede it. "Our Own Commissioner" actually has the imper- tinence to make that statement in face of the fact, as solid as the rock of Gibraltar, that the very caretaker of the club premises, and who with his family lives thereon, and who works hard to give it all the attrac- tion possible. is employed at the Viaduct establishment. I dare be bound to say, that during hi" many years con- nection with the works and with the club, he has never once been tampered with in any shape or form, and, that he has never received any threats or notices affect- ing the political position he occupies. His case is not the exception. but the rule. Would it have been so if "Our Own Commissioner's" statements were correct? Not quite. In conclusion, I will only add that many other inaccu- racies could be peinted out, but these are evidence of the malignity with which the attack has been made on Messrs. Emmett and Harwood. The facts speak for themselves, and should prove an interesting study for "Our Own Commissioner."—Yours, Earlestown, January 9th, 1890.
O-NK WHO KNOWS.

, A coroner's jury at Tavistock, on Wednesday night, returned a verdict of manslaughter against Alfred Davis, navvy, for causing the death of Jane Caser, an aged woman, who was brutally beaten last week.

ALLEGED MURDER OF A MOTHER-IN-LAW. Maria Brown, aged sixty-two, of Fulham Market, is reported to have been kicked to death by Elijah Snel- ling, labourer, her son-in-law, on the highway on Wed- nesday afternoon. A woman named Hardly heard shrieks, and saw Snelling close by the field where Browne's body was found. Sergeant Gooch, of Harleston, and other officers arrested Snelling the same night at Rushall. On Thursday Snelling was brought before the magistrates at Harlestou. He has a repute of being a violent man.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. That the members of I'Vidnes Conservative Club have decided to form themselves into a limited liability company, and in the event of a "smash up" each member will only be called upon for the sum of 10s.

That through the death of Mt. Imison, the Church in Widnes has lost one of its most ardent supporters and one of its most active and ardent members, and his place will not be easily filled. That universal sympathy is expressed for his bereaved wife, and fatherless ones, who are all very young.

That Runcorn School Board was dissolved on Tuesday, after three years' work, and several vale- dictory addresses were delivered. Only three of the seven retiring members will return to the Board. That the chairman showed a capital record of work accomplished during the triennial period, and the facts and figures he gave must be gratifying to the ratepayers. That Runcorn Guardians, on Tuesday, will again have served up the schoolmaster business. This is becoming a standing dish," but there is no fear of it becoming stale so long as it excites so much personal feeling.
THE TUNNEL WORKS AT CUERDLEY.

Yesterday Messrs. Cochrane and Company re- commenced operations in the Tunnel Works at Cuerdley, for the conveyance of water from the Vyrnwy Reservoir to Liverpool. The works have been stopped some time on account of the death of the head of the firm of former contractors. Much difficulty has been experienced on account of the silting of the tunnel4anl at one time several of the men had a very narrow escape. The works have been in operation about eighteen months.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 11, 1890..
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY 11, 1890..
THE PROPOSED EXTENSION OF WARRINGTON. RATEPAYERS OF PADGATE PROTEST.

ePealdaguas tees, iwn a st the ee dwaat rrt ihnegSt toon On Thursday evening a meeting of the ratepayers c kßso rI on g, ht extension c ons i er othf Bill relating to the township. Mr. W. Royston pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. J. C. Sutton (county councillor for the district), John Houghton and Thomas Bennett (overseers), J. Hut- chins, T. Yates, G. Mather, J. Hatton, T. Smith, T. Daintith, T. Lythgoe, T. Taylor, A. Taylor, A. Brime- low, and G. Brimelow (assistan, overseer). The CHAIRMAN said the object of the meeting was to consider a portion of the Bill submitted to Parliament by the Borough of Warrington, and by which it was pro- posed to include a part of the Padget° township with- in, the municipal area. If the Bill was carried as it stood it would make a great alteration in the township. It would take something like 80 acres of land, with a gross rateable value of £6OO. Of course they expected that other townships, Sankey and Orford, would take up the matter on their own account, whilst they at Padgate, would interest themselves only so far as they were concerned. His chief objection to the scheme, was that the Corporation should take so much purely agricultural land, which it was scarcely passible would become building land, for it was under the level of the river. He did not say the Corporation were not within their rights in extend- ing their limits, but if they had taken the more populous part of the district he should not have thought so much about it. He supposed the object of the Corporation was to get Warrington 50,000 inhabitants, so that it could be made a county borough. (Hear, hear.) Mr. J. C. Sumner said it must be remembered that the borough of Warrington were acting solely in their own interest, arid the/overseers of Padgate were simply doing their duty in calling the ratepayers together to look after their interests, and refuse to concede any portion of their territory, unless reasonable grounds were given for its forfeiture. If he understood aright, there was a clear and well defined boundary round their parish. (Hear; hear.) There was something in their desire to stand by an ancient boundary,—a natural one, which everybody understood. If that boundary was once disturbed, there was no knowing how it would in future be further inter- fered with. If the change proposed was made it would have the effect of creating a consider- able amount of additional work to the Over- seers of the Poor and also to the Assistant Overseer. had, he said, all along opposed the breaking up of the county, but there was no doubt that Warrington would seek to be declared a county at the earliest pos- sible moment. He thought the alterations were being made in the boundaries of places now with an eye to the formation of District Couecils. As a county borough Warrington would take the whole of their district as a separately governed one for all purposes, therefore Padgate would absolutely forfeit the land in question if the concession was once made. He was a member of the Parliamentary Committee of the County Council., and he had raised a discussion at a meeting held that day about the great cost local authorities were put to in having Government inquiries into new schemes, and the Committee had unanimously passed a resolution appointing a deputation, of which he (Mr. Sutton), was a member, to wait on the Local Government Board and urge that such expenses should be reduced as much as possible. The Committee of the Council had also considered the applications of certain boroughs to be made county boroughs, and had decided to oppose them all. The rates in the municipal borough of Warringten amounted to 3s. for the year, whilst outside the borough they were only Is. *ed. The improvement and sewers rate, in addi- tion, was 2s. 6d. in the £ per year. The Warrington Town Council had just obtained sanction to borrow some £25,000 in connection with street improvement purposes and Longford works, so that he believed the rates would be higher for the ensuing year. He would suggest that the following resolutions be pas§ed by that meeting :—" At a township and vestry meeting, duly convened, the ratepayers and inhabitants of Poulton- with-Fearnhead, in the Warrington Rural Sanitary Dis- trict unanimously protest against so mu& of the Bill submitted by the Corporation of Warrington to Parlia- ment as provides for the inclusion of a part of the town- ship in the municipal borough. They submit that no sufficient reason exists for such a disturbance of areas, and that the effect would be to do an injustice to the township and to the owners and occupiers of the land and premises proposed to. be included within the municipal area. They also submit that in view of the contemplated formation of District Councils, the probable proposal of the Corporation of Warrington to be constituted a County Borough, and of the changes that may at no distant period be effected in the systems of Local and County Government, it is undesirable and in all respects unreasonable to interfere at the present time with the local administrative areas in the way proposed by the Warrington Bill." And, further, "that the Parish overseers be asked to submit a copy of the proceedings to the Local Government Board, the Lancashire County Council, and the Warrington Union Rural Sanitary, Authority, and to request their support with a view to an amendment of the Bill in res- pect of the proposed extension of municipal boundary, and that the overseers be further empowered to take such other steps as they may deem advisable.' Mr. Hueemes said he naturally felt, as owner of the land proposed to be added to the borough, most con- cerned about the 'matter ; but he really looked upon the question as a fight between the borough and the small township of Poulton as to the possession of certain pro- perty for the increase of their rates. (Hear' hear.) He thought it would be a hardship on the township if some of their valuable rateable property was taken from them. Mr. Surroi4 said it would not be advisable to fight the matter in Parliament, but they would be quite as well off if they asked protection of the Sanitary Authority of the District, the County Council, and the Local Govern- ment Board. On the proposition of Mr. J. nonenreme, seconded by Mr. G. Mantert,the resolutions given above were carried unanimously. Mr. Server; said that Mr. Frank Roberts, C.C. for Warrington, wsis present at the County Council meeting that day, and he intimated to Mr. Roberts that he thought it right that the cottage property near the Ship Canal should be taken into the borough. But he was opposed to Orford, Sankey, and Padgate being disturbed. With re- gard to the resolutions passed that evening he would see that they secured the attentiOn of the County Council.

div.head: ILLNESS OF MR. BLECKLY.
div.p: THE ILLNESS OF MR. BLECKLY.

It is with regret that wo state that Mr. Henry Bleckly, whose health has for some time been a source of great anxiety to his friends, is now in a very serious condition. He is at his residence at Altrincham—Bell Field—where he is attended by Drs. Leach and Ransome, but little hope is enter- tained of his recovery. Several members of the family are staying with him. Mr. Bleckly who is 77 years of age, passed a restless night on Thurs- day.
ILLNESS OF SIR GILBERT GREENALL.

We regret to hear that Sir Gilbert Greenall, M P., has been confined to bed with illness, accompanied by an attack of lumbago. At his advanced age—be is over eighty—it is scarcely necessary to say that his illness is a matter of great anxiety.

div.head: INFLUENZA.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA.

We do not bear that influenza—at all events of the Russian sort—is making any serious ravages in Warrington. Postal officials throughout the country have been strangely susceptible to the much-talked- of malady, and we understand that some of the local officials have not altogether escaped; though none of them have been prevented from attending to their ordinary duties. Another suf- ferer is Mr. J. C. Parr, of Grappenhall Reyes, who wrote to the Daresbury Highway Board that he was prevented from attending their meeting, on Thurs- day, by an attack of influenza. It is also stated that a dramaticicornpany that was to have performed at the Theatre Royal, Warrington, telegraphed can- celling the engagement on account of one of the leading members of the company being " down " with the infection.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.

The report of the directors of Parr's Banking Company, Limited, to be submit ted to the proprie- tors at the next ordinary general meeting of the Company, to be held at noon on Friday the 24th inst., is as follows :—" The Director', in sub- mitting to the shareholders the annual balance sheet, certified by the auditor, have to report that the position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £21,912 6s. 11d. brought from previous actount, the net balance of pro- fits, after providing amply for all tad and doubtful debts, and-rebating the current bills at six per cent. is £136,602 3s. sd. The distribution of this sum recommended by the Directors, is as follows : Interim half-year's dividend of Th per cent., declared 26th July £42,000: dividend to be now paid of 10-1 per cent., tree of income tax, making 18 per cent, for the year £58,800; bonus of 4s. per share (one per cent.), free of income tax £5,600; to property account £5,000: balance to next account £25,202 3s. sd. ; total £136,602 3s. sd. The directors who retire at this time by rota- tion are Colonel McCorquodale, Mr_ Edward Greenall, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, M.P., Sir Thomas G. Frost, and Mr. John Thompson. Mr. Thompson does not offer himself for re-election. The other gentlemen named are eligible and are recommended for re-election. A sub- branch has been opened at Great Crosby.

div.head: PENKETtI.
div.p: PENKETtI.
THE ART CLASSF,S.
The Penketh Art Class resumed on Monday, with a fair attendance of members, after a holiday of three weeks. DAY SCHOOL ENTERTAINMENT.

Last evening an entertainment conducted by Mr James Wilson and Mrs. Wilson, was given by the children of the day school. The programme *as varied and pleasing, and consisted of musical drill, songs, recitations, Szc. There was a good attend- ance, and too much can hardly be said of the way in which the children are trained, and the cheerful- ness with which they go through their different performances. PENKETR KUTUA.L IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday evening. in connection with the above society, a meeting was held in the Day School when a paper was read by Mr. R. Posnett, entitled " Fiction.' The paper was an excellent one, and afforded great Pleasure to the members. Mr. Fitton, of Runcorn, occupied the chair. At the close several of the members engaged in an animated discussion amongst them being Mrs. It. Garnett, Messrs. C. K. Parker, Suoddy, Watson, &c.

div.head: SEWER BROKEN INTO.
div.p: A SEWER BROKEN INTO.

On Wednesd;rafternoon as the machine of Mr. Whalley, of Mill Green, Bold, was coming from the farm of Mr. Pilkington, Penketh Hall, one of the large wheels got on the sewer that had been lately filled up. The wheel immediately sank in the ground almost turning the engine over. Under the superintendence of Mr. Whalley, who happened to be present, the engine was, after some difficulty, extricated. Portunately no one was hurt.
PENRETII PENNY BANK.

The balanje--Jieet—of- this bank, the year ended 1889, shows that there is a substantial sum invested of .£971 13s. Bd., belonging to the inhabi- tants of Penketh. The managers are now giving as an encouragement to the promo non of thrift and saving—interest at the rate of .£.3 per cent They wish especially to encourage small deposits,. even as low as one penny, believing that a habit of sav- ing commenced early in life often leads to future thrift.

div.head: I. M. C. A.
div.p: THE I. M. C. A.

Last evening week the members of the above society enjoyed a social night at Bethany House. The entertainment consisted of songs, recitations, and readings, by Mr. Dow (of America) and mem- bers of the Association. Mr. Carr (of New York) addressed the young men. Refreshments were pro- vided by Mrs. Coop, whose interest in the young men of the neighbourhood has been the cause of the Association being started and carried on success- fully. The evening was thoroughly enjoyed by every member present. THE CONSERVATIVE CLUE.

The members oi the Penketh Conservative Club held their annualumeeting on Tuesday evening, Mr. Houghton in the chair. There was a fair attend- ance of members. The balance sheet of the past year was read, showing a balance at the end of the year in favour of the club. The following mem- bers were appointed officers for the ensuing year: —President. Mr. Jonas Forster; vice-presidents, Messrs. Alexander Thorpe, Thomas H. Wilson, and Peter Boardman; Committee, Messrs. Fredericr Thorpe, F. Buzza, Jesse Sampson, James Wood- ward, J. Appleton, J. Moores, Higham, T. Welsbv, A. Appleton, J. Fisher, J. Parks. Secretary and treasurer, Mr. Richard Boardman. The usual votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: WARRINGTON MEDICAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON MEDICAL ASSOCIATION.

The Warrirlgton Amalgamated Friendly Societies' Medical Association held their annual meeting on Thursday evening, at the Temperance Hotel in Sankey-st., when there were present Messrs. P. Edgar (president), J. Albinson (vice-president), W. Bibby (sec.), A. Stirrup areas), S. Dunbobbin, and W. lrolmea. (trustees), W. Barlow, J. Caldwell. J. Burgess, J.Hill, T. Wadsworth, I'. Langley. W. Boyle and others. The association now has 1.,938 lodge members, and 1,740 dispensary members, making a total of SA7B, and is worth £374 ss. 11d.

REPORTS. The 12th report of the Committee stated that the work of the association continued to he carried on in a very satisfactory manner, and that steady progress had been made in every department. On reference to the accounts it would he seen that the income for the past year from all sources, had been £614 18s. 104 d., and that the expenditure for the same period amounted to .E 560 14s. id. leaving a balance of over £54" in favour of the Society. The medical officer and dispenser still continued to give satisfaction. The Committee felt that that report was the most impor- tant one that had been submitted since the formation of the Association. A step, contemplated ever since the establishment of the society, and which was more fully gone into in the last report—the acquisition and purchase of the Palmyra-square prmerty--had been achieved, and the Committee hoped that such investment would be both profitable to the lodges (particularly those who had made advances), and the Association, and that the same might be the means of further cementing the lodges and members more firmly to the Association than they had hitherto been. The Committee expected to transfer the work of the Institution from Friars-green to their new premises about the middle of March. Due notice would, however, be given of the particular time when such change would take place. The report of the Medical Officer (Dr. Kishey) stated ' that the work had been very heavy during the whole of the year, and up to the present time was still in- icreasing. A great deal of work fell on Mr. Lake, the 'dispenser, who had dischargA his part with every care and attention. With the exception of measles, the num- ber of infectious cases had been very small'. The total number of prescriptions had been 16,975, of visits inihe 4.963, and of deaths 41. The number of surgical cases "was about the same as last year. Of the 41 deaths,2l were of men, 3 of women, and 17 of children. The num- ber of deaths exceeded those of last year by 11, but that was chiefly owing to the fact that several deaths had occurred among those suffering from chronic complaints, such as heart disease, Ric. These reports, together, with the statement of ac- counts, were adopted. ELECTION OF OFFICERS, &C. The following were elected officers :—President, Mr. Joseph Albinson, vice-president, Mr. George Roughley ; auditor, Mr. Thos. Roberts; secretary, Mr. Bibby; and treasurer, Mr. A. Stirrup. The meeting terminated with the passing of a cordial vote of thanks to the retiring president for his valuable services during the past four years. Several delegates, of whom there were a good number present, spoke in favour of the proposition. The compliment was suitably acknowledged by the retiring president.

Considerable excitement was caused about noon on Thursday in Gray's Inn-road, London, by a man jumping from a window some 501 t. high. He was picked up dead. George Child, one of the men who escaped last wetk I from a Glasgow prison van, was apprehended on IThursday morning at Glasgow. The fourth mall ia stilt I at lsrge.

THE MAYOR OF WARRINGTON ON
SUNDAY SCHOOLS.

On Monday evening, the annual congregational tea party in connection with Emmanuel Church, i was held n the schoolroom over Arpley Station. About 230 sat down to tea, after which a concert was given, his worship the Mayor (Alderman Fran- comb) in the chair. The room had been very taste- fully decorated by Mrs. O'Brien, and the most pro- minent motto on the walls was "Welcome to our Mayor." The Mayor, in opening the proceedings, said there was no institution in the country which was doing so much good as the-teaching of children in the Sunday schools. They all knew very well that it was impossible for children to be taught re- ligious subjects in day schools, in which the pay- ments were made on results, and it was impossible to impart Scriptural knowledge there as it should be imparted. That was why their clergymen, and others should endeavour to impress upon children the necessity of a regular attendance at the Sunday school, and urge them not to leave it when they became 14 or 15 years of age, but go on till they were 20; and even after marriage, if possible. (Ap- plause.) The .Mayor referred to _his.experienccof

'Sunday. schools in Blackburn. He had lived fbr some years in a district near Blackburn, and he had never seen such a place for Sunday schools. In one class there were from 60. to 70 nerscns, and quite half of them were married; and it was astonishing to find such a large amount of money collected;. showing that the people thoroughly:appreciated the work, and believed in it. Though theywere princi- pally cotton operatives, they succeeded, after four or five years" work, in building a church for them- selves; and he did not think there was a person who attended the services, who could say that be held a higher position than that of a foreman in a cotton factory and that showed, that where people were banded together good must result. 'Unity was indeed strength. (Applause.) Later in the evening the Rev. 'P. Lake Good delivered a short address. During the evening several glees and chqruses were given by the choir; songs by Miss Ditdhileld and Miss Nixon ;- and Messrs. D. Ikin, Walter Bellian, Charles Davenport, and John Bosomy an oration "American. HUMOUT," by Mr. Clare ; and recitations in the Lancashire dialect by Mr. J. Brierley. Mr. G. Riley was at the piano.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB TOEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB TOE- BATING SOCIETY.

On Tuesdhy evening the,meetings of this Society were resumed. after suspension for the Christmas' and New Year's festivities. The chair was taken by Mr. John Walker, and there was a large attendance. The debate was opened in opposition to Home •Rule by Mr. T. C. London who proceeded to show that there had been a great change of opirlion in the Liberal party upon the question. He argued that there was no need for a Home Rule Bill, seeing that Ireland was getting peaceful when the bill was introduced, and that there, was a. possibility, of settling.the land question upon a reasonable basis. All that was needed was to give Ireland local self- government and not Home Rule. Other nations, such as germany, Russia, and the United States were aiming at consolidation, and he contended that nothing should be done to jeepardise the British empire by treating Ireland as a separate nation. He urged that there was no satisfactory definition as to what was meant by Home Rule, and, quoting from the 'provisions, of the bill introduced in the House of Comarms by Nit. Gladstone, he strongly maintained that such a limited bill would not be acceptable to the Irish people, and that it would speedily be followed by a - demand for legislative independence. The removal a Irish members from Westminster was objectionable, and it was scarcely less objectionable to include them seeing that they would then be having more control over , legislation than others members of Parliament. In his judgment the land question was at the root of all the difficulties they had in Ireland, and 'if all parties would combine to settle the land question upon a just basis, to get rid of Dublin Castle rule and to remedy other grievances, Ireland would have obtained everything she could reasonably demand. They ought not, because they found difficulties in the way yield to the counsels of despair by granting Home DIGGLE supported M. London in his view of.the ques- tion, and he urged that the Irish were better treated with regard to land'tenure than thepeople of this coun- try. They had everything they really needed, and if they would only obey the law like other people there would •be nothing ,to complain. about.—The speakers in support a Home Rule were Councillor T. Flood, Messrs. W. H. Butler, J. Pemberton, and the Chairman. It was shown by them that it was no new thing for Ireland to have a Parliament of her own, and that a Parliament had been of such great advaataee to the country, that when she managed her own affairs she made progress by leaps and hounds. As to the Liberals having changed their opinions, it was desirable that they should do se when till,- found' it needful, and Heine Ride had come upon the party-, ,as other reforms had come, as a matter of evolu- tion in politics. The difficulty those who opposed Home Rule were in, was that they talked about. giving a measure of local self-government • while at the same time they urged that any power that' was granted to the Irish would be used against the English. Government. It was shown that there was a difference between landtenuroin Ireland and in England; inas- much as the peasantry in Ireland had in meet' cases drained the land and built the houses in which • tl*ty lived,and were being evicted from property which • really belongsd to them more than to the landlofd. Having tried 85 coereibn bills it was felt that the time had come, when a new.course should be tiken,and a trial should aoe. given to a policy of conciliation. The proceedingscloaect with a very cordial vote of thanks to Mr. London for his able address, and with a resolution to adjourn the debate until Tuesday night next. The proceedings wilh as heretofore,.beopen to visitors of all shades of opinioet.

At the clbse of this performance, the annual distribution of prizes fstr the best attendances during the year was naoide by Mr. Thorp. MR. GLADSTONE ON AGIIICULTME.

The farmers attending the rent audit dinner in con- nection with the Hawarden estate, which was held on Thursday evening, were favoured with the company of Mr. Gladstone, who on similar occasions during the last six or seven years has been an absentee, The right hon. gentleman, who was very cordially welcomed, responded to the toast of " The,health of Mr. and' Mrs. Gladstone." He warmly acknowledged the friendliness of the expres- sions used with regard to Mrs. Gladstone, who he hoped would be kept among them Inc many years to come, Turning to the relations of landlord and tenant, he saw no reasons why questions affecting them should not continue to be amicably settled. With re- gard to the proposal for the nationalisation of land, if it could he carried out for the good. of the whole commu- nity, the landlord would have no right to object if he got fair compensation for the transfer of his property ; but for his own part he could not see his way to such change, because he had not yet been able to understand in what way the State was to be made a good and ca- pable landlord. He was convinced that the present sys- tem of owner and occupier was a good one. He believed, too, that we we are gradually moving towards an im- proved state of things in agricultural matters, and he looked with pleasure to every change, small or great, which would tend to keep up the demand for agricunu- ral labour, and to check what could only be a great mis- fortune—the decay of the agricultural industry.

The remains of Father Perry, this Jesuit astrowner, who died in French Guinea, whither he had gone tint the purpose of observing the recent eclipse, are being brought to Engle:ad. The body will be conveyed to Stonyburst, and interred in the little cemetery attached to the college.

div.head: COLLAFEB, OF THE IRON BOOM.
div.p: COLLAFEB, OF THE IRON BOOM.

The Scotch iron market has had an elciting forenoon,„ prices having collapsed in a remarkable degree owing to, large selling orders. Scotch fell from 6s. to 635. 1d.,, Cleveland from 635. 9d.. to 625. 3d., and hematite horn, 80s. 4id. to 78s. 10d. The feeling is that values may yet go lower, as the demand is falling off.

div.head: INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.

There appeaWt(Tb-e—n-oTha-i-JailOrT&Tibe influenza epidemic is abating, but, on the contrary, its area, as reported on, seems to be extending. Ther disease has now got into Salford. Sandringham, it is alged,has not been snared, several cases having occurred Were. Prince George of Wales has been one of the sufferers, while Princess Victoria is the latest victim. The Rev. Fred. A. T. Ffervey, M. A., domestic chaplain to the-Prince and Princess of Wales, has been, another of the sufferers. Sir Robert Peel, Sir Donald Currie, and Sir John Puleston, Ml'.., are now convalescent.. Influenza is prevalent in the large factories of Greenwich and Deptford. Yesterday two' deaths from influenza were • reported from West Kent. Mr. Joyce, aged 31, died at New Cross after two days' illness, the doctor certifying the cause to be influenza. A girl, aged 12, has died at Selvedere from the same cause, while a: third death, that of a gardener, is reported from. tford, but is not yet authenticated.
• The Hon. Percy Al!sop, M.P.,.and Earl Cadcgan are confined to the house with iniluenza.
, The epidemic of Russian influenza has attacked the ,-Carabincers stationed at Leeds,,and 20 of the soldiers are in hospital.
THE LONDON SCANDALS.

' Yesterday, Arthur Newton, Fiederick Taylorson, and Adolphus, De Gallo again appeared at Bow-st., to answer thetharge of conspiracy in connection with the Cleve- Nand-street scandals.—Mr. Swinscoe, mother of the boy Swinscoe, was called by the Treasury. She sain•that Perkins and Wright fetched her son one day in December. No one spoke to her till then about his going abroad.— Mrs. Emily Parkins, widow, said her son went away one morning. No one had been to her to obtain her consent to his going abroad.—Mrs Elimbeth Allies said Constable Hands called for her son on the 2.3 rd August last. Her son had' been away ever since. Two other men afterwards called,., but she could not identify either of the defendants. with them.—Earnest Allies, brother of Algernon Allies, itilentified,De Gana and Tayterson as the men who called inqairing kr his brother. —William Allies, coachman, Sudbury, father of Algernon, said after the conviction of Newlove- and Veck, Taylor- son called and said some person wished to do his son some good and try to retrieve his character, and asked if he was agreeable that his son should to away. He said he was. He afterwards had correspondence with Newton, and asked the latter to get him an interview with his son.

div.p: TERRIIILE ACCIDENT INsAMERICA.

. 14 WORKMEN DROWNED. Nmv Yonx, FRIDAY. —A terrible accident "has causal the death of 14 workmen engaged in constricting a bridgeacroas the Ohio river, to connect the towns of Louisville and Jeffersonville. The water thadermined the caisson in which they were working, and rushed in witirsuch force that it was impossible for all to escape. The only exit was a valve door, through which oviy one man could pass at a time, and by this opening four men escaped, the foreman gallantly shouting, All short men gmfirst." The foreman himself and thirteen others were drowned in the caisson, the water overtaking them be- fere they could struggle through, the valve. The sur- vivors described the sthiggles of the doomed men as terrible to witness.

div.head: ALARMING ILLNESS OF THE KING OF SPAIN.
div.p: ALARMING ILLNESS OF THE KING OF SPAIN.

• A telegram from Madrid on Thursday morning states: .--During last night the condition of the young King became very much worse, all the symptoms being greatly aggravated. The fever rose rapidly, and high convul- sions were frequent. The weakness of the little patient was extreme, and the exhaustion so great that at two , o'elock life was thought to be extinct. He rallied slightly later, and life is now only maintained 11,y artificial means. The doctors in attendance despair of saving him, and it feared that the end must come Within a few hours. 'Senor Sagasta was summond to the palace at midnight. and still remains there in attendance. Nothing of the serious condition of the King is given in thisunorning's papers. MADRID, FRIDAY MORNINO---During the night, the little King was again utterly prostrated by a syncopal attack, leading the physicians to believe that he was actually dead. He rallied, hewever, thoughTtow terribly weak. It is believed that he has not sufficient strength to withstand anOther attack. special measures have been taken to prevent any political coup •being success- fully attempted.

THE SHIP CANAL. THELWALL MISSION. On Sunday, special missionary services were held in the Ship Canal Mission, Thelwall. The morning preacher was Mr. W. H. Holt (the now missionary for the Thel- wall section), whilst in the evening the pulpit was occu- pied by Mr. G. Manning. The services were continued on Monday and Tuesday evenings, when addresses were given by Mr. Livesley, of Ellesmere Port, and have been continued each evening during the week.
